News.title: Cross Country cancels trains on ‘almost all routes’ after major power cut in city centre – as thousands face disruption
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAVEL CHAOS Cross Country cancels trains on ‘almost all routes’ after major power cut in city centre – as thousands face disruption

TRAINS across the UK have been cancelled after a major power cut at train operator CrossCountry’s control centre sparked travel chaos.

The power cut started yesterday in Birmingham and is affecting a large number of system used to manage the railway.

Major routes cancelled include services between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton.

Routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh are also affected.





Cross Country explained that only services going to Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport will run a “near-normal” service.

Significant reductions to services and cancellations are expected across almost all routes.

Travellers are being warned to plan ahead with their journeys.

Those planning to go by train may wish to take an alternative route and be aware of longer travel times.

A CrossCountry spokesperson said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located.

“As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.

“Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday 23 August.

“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all CrossCountry routes throughout the day.



“We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.”

News.title: Teen joyrider who died in A66 crash that killed seven including two cops posted TikTok clips of high-speed police chases
News.content:
A TEENAGER who was one of seven killed in a head-on collision with a police car during a pursuit uploaded videos of previous high-speed chases.

Two police officers died in the crash in the early hours of yesterday morning after they hit a Volkswagen Passat which was driving the wrong way on the A66.



PC Matthew Blades, 38, and PC Tom Clough, 37, and the five occupants of the Passat were all declared dead at the scene near Middlesbrough.

One of the youngsters killed in the crash, Makai Saddington, previously posted several videos to TikTok which appear to show him in a high-speed police chase.



In one video, from months before his death teens can be seen driving through a housing estate at speed while a police car with blue flashing lights follows.

The Audi then peels off onto a grassy playing field in an attempt to lose the chase.





Another clip features a green Nissan being driven around before it is torched.

Images posted to the account show Saddington and a friend in black balaclavas posing in a car.

This comes just days after five teenagers were killed after driving their car the wrong way down the motorway and ploughing into a family who were on their way to the airport.

Sisters Niamh and Alma Kinsella, both in their 30s, Ella Hendricken, in her 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son Yemi remain in hospital in a critical condition after they were hit on the M9 in Ireland.



The victims of yesterday’s crash have been named locally as Michael Ray, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy but their identities have not been confirmed by police.

Saddington’s aunt has paid tribute to him after it was revealed he was one of the five youths from a cluster of deprived estates in east Middlesbrough killed in the A66 smash.

The 18-year-old was born and raised in Pallister Park, Middlesbrough, brought up by his mother Alisha Morgan.

Saddington’s aunt Sharon Morgan wrote on social media: “Today is a day I never thought I would have to face.



“I’m heartbroken to say that we lost my beloved nephew today, our Makai. There are no words that can truly express the pain of losing someone so young, so loved, and so full of life.

“You brought so much love and happiness into our family, and your memory will stay with us forever. This loss has left a space in our hearts that can never be filled.

“Rest peacefully, my beautiful nephew. You will never be forgotten. Until we meet again, fly high love ya aunty Sharon…

“Keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we try to get through this heartbreaking time, especially our Alisha, his Mam.”



Locals plan to release balloons in his memory at a park near his home next week.

A mile from the scene of the crash residents of Lime Road were woken at 3.36am by the sound of screeching tyres as the motor took a corner into their narrow street.

Ellie Westerman, 24, said: “The car must have been travelling at between 80 and 100 mph down our narrow street.

“The noise woke me and I shot out of bed, you could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going.



“It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area and it’s tragic people have ended up dying.”

Another resident said: “The screech of tyres woke me up, the car being followed must have taken the corner into our road at a tremendous speed.”

Local resident Neil Hutchinson, 47, said: “The police cars were tearing down the street at half past three with lights flashing and their sirens going.

“You could tell from the noise that they were travelling at high speed.”

The IOPC said it is believed officers spotted a suspicious vehicle and began a pursuit before the car travelled onto the A66 and collided with a police vehicle.



Cleveland Police said the police car was travelling in the correct direction and contained the two serving officers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear of the deaths of two police officers and five members of the public after the horror crash.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He posted on X: “Devastated to hear that two police officers have lost their lives while on duty in Cleveland this morning, as well as five members of the public.“My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland Police.

“Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”

News.title: Dark side of Below Deck life with girls jumping ship to flee sex parties & hostesses facing grim demands from super-rich
News.content:
AMBLING along the immaculate pathways of Puerto Portals’ polished marina village, I was flanked by rows of gleaming superyachts, each one looming from the water like a floating monument to excess.

Their lacquered hulls shimmered beneath the Majorcan sun – vast, extravagant and seemingly designed to seduce anyone who wandered close enough.





Around me, crew members toiled in the afternoon heat, buffing away the faintest blemish from immaculate decks, and stewardesses stood ramrod straight in flawless uniforms, poised like ceremonial guards awaiting their next command.

Soon they would sail beyond the harbour and into the vast, lawless expanse of the open sea, where the glittering facade of luxury can become considerably murkier.

Because beneath this sun-drenched display of wealth in the Brit holiday hotspot lurks a darker world where those employed inside these floating kingdoms are at the mercy of those who pay them – and risk being subjected to sexual abuse and vile demands.

Captain Ruben Heller, who jumps down from the top deck of the yacht he is prepping to talk, told me he has witnessed things aboard yachts that he described as unimaginable, admitting that crew members often learn to “turn a blind eye” at the ingrained culture of prostitution and sexism.

The South African captain warned that, far too often, wealthy yacht owners make increasingly revolting demands of stewardesses who arrive aboard chasing a dream career.

He recalled how a friend working as a stewardess on a superyacht was subjected to one particularly disturbing request – she claims from a rich Saudi.

Ruben said: “He wanted her to pick up his poo from the bed.”

The woman reported the incident to the captain, but was allegedly told: “It must’ve been an accident, just sort it out.”





But according to Heller, the bizarre ordeal did not end there – with the same request allegedly happening repeatedly.

Eventually, the captain confronted the Saudi, who then asked to speak directly with the stewardess.

She allegedly told him: “This is disgusting. I can’t do this. This is not normal.”

And he replied: “What do you mean? How much will it take for you to do that for me?” Captain Heller recalled.

The captain claimed the man then doubled her £5,000 salary to £10,000.

“She couldn’t say no, so she continued to do it,” he said.

Captain Ruben added that he had also encountered numerous owners who summoned prostitutes whenever the opportunity arose – with some even sending their own families away so they could indulge in secret liaisons.

He said: “One boat that I worked on, the owner had his wife and kids on board, they left on a business trip, but there was definitely something else under that, and a load of girls came on. I took them around for a couple of days.



“It was interesting to see the contrast between being with the family and then switching to being with a mistress.

“Some of the women were prostitutes. You see on the cameras things happening on the exterior. There’s a lot of alcohol, sex and drugs involved, but we don’t ask any questions, there’s some things we don’t want to know about.”

Ruben told me a story involving a man whose wife and kids had taken a day off the vessel and he had decided to invite some prostitutes on board.

He said: “The wife came back early and suddenly the girls were forced to climb down the anchor and into the ocean so they didn’t come face-to-face with his wife.”

One British stewardess, who has decided to remain anonymous for protection reasons, said she knew there would “one day be a documentary about all of this”.

The series Below Deck was the first to shine a light on the darker side of the yacht industry – with crew members speaking out candidly about their roles and relationships.

But the anonymous stewardess said: “It’s quite a hidden industry. People think they know about it, but they don’t.

“If you work on a private boat, everything is kept a secret.”



The so-called “yachtie”, who has worked in the industry for just a year, warned that while billionaire owners may be involved in dangerous or disturbing behaviour, she believes another part of the industry deserves far greater scrutiny – the captains.

“Captains who have been at sea for however many years are stuck in their old ways,” she said.

She claimed she had heard of cases in which captains invited young stewardesses aboard for interviews before allegedly sexually assaulting them.

“When you’re at sea, law sometimes doesn’t exist,” she added.

The stewardess also described an industry that has become increasingly saturated, with scores of young people desperate to secure a coveted position aboard a luxury yacht – sometimes at any cost.

She told me: “These young girls and young people will go into the industry and grab whatever they can get. And it can be very dodgy.

“It’s common that the captains will slip a hand up a skirt sometimes, it’s normalised.

“When you have floods of people coming into the industry, it means a lot of mistreatment can go unnoticed.

“Because it’s such a desirable job, they put up with certain things. Stewardesses are likely to deal with abuse because they feel they have to tolerate it to keep their place in an industry many dream of breaking into.”

Kirsty Molloy* thought she had found the perfect ticket to life at sea when she snapped up a job with with Craig Taylor* – a supposed “38-year-old” surfer and skipper sailing around Fiji with an international crew.



Kirsty arrived at the boat buzzing with anticipation, only to discover that the man waiting for her looked considerably older than the slick photograph used on his profile.

Days into the voyage, Taylor allegedly became drunk and unleashed a torrent of abuse at Kirsty in front of fellow crew members.

She said he screamed at her and also threatened to dump her on the nearest island – whether it was inhabited or not.

Taylor, who was actually in his mid-40s, was later arrested by Fijian authorities and charged with one count of causing actual bodily harm to another female crew member Kirsty had worked alongside.

According to The Guardian, Molloy later found out Taylor was a convicted sex offender who was jailed for 18 months after breaking into a woman’s home and sexually assaulting her.

For all its glittering decks and champagne sunsets, the superyacht world has a darker underbelly – and those who work aboard these floating palaces can find paradise comes at a price.

*Some of the names in this article have been changed.

News.title: Chopper crash that killed Brit newlyweds in Greece may have been caused by ‘damaged rotor blade from earlier incident’
News.content:
A DAMAGED rotor blade could have caused the chopper crash that killed Brit newlyweds honeymooning in Greece last week.

Alexander Cromie, 31, and Marie Ebert, 30, died alongside a Greek pilot in a horror helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday.



Witnesses saw the Bell 206 spinning out of control, suggesting a tail rotor failure, before it plummeted to the ground.

Horrifying footage showed the aircraft hurtling towards the ground and exploding in a fireball.



Investigators are reportedly considering if the deadly crash is linked to an incident involving the same chopper just 11 weeks earlier.

Straps had been put in place after the helicopter landed on Paros on June 1 to stop tail blades moving in high winds.

But, according to a report filed with Greece’s Civil Aviation Authority, the pilot did not ensure the straps were removed before starting the engine to fly passengers back from the island.

Records suggest the chopper stayed in Paros for three days after the incident with the straps.

It was then given an air-worthiness certificate just over a month later, on July 2.

As a precaution, Greece‘s civil aviation authority has ruled that “visual and functional checks” on tail rotors must be carried out before every flight in the country involving a Bell 206 helicopter.



A serious fire destroyed most of the chopper, complicating efforts to investigate the crash.

The small private aircraft crashed while attempting to land on a helipad in Sifnos at around 6.15pm local time.

Both Brits and the pilot were confirmed dead at the scene as fire crews rushed to extinguish the inferno.



Alex was a vice president in private wealth solutions for US-based investment management company Blackstone.

A spokesperson for the company said: “We are shocked by the tragic passing of three people including our colleague Alex Cromie and his wife Marie Ebert, who were celebrating their honeymoon.

“Alex was beloved by everyone who knew and worked with him at Blackstone, and our thoughts and prayers are with his loved ones.”

Bristol-born Alex graduated in economics at Sheffield University before launching his career at banks including NatWest and BNP Paribas.

Marie landed her role as senior specialist in market reputation at top London firm Bain & Co last July after forging a career in asset management, private equity, and consulting.



They paid tribute to the Brit, saying: “We are shocked to read reports of a tragic accident in Greece regarding one of our colleagues and her husband.

“Our thoughts and support are with the families involved at this very difficult time.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Deputy Mayor of Sifnos, Manolis Fountoulakis told ERTnews: “According to the testimonies of the residents of the area, they heard the noise of the helicopter, it was a strange noise.

“It probably had a mechanical failure in the air. This is because the propeller was doing something strange… it was making a very loud noise.”

News.title: Tragedy as tourist, 68, dies after car gets stuck in mud on remote road in Death Valley during 46C temperatures
News.content:
STRANDED IN DESERT Tragedy as tourist, 68, dies after car gets stuck in mud on remote road in Death Valley during 46C temperatures

A TOURIST has tragically died after his car got stuck in mud on a remote road in Death Valley.

Pierre Michel Formosa, 68, and his travel companion were left stranded in the California desert when their vehicle became stuck.



The pair from France were were left with no choice but to to walk across the salt flats to seek help, the National Park Service said.

With temperatures breaching 46C on August 17, after a short time Formosa was unable to continue and so his companion went on alone.



Sadly by the time the victim’s friend secured assistance at a national park visitor centre and a search was launched, Formosa had died.

He was pronounced dead at the scene.



Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said: “Our deepest condolences are with the family and friends of the visitor who died.

“This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous.

“Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances, and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience.

“We’re grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones.”



The Inyo County coroner will determine the cause and manner of death.

Prior to the tragic discovery, his companion flagged down a passing motorist for help after which he helped report the emergency at the Furnace Creek Visitor Centre shortly after 2 p.m.

A rescue operation launched immediately, deploying helicopters and multiple ground units.

Death Valley is a desert in eastern California.

The World Meteorological Organisation lists it as the place with the hottest ground temperature ever recorded on Earth.



It is located in the Mojave Desert in California, got its name from pioneers who got lost in the area.

After their near-death experience in the 1800’s, one of the men in the group nicknamed the area Death Valley.

One proclaimed “goodbye, Death Valley,” and a name was formed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 2020, a travel writer, named Claire Nelson, broke her pelvis while hiking alone in Joshua Tree, an area four hours south of Death Valley.

She survived for days with little food and water and was forced to drink her own urine.

News.title: Mum of Brit, 23, shot dead at dad’s Texas home will fly to US in fight to reopen case after being ‘let down’ by UK cops
News.content:
'NOT BEING HEARD' Mum of Brit, 23, shot dead at dad’s Texas home will fly to US in fight to reopen case after being ‘let down’ by UK cops

THE MUM of a 23-year-old Brit shot and killed by her father is set to fly to the US in a bid to reopen the tragic case.

Lucy Harrison’s mum, Jane Coates, is hoping to campaign for a fresh investigation more than a year on from her daughter’s tragic death.



In January of 2025, Lucy was shot in the heart by her dad Kris at his home in Texas.

Kris, 52, claims the horror occurred accidentally while he was “showing off” his firearm to his daughter, who had been visiting him in on holiday.



Lucy tragically died on January 10 last year – the same day she and her boyfriend were due to fly back home to Warrington, Cheshire.

US cops dropped their probe without charging Kris, but a British coroner later ruled his actions “reckless” and delivered an unlawful killing verdict.

And Jane has since accused the American authorities of “ignoring” evidence that she claims contradicts Kris’ version of events.

Now, 19 months on, Jane is heading back in the hopes of speaking to a district attorney and fighting for a fresh investigation.



Speaking to the Daily Mail, the mum said: “I think it’s not being heard – just raising all of our concerns and nothing being acted upon, and feeling like we’ve just been deserted by the British authorities.

“Receiving the unlawful killing outcome was a day full of complete mixed emotions, but one where finally Lucy’s truth and voice has been heard in some capacity.

“But from then it still hasn’t moved things forward in terms of my request for a reopening of the investigation in Texas.”

Joined by Radd Seiger, previous advisor to Harry Dunn’s family, the pair will travel to Texas and ask officials to accept the coroner’s outcome.

Cheshire Coroner Jacqueline Devonish concluded in February that the shooting was “reckless”.



Kris, a British citizen, chose not to attend the inquest in the UK as he said it would be too emotionally difficult.

Lucy’s boyfriend Sam Littler gave The Sun a harrowing account of being at the police station after the shooting: “I was 23 years old, alone in Texas, and had just found out that my girlfriend had died”.

He added: “From my understanding, it felt as though the situation was already being viewed as a ‘terrible accident’ before I was questioned as a witness.”

Kris and Lucy were alone at the time of her death and the 52-year-old said he had been showing a firearm to his daughter.

Sam has now questioned whether the Grand Jury in Texas was given the full evidence before it decided not to press charges.



Jane has campaigned loudly for justice for Lucy, calling on ministers for public support in the case.

The family have requested various meetings with senior officials including Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokeswoman said: “Our thoughts remain with Jane and her family for the tragic loss they have suffered.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We were in contact with the family and provided consular support.

“We will always look to learn lessons to improve the consular support we offer to other families in the future.”

News.title: Bloodthirsty cartels battle for new billion-dollar empire as snipers shield gold-rich valleys & guards are gunned down
News.content:
DANGER ZONE Bloodthirsty cartels battle for new billion-dollar empire as snipers shield gold-rich valleys & guards are gunned down

COCAINE cartels with gold rush fever are violently muscling into the Amazon basin’s legal mines to get their cut of a multi-billion dollar trade.

Heavily-armed gangs patrol barbed wire fences protecting mines deep within the rainforest, where they run a ruthless racket to extract their most prized asset.



Organised crime groups are extorting miners, politicians and seizing control of the gold supply chain that is so valuable to Latin American countries.

Despite being in the middle of a cocaine boom, experts say the gold trade has become the most lucrative revenue stream in the cartel’s arsenal.



Gangs operating from the heart of the Amazon basin in Peru, Ecuador and Colombia, to infamous Mexican cartels, are all getting a piece of the action.

Jennifer Scotland, a research analyst for RUSI, the world’s oldest security think tank, told The Sun: “Gold has surpassed cocaine revenue in Colombia and Peru. It’s become an attractive source of revenue for crime groups.”



Gold mining has long been exploited by cartels as a means of money laundering from drug trafficking.

These groups can finance mining communities and invest in equipment with dirty cash to extract and sell gold in legitimate markets.

But gold mining alone has become a more stable source of revenue than the pervasively violent drug trade.

Scotland said: “It’s become an increasingly important revenue stream.



“Compared to cocaine, these are relatively low-risk, high-reward crimes that have been historically less prioritised by policymakers and law enforcement.”

Cocaine prices in Europe have taken a steep fall over the last decade, dropping from £38,300 to £11,800 per kilo between 2014 and 2025, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

Gold’s value has gone in the opposite direction, nearly quadrupling from £31,000 to £103,680 per kilo from August 2016 to time of writing.



Guards at legal mines have been forced to carry military-grade weapons to protect mine-shafts amid the gold boom.

Luis, the head of security at a mine deep in the Ecuadorian forest, was ambushed and shot five times after refusing to pay bribes or work for the gangs.

He told The Times a few weeks earlier: “In these mountains, it’s the criminal groups, not the state, that’s in charge.”

Last May, 13 security contractors were kidnapped and killed in Pataz, northern Peru.

The government immediately sent in the army to control the region and enforce a 30-day mining pause.



On top of violently seizing existing gold mines, criminal actors have also created their own illegal extraction sites.

Last June, imprisoned Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Joaquin “el Chapo” Guzman, seized control of La Cienega, a lucrative 14,000-acre gold mining region of Mexico‘s Sonoran desert.

The cartel’s Los Chapitos faction operated heavy machinery around the clock and drained the area of millions in gold before a major military and police sting targeted the operation.



In Ecuador, the dominant Los Lobos cartel controls the processing hubs of major mining districts, giving them near-complete command over the supply chain.

Scotland said: “We have seen criminal groups forcibly inserting themselves into mining communities, forcing them to pay taxes and using violence against local miners or politicians who refuse to cooperate.”

Cartels are also increasing their power bases and often usurping local governments by driving a wedge between them and the people.

Scotland said some communities had historically been “stigmatised” and prevented from accessing natural resources – which criminals exploit to gain favour.

She said: “In those cases, criminal groups have kind of provided informal mining communities with equipment and finance needed to mine in protected areas.



“This has resulted in clashes with mining companies.”

Gangs have been able to take over these mines by presenting themselves as an alternative source of money, equipment and protection to the locals.

Their growing influence is part of a wider battle for control between organised crime and the state across parts of South America.



Colombian Defence Minister Pedro Arnulfo Sanchez begged the US government to sanction illegal mining after gold bought by US mint was traced back to criminal groups.

“The harsh reality is that criminal mining is defeating the Colombian state,” Sanchez told The New York Times.

Across the major South American crime hubs, gangs are increasingly challenging state authority.

But Scotland said the problem is not as simple as criminal groups replacing governments.

“I think it’s important to note that the state doesn’t necessarily go away,” she said.



“It’s not a question of state institutions being captured by organised crime.”

Instead, gangs have exploited corruption by receiving mining licenses under the table and paying officials to turn a blind eye to illicit extraction.

The sheer size and remoteness of mines also makes policing difficult.



Scotland said: “These areas tend to be vast rural areas and it’s hard for law enforcement to monitor them.

“And, for example, when one illegal mine is destroyed, they’ll often be another one cropping up the next day somewhere else.”

The criminalisation of the trade also means governments lose millions in crucial tax revenue.

Scotland said: “Countries aren’t reaping the benefits from tax revenue because it’s the criminal groups that are taxing these activities instead of the state.”

The gold rush has also come at a human cost for poor communities.



Scotland said: “You see forced labour, forced displacement of communities, sexual exploitation and human trafficking.”

Criminal operations are not bound by the same legal requirements as legitimate mining companies.

One of the biggest threats comes from mercury, which is widely used to separate gold from ore.



Scotland said: “You see widespread use of mercury to separate the gold, which pollutes local water sources, damages crops, and causes health problems.”

She warned that organised crime groups are now looking to extract and traffic critical minerals used by defence and technology industries.

Cassiterite, a mineral that was once treated largely as a waste product from gold extraction, has become an export product in its own right.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Criminals are also targeting copper production in Peru, fuelled by high prices amid a growing demand for green energy.

Scotland said: “This is definitely a risk going forward as demand for critical minerals starts to increase and they increase in value.”

News.title: ‘Smoking gun’ evidence of Putin’s bid to hit German airport with ‘Semtex-packed drone’ as plot ‘linked to blitz on UK’
News.content:
EVIDENCE of Vladimir Putin’s plot to hit a German airport with a Semtex-packed drone has reportedly been linked to a series of parcel bombs that targeted the UK.

Mad Vlad’s suspected attempt to blast a plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport with an explosive-laden drone failed.



A canny airport bus driver found the drone on August 4 after it smashed into the wing of a parked Ukrainian cargo plane.

It had failed to detonate, but held important clues about who was behind the plot.



The hero airport worker found the drone by a huge Antonov An-124 that was set to fly military supplies to Ukraine.

He reportedly managed to get close enough so he could bravely kick the drone as it hovered, before pinning it under his foot and alerting airport security.

Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said a “ripped” detonator on the explosive package was the only thing that prevented the device from going off as it hit the tarmac.

Investigators have analysed the drone and found traces of DNA that match at least one person suspected of being involved in a Kremlin-backed plot to send parcel bombs in the UK, according to the Mail on Sunday.



One parcel burst into flames as it was set to be loaded on a DHL flight to the UK in July 2024 at Leipzig airport.

A second caught fire just two days later in the UK. It had already reached a DHL depot near Birmingham.

In Poland, two similar parcels were discovered.



All were posted from Vilnius, Lithuania, and were thought to be part of a “practice plot” ahead of a suspected plan to sabotage flights to the US.

Investigators identified 22 suspects in Poland and Lithuania who are thought to be working for Russia‘s GRU spy service.

The same network is now thought to be behind the latest Leipzig drone attack.

German security services expert Professor Peter Neumann told the Mail: “They found DNA on the Leipzig drone and… the person that matches that DNA is a person who is suspected in Lithuania of involvement in the parcel bomb plot of 2024.”

Five men are on trial in Lithuania suspected of involvement in the 2024 parcel bomb plot.



Professor Neumann called the DNA the “smoking gun” that shows “the parcel bomb attack was basically led by the Russian GRU”.

German MP Roderich Kieswetter added: “The pattern of behaviour matches with the Russian conduct of such operations.”

Lithuania’s prosecutor’s office confirmed “the drone incident at Leipzig Airport is linked to Lithuania”.

The astonishing failed Leipzig bomb is thought to have been engineered with roughly 600grams of Semtex squeezed into a sweetcorn can.

Investigators reportedly found a stash of similar can bombs smuggled into Poland by Russian spies.



The bomb was controlled by a phone sim card and antenna, with plotters hiding a phone signal booster in a nearby tree, investigators believe.

This would have helped saboteurs control the bomb from a distance.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And investigators think a second drone hovered above Leipzig-Halle airport to send live images to the plotters.

This drone collided with a cargo plane from Marseille, which was forced into an emergency landing in Hanover and left with minor damage.

News.title: 'I had my first swimming lesson in 20 years - everyone like me should do the same'
News.content:
'I had my first swimming lesson in 20 years - everyone like me should do the same'

The importance of swimming has been highlighted this year as the Royal Life Saving Society warns that extreme weather is a major influence in the number of drownings

I took my first swimming lesson in 20 years

One in three adults can't swim the full length of a 25-metre swimming pool, and I'm among them - despite having received lessons up until age 11 at my inner-city school.

‌



That's why this week I decided that, as part of our Save Lives for Sam campaign, I would take my first swimming lesson in 20 years. I've had zero confidence in my swimming ability for a long time, and that lack of confidence has seen me dangerously panic and flounder when attempting to swim during summer holidays. So I was keen but scared to venture back into the water of even a controlled environment like a pool.

‌



But I was able to rediscover some of my lost skills thanks to the incredible tutoring of an experienced teacher at Highbury Leisure Centre in Islington, North London. As thousands of Brits like me head out to the seaside this summer, I can only recommend that they do the same - especially if they've never learned how to swim before.

‌



Boy swept out to sea survives after using swimming skill he'd learnt only days before READ MORE :

View 6 Images I had happy memories of childhood swimming, but no confidence about entering the water as an adult (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

I have happy memories of learning to swim as a child, and got some high praise from my family and teachers for being relatively good at it.

I was even lucky enough to get one or two of those coveted Frosties badges while Kelloggs were sponsoring the Amateur Swimming Association (ASA) back in the 1990s and early 2000s.

‌



But I've spent all of my 31 years in London, meaning that like most inner-city Brits, I tend not to encounter many opportunities for a swim.

Swimming as a skill has become more vital than ever, especially during years as hot as this one, when people try to beat the heat on the coast, whether here in the UK or abroad. According to the Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS), our partners on our Save Lives for Sam campaign, most drowning deaths occur during extreme heat.

View 6 Images My teacher Martine gave me the best possible swimming refresher (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

‌



Dozens of people have died this summer alone, with 52 deaths of both adults and children since May 24 and August 9. Among them are six-year-old Saja El-Khawasm, who died days after her parents Hassan, 55, and Zeina, 37, and sister Sara, 14, perished after getting into difficulty in the sea in Shoreham, West Sussex on Tuesday.

The charity has found that three times more people drown accidentally in the UK during extreme heat compared to typical summer conditions. I've gone running to the sea myself in recent years, and discovered while there that I was woefully unprepared to enter the water.

So this month (ahead of another summer holiday) the RLSS put me in touch with their partners at Greenwich Leisure Limited, to organise some lessons with a teacher, Martine.

‌



View 6 Images Martine helped me through the basics, from breathing to the different styles of swimming (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

Martine teaches across age and ability, ranging from the very young to older people who want to brush up on their skills later in life, when swimming can serve as an essential health boost.

Before we got into the pool, she outlined to me just how important it is for people know how to swim. She told me: "Swimming is a life skill, it's a survival skill. It's something that, if you learn as a child, you're lucky. It's something that never really leaves you."

‌



Those who haven't learned as a child - including a large number of children from the UK's most deprived areas, who the RLSS' Child Drownings report found drown at twice the rate of the least deprived - face danger as adults.

Martine added: "If you consider those children who haven't had any experience at all, as they go into adulthood, there's nothing there. So any time spent near the water is potentially dangerous, because if they fall in, they won't know how to save themselves, or how even to call for help, how to alert. All of those things are really important."

View 6 Images My swimming journey restarted decades after my last lesson (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

‌



She was incredibly encouraging from the moment I entered the pool, allowing me to get acquainted with the chilly chlorinated waters and teaching me the appropriate way to breathe.

Unlike most forms of exercise, including going for a jog, swimming requires measured and practiced breathing. I learned nearly straight away when I attempted my first front crawl in decades how important it is - if you don't breathe properly water can flow into your nose and mouth.

Water flooding into your orificies creates a unique panic, one that made me abandon mid-length and stand up in the shallow end.

‌



View 6 Images Learning to breathe and float are big parts of swimming (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

In any other situation, like in a river, lake or swimming in the sea, a move like that could have been dangerous. But Martine calmly helped me through the moment, and out the other side I came, ready to go for a second punt at the front crawl and back stroke - which she had taught me earlier in easy-to-follow stages.

When I was able to get to the middle of the pool, we moved onwards to the deep end. There I learned my most important lesson; that I can still manage a serviceable breaststroke.

‌



I realised after Martine gave me a short demonstration that I remembered many of the important motions. So clearly, there was some tutoring tucked in the back of my mind that the lessons had helped resurrect, and Martine explained to me that many people will find the same happens to them when they try swimming.

View 6 Images With some help, I started relearning the breast stroke and front crawl (Image: TIM ANDERSON)

But they also hammered home how vital it is that people have a solid understanding of the most important basics first.

Article continues below

I was eventually able to swim an entire length of the pool, a milestone I didn't think I'd be able to achieve. I've been figuratively and literally buoyed by the experience. The only negative was that there was no Kelloggs badge my mum could sew on to my shorts this time though.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Josh Tarling makes heartbreaking Vuelta admission a week after brother's cycling death
News.content:
Josh Tarling makes heartbreaking Vuelta admission a week after brother's cycling death

Josh Tarling was in action at La Vuelta a Espana just days after his brother and fellow professional cyclist Fin Tarling died in a collision during the Volta a Portugal

View 2 Images Josh Tarling put in an outstanding performance at La Vuelta just days after his brother died (Image: Eurosport)

Josh Tarling confessed his remarkable Vuelta a España opening stage performance held little significance for him in the wake of losing his brother and fellow professional cyclist Fin Tarling. The display came mere days after Fin's heartbreaking death during the Volta a Portugal last week.

‌



Fin, 19, was killed in a high-speed crash with a van during the eighth stage of the race last Friday. The vehicle had made its way onto the course ahead of the incident, under the impression the cyclists had already passed.

‌



Josh chose to race in the Vuelta despite the heartbreaking news, to occupy his mind while grieving. The 22-year-old Netcompany Ineos rider took his place on the start line for the three-week Grand Tour and delivered a stunning opening day showing.

‌



Cycling star Kim Le Court soars to stunning stage three victory at Lloyds Tour of Britain READ MORE :

Sprint superstar Lorena Wiebes sparkles in Blackpool to grab second Lloyds Tour of Britain stage victory READ MORE :

The rider battled his way into the lead with a superb effort before being forced to watch as Ethan Hayter and then Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar edged past him by the finest of margins. The Welshman came up just four seconds shy of Pogacar's victorious time.

However, following last week's heartbreaking news, the outcome held little meaning for Josh, who was embraced by Pogacar on the podium at the conclusion of the first stage.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



When questioned about what the ride meant to him, he told Eurosport: "Not a lot. No, I'm happy with it. And I'm happy I could try and get my head busy with other stuff.

"So yeah, obviously I'm happy and I'm thankful for the team and everything, to let me come and let me give it a good crack."

Legendary Welsh cyclist and Netcompany Ineos' racing director Geraint Thomas said he couldn't be prouder of him. Thomas described Tarling's grief as 'unimaginable', and said that the team would do their utmost to provide a sense of normality to help him through the coming three weeks.

‌



"For a start, it's just great to have him here," Thomas told TNT Sport. "You know, he was really keen to ride, he just wanted to get back to the day job, so to speak, and find comfort in the process and being around the team and everything being as normal as possible. So we fully backed him with that and it's great to have him here.

View 2 Images Joshua Tarling finished third on stage one of La Vuelta (Image: Laurent Coust / Europa Press via Getty Images)

"Obviously, it's been unimaginable what he's gone through the last week or so. But to put in a performance like that at the end of the week he's had is just fantastic, really, it just shows the class of him as an athlete and as a person. Couldn't be prouder.

‌



"I think the course suited him. Technically, he's one of the best and I think yesterday was probably the first time he's ridden a bike properly in a while, so to still put that in? It's insane, really.

"We'll just continue to be normal around him and support him as best we can. It's the start of hopefully a great trip for these eight boys on the bus."

‌



Josh's participation in Ineos' squad had the full backing of his family. "On Saturday Joshua will be riding the Vuelta," his mother Dawn posted on Instagram.

"He has chosen to do so in honour of his brother Fin, with the full support of his family, surrounded by a team who have been incredibly supportive of whatever decision he made.

"I could not have wished for two boys who were closer growing up and into adulthood we have watched with pride as Joshua has been the most loving and supportive big brother to Fin. Following this devastating news he has been an incredible strength for us all.
