"Finlay was so incredibly proud of his big brother, and would be watching nose to the tv and shouting as he competed. So it is right that Josh honours that love and pride by doing what Fin always loved watching him do."

News.title: Disgraced Royal Marine's 'magic in action' using horses to heal shattered forces veterans
News.content:
‘Magic in action’ is how a disgraced ex-Royal Marine describes his work with horses to help shattered army veterans feel whole again. “Taught manners” by a bolshy Shetland pony as a child, Jock Hutchinson turned to horses for salvation after a number of knocks left his life in ruins.

Now, on a remote Scottish farm, the 63-year-old Stetson-wearing equestrian and his wife, Emma, run HorseBack UK, a charity using horsemanship to support military veterans with PTSD and life-changing injuries. They also work with disengaged youth and community groups. He says: “When I was at my lowest ebb, salvation came in four legged form. I was kicked out of the Marines for smoking drugs, then suffered a breakdown and lost everything. But I found hope, purpose - and indeed my future - in the horses I’d loved as a child.”

Growing up in Dunfermline, Scotland, he says: “My father was a carter, a horse and cart man, and my mother was from farming stock. Horses were my first friends, I’ve always loved them. I rode at two or three years old.” Childhood was turbulent for Jock, who got his first pony, a Shetland called Star, aged 10.

Gillian Anderson as 007 tipped by Royal Albert Hall Bond Prom conductor READ MORE :

Mark Gatiss reveals physical toll of playing post-war detective in hit series Bookish READ MORE :

View 7 Images Jock Hutchinson with one of his horses on his Scottish farm (Image: Supplied)

‌



He says: “I would ride it when I needed to leave the house. My mother had bipolar depression, which is a horrible illness, and had an impact on the whole family.” But Star was a forceful character. He says: “I was taught manners by a Shetland pony.”

His dad bought his next horse in the pub, when Jock was 13. He says: “I couldn't catch him at first - he was wild. I'd run around the field going, ‘Billy, you b******, come here.’ Thus he was christened Billy the B******.

“I had to work it out all by myself and spent a huge amount of time lying on grass looking up at the stars going, ‘God damn, that hurts.’ He was not an easy fellow. But we became great friends.” And Jock has broken bones to show for his early ‘trial and error’ approach to taming horses.

View 7 Images Jock Hutchinson , left, in the Royal Marines

‌



He says: “All my ribs are plated on the left side. I've got two vertebrae plated. My pelvis is plated. I'm not leaving my body to science, I'm leaving it to Meccano.” At 22, Jock joined the Royal Marines, which he loved, saying: “It gave me an identity and a purpose in life that I hadn’t had before. It made me proud of myself and proud of being in a team.”

After a year as a troop commander, he worked training recruits before becoming a helicopter pilot, for which a childhood spent with horses came in handy. He says: “A helicopter really responds to what you do. And if you over control it, you'll fall out of the sky. You've got to manage the tension, especially when things are getting a bit hairy. That's exactly the same as a horse.”

Going on to fly operationally for the Army, Navy and Marines, Jock’s career ended abruptly. He explains: “I got kicked out for smoking marijuana when I was 30.

View 7 Images Princess Anne with Jock Hutchinson when she visited HorseBack UK

‌



“Telling my father was the hardest thing I’ve done, but he was so supportive.” Now branded a drug user, he continues: “It was extremely painful because I lost my job, my identity, my pride, my confidence, everything in one go.”

At first, he sold Christmas trees, before starting his own security business. But when he was 45, he suffered a stress-related breakdown. He says: “I completely spiralled. I was sleeping under my desk, out of my mind with stress. “Everything got too much, and I had a breakdown. I folded the business and went from having everything, to almost nothing. “But the worst thing that ever happened to me led to the very best.”

Deeply depressed, Jock turned to a tried and tested tonic, buying himself a horse. He says: “I’d ride and ride, and piece by piece, I put myself back together.”

View 7 Images Jock Hutchinson with one of his horses (Image: Supplied)

‌



Living with wife Emma, 38,a former police officer, in Aboyne, Aberdeenshire, in the Scottish Highlands, they started a business breeding horses. Then a dilapidated farm caught their eye.

Jock says: “It was a wreck. Then, a visit from some military friends recently back from Afghanistan gave me an idea. Could other injured military personnel benefit from being at the farm among the horses? On a bit of a whim, we rented this place, even though it was a pile of rubble.”

Jock, whose three daughters with Emma were born on the farm, continues: “Word of my plan spread, and I was introduced to 15 young ex-service men who were recovering from life-changing injuries nearby. We invited them up to the farm for a day out. Something clicked. It was magic in action.”

View 7 Images Jock Hutchinson has written a book, Free Rein, about his experiences

‌



Soon Jock realised the healing powers of his ‘Scottish ranch.’ He explains: “These guys were getting the best medical care and they were extracted from the battlefield in seconds. “They got the prosthetics, they got compensation, but they had no future. Their mental health was shot, they had PTSD. They had no community to go to and I knew I had the chance to change that.”

When Jock’s father died in 2009, he left them the money to start the charity. He says: “We couldn't afford contractors, so we just did it all ourselves. Before long, we had somewhere that veterans could come and spend time with the horses.

“HorseBack UK was born. We help to heal physical and mental injuries, manage post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and ease the transition back into civilian life.” HorseBack UK now has 40 horses Many of them, including seven ex race horses, were rescued by the couple. Last year the incredible charity hosted 600 people.

And in 2015, Princess Anne opened one of its rehabilitation arenas.Jock says: “My life was saved by horses over and over. “Now, not only are we saving humans, but we’re saving horses… and then they're kind of saving each other. Horses are the best teachers in the world.”

‌



VETERAN JASON HARE

View 7 Images Afghanistan veteran Jason Hare had a life-changing experience at Horseback UK (Image: Supplied)

Veteran Jason Hare, 45, the course director and one of the lead instructors at HorseBack UK, says: “Back in 2010, I was in one of the first groups of injured troops that came to Jock’s place. “I’d sustained life changing injuries on my third combat tour of Afghanistan. I stepped on an improvised explosive device while leading my team and lost my left leg below the knee, had digits blown off my right hand, and my face was degloved.

“I had 11 operations over the following six years to be rebuilt. I learned to walk and adjust to my new body, but rehabilitation is tough, especially mentally - and I needed a break. I’ve always loved horses, so when Jock invited the injured recovery troop, I accepted. And something magical happened.

‌



“A horse has empathy and a personality. Being around these sentient beings, learning how they behave and how you need to communicate with them, took me out of myself. There was a calmness, a certainty to them. On site, the veterans would work with them on the ground, and we learned to ride.

“Winston Churchill said, ‘There is something about the outside of a horse that is good for the inside of a man,’ and it’s absolutely true. When Jock asked if I wanted to work with him at HorseBack UK, I jumped at the chance.

“When I first sustained my injuries I didn’t want to be here. Now I know my purpose is to help other veterans who need horse power too. What happens on Jock's ranch saves lives..”

*Free Rein: How Horses Can Help Save Your Life by Jock Hutchison (Bloomsbury Publishing, Hardback, £22)

News.title: 'Seedy' bar manned by Kate Moss and Peter O'Toole and loved by Tracey Emin and Ronnie Kray
News.content:
IT was the infamous haunt of Princess Margaret and David Bowie, the seedy Soho drinking den where a young Daniel Craig once pulled pints behind the bar. A magnet for artists, actors and a heady mix of highlife and lowlife, the Colony Room Club earned a reputation as the most notorious watering hole in London - and the most fun.

Opened in 1948, it survived decades of debauchery and scandal before closing in 2008, then reopening in 2023. Now, three years after it was gloriously brought back to life, the doors have closed once again. Few people alive know the place better than Darren Coffield, the artist behind the 2023 revival and author of Tales from the Colony Room: Soho's Lost Bohemia. He first climbed the stairs in 1988 as an art student.

Darren said. "What fascinated me was it was living history." It was a tiny, cramped, smoky room at the top of a dingy staircase - but no-one went there for the decor. The colour was in the people. You'd sit in there and you'd start chatting to a journalist who worked on the Profumo affair with Christine Keeler. Or, another afternoon, Francis Bacon might walk in, or John Hurt."

View 5 Images Gangster Ronnie Kray at the Colony Rooms with theatre director Joan Littlewood and club owner Muriel Belcher (Image: ©The Colony Room Archive®)

The Colony had been attracting royalty and gangsters, artists and actors since it opened. At the height of his fame as Doctor Who, Tom Baker would arrive in the famous hat and scarf, a toothbrush in his top pocket to signal he was looking for a bed for the night. Once he wandered out of the Colony in the full costume, and was stopped in the street by three Japanese tourists.

Darren said: “He always carried a stack of publicity photos, so he whipped a couple out, signed them, and handed them over. But it was quite clear they had no idea who he was. They just wanted to get to Oxford Street."

The whole spirit of the place flowed from one woman, owner Muriel Belcher, who was once described as 'the rudest person in England.' Comedian Barry Humphries, better known as Dame Edna Everage, said: "It provided an atmosphere of delectable depravity for the select company of alcoholics and would-be artists who managed to win the reluctant approval of Muriel Belcher, the gorgon-like proprietrix."

Jazz singer George Melly was fonder. "Muriel was a benevolent witch, who managed to draw in all London's talent up those filthy stairs." But there was a kind side to the self-styled Queen of Soho."

View 5 Images Melvin Bragg and Tracey Emin at the Colony Rooms Club in 2001 (Image: ITV/Shutterstock)

Darren said: "A lot of people who drank in Soho went there because they were orphans, or they had been orphaned by their families, who turned their backs on them, because they were gay or left wing or communist. And so she became this sort of de facto mother and looked after them."

Inside those famous green walls, the normal rules did not apply. David Edwards remembered the afternoon Francis Bacon stormed in, fuming from a shopping trip.

"One afternoon Francis walked in the club, annoyed and pulling his collar. What's wrong Francis? Harrods, I'm never going back there again," David said. "He'd bought a lot of clothes, but when he got home he'd decided he didn't like any of them. I bought so many suits and shirts and threw the lot in the dustbin. You'd never seen the club empty so quickly. The next day everyone was up the club parading around in their new suits and shirts from Francis' dustbin."

Then there was the Lost Property cupboard, catalogued by member Michael Clark. "Vacuuming the carpet one morning, a front tooth was found; it had been knocked out of a member's mouth the night before," Michael said. "It was returned later that afternoon."

View 5 Images Group picture at the Colony Room Club in the 1980s includes Doctor Who actor Tom Baker, artist Francis Bacon and journalist Jeffrey Bernard (Image: Neal Slavin)

Another member, known as Brian the Burglar, would take orders from regulars at Christmas. He claimed to have burgled Margaret Thatcher's home in Chelsea, but he wasn't fussy. Drinking with a stranger one afternoon, he said he needed the toilet. Instead, he left, burgled the man's flat, then returned and carried on drinking with him.

Muriel kept her nerve the day a man burst in claiming to be armed. "A man came barging in the door one day, shouting, ‘hands up I've got a gun! Someone called the police while I kept him talking. Within five minutes the whole of Dean Street was blocked off," Muriel said. "But when they searched the man, the only offensive weapon they could find on him was a pencil. I didn't press charges and later that night he came back and asked me if I would give him a job playing the piano for a pound a week."

Peter O'Toole did a shift behind the bar the night before he took on the play Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell, named after the Spectator columnist and Colony regular whose no-shows became West End theatre. "At that stage he wasn't drinking any more," Darren said. "He was just pouring drinks for everyone. Over the years people were so drunk it was easier to lock them in. They weren't going to drink anymore, they were paralytic. So they just locked them in with the booze, which would never happen in the Groucho Club, would it?"

For all the laughter, the room could be merciless. The seats faced inwards, and nothing stayed secret for long. "It was like a theatre of cruelty, to see people literally have divorces in front of your eyes," Darren said. "It was such a small room, all the seating faced inwards, so it was almost like a gladiatorial arena. It wasn't the kind of place you'd go to and pour your heart out, because within five minutes everyone in the room knew what was going on in your personal life, and you'd become the subject of learned discussion."

View 5 Images Actor Peter Davison with Colony Room Green club owner Darren Coffield (Image: ©The Colony Room Archive®)

The Colony outlived Muriel by nearly 30 years. When she died in 1979 the club passed to her barman Ian Board, and on his death in 1994 to Michael Wojas. Under Michael it became the unlikely clubhouse of the Young British Artists. Trainspotting author Irvine Welsh drank there, The Clash drank there, and model Kate Moss was coaxed behind the bar to serve.

Behind the bar, the help was as starry as the drinkers. Over the years Tracey Emin, Kate Moss and a young Daniel Craig all did unpaid stints pulling pints, long before he became James Bond. The guest list down the decades was just as loaded, taking in Noel Coward, EM Forster, John Hurt, composer Ian Dury, Bond creator Ian Fleming, and even Cambridge spies Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean.

By 2008 the money had run out, and the doors shut. But in 2023, Darren rebuilt it in a basement just off Regent Street, tracking down the original fittings a former owner had sold to an American dealer. The green walls returned, along with the ban on phones and the 2008 drink prices. And the stars came with them.

"People came from all over the world to come and see it," Darren said. "Lisa Stansfield came back and drank there. Bobby Gillespie from Primal Scream came down. Even half of Blondie turned up one night." This year, the owners shut it down and changed the locks. "It's gone. They shut it down. They gave us eight days notice," Darren said. "And then they changed the locks on the doors so we couldn't go in and get the artworks out. But we'll rebuild again."

News.title: 'I had 9 organs removed after true cause of pain discovered'
News.content:
'I had 9 organs removed after true cause of pain discovered'

Claire Gerring was initially suspected to have endometriosis

View 4 Images Claire Gerring in hospital (Image: Claire Gerring/SWNS)

A woman's condition turned out to be so rare that it required nine of her organs to be removed during “the mother of all surgeries”.

‌



Claire Gerring, 42, had initially been referred to John Radcliffe Hospital after an ultrasound in November 2022 with suspected endometriosis and was put on the wait list in May 2023 for an investigative laparoscopy. But after intense pain on her right side, a positive Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) test led to a colonoscopy.

‌



Doctors discovered her appendix was inverted and a CT scan revealed she had malignant tissue on the organ and needed investigative surgery. A biopsy on May 6, 2025, confirmed she had stage four Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP) - a rare cancer that typically originates from a tumour in the appendix.

‌



We can all eat more cheese, gut health clue to Alzheimer’s, breakfast staple cuts cholesterol, and erectile dysfunction pills help you live longer - all this and more in our science newsletter

She was referred to Basingstoke and North Hampshire Hospital, as it is one of only two hospitals that specialise in PMP. The cancer in her appendix had ruptured, meaning there were other nodules in the rest of her body.

View 4 Images Claire after her first hospital discharge (Image: Claire Gerring/SWNS)

‌



On July 15, 2025, Claire, who is mum to sons Oscar, 15, and Spencer, 14, underwent a 10-hour operation to remove nine organs - her appendix, ovaries, fallopian tubes, gall bladder, spleen, uterus and cervix.

She also had removed her greater omentum, belly button, peritoneum lining and part of her bowel Her liver was also partially cut away, as well as having her diaphragm scraped and bladder stripped.

During the surgery Claire had HIPEC chemotherapy – heated chemotherapy circulated around her abdomen. After four-and-a-half weeks in hospital, she was discharged and has been left with bowel problems, but has no evidence of disease at the moment and will be monitored for the next 20 years.

‌



Claire, a hairdresser from Wantage, Oxfordshire, said: “I felt really quite scared and quite alone after my diagnosis. When you’ve got a rare cancer and it’s not something you’ve heard of before, there are not a lot of people to talk to about it.

“I was told by surgeons before my operation what they would remove. On top of that they cut part of my liver away and scraped my diaphragm and stripped my bladder.

“It’s a lot to process. It’s quite scary, but I’m lucky I had professionals who knew what they were doing. It’s called the mother of all surgeries because of the severity of it."

‌



After struggling with pain in her side and asking for her laparoscopy surgery to be expedited by her GP, a positive FIT test and colonoscopy in March 2025 revealed Claire’s inverted appendix, which needed a CT scan. Her original endometriosis surgery was set to go ahead on April 11, 2025.

“But on April 10, I phoned up just to double check they’d got my CT scan results back as the next day I was now having investigative surgery,” Claire told Talk to the Press. “That’s where I was told I had malignant tissues in my appendix.

“At that point I wasn’t too worried because I thought, ‘well I don’t need my appendix’. Thirty seconds later, my gynaecology lady rang and said ‘Claire this is serious’ and that my surgery wouldn’t be happening tomorrow."

‌



View 4 Images Claire with her husband, Tom (Image: Claire Gerring/SWNS)

Investigative surgery on May 6 revealed the cancer was not contained to her appendix.

“When the tumour ruptures it releases mucin, which is a jelly-like substance,” Claire said. “It’s often called ‘jelly belly’. Your abdomen fills up and coats all your organs with mucin."

‌



As a result, Claire needed vital cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC to remove all her affected organs.

"I’m coming up to my year's anniversary and I’m still left with complications in my bowel and I’ve been back in hospital in between,” she said. “With a lot of cancer you’re told you lose weight, but with this one I put on weight and looked four months pregnant.

“I thought I’d just got to 40 and it was my middle-aged spread. But it was actually inside my abdomen.

‌



“Recovery is a slow process, obviously, like most surgeries, if you have your appendix out the recovery time is six to eight weeks.

“Times that by 11 (and) it’s a long time. I had a bowel obstruction and was back in hospital for a 10-day stay recently.

“I’m still grateful, it’s a small price to pay. Basically what they say is you’re never back to your old self, you just get used to the new you."

‌



Now a year into her recovery, Claire has thrown herself into fundraising for charity Pseudomyxoma Survivor, throwing a masked ball on July 11, 2026.

On the night, she said: "I just feel my main purpose for doing this is raising awareness about the rare cancer and Pseudomyxoma Survivor. I believe deeply that if you’re willing to take, you must also be willing to give back. And here I am today, standing in front of you, living that promise.

"I feel so passionate about giving back to this charity which stepped in and helped me at the point in life when it felt uncertain and alone. They also support research and have recently given £100,000 towards — would you believe it — the research project is called The Beacon Project.

‌



"They are creating a blood test to detect the cancer and recurrence way before CTs can even pick it up. Tonight, we are part of supporting these amazing breakthroughs."

View 4 Images Tom, Spencer, Claire and Oscar (Image: Claire Gerring/SWNS)

She has raised £16,002 so far for the charity through Just Giving and other events.

‌



Maddy Lomas, trustee at Pseudomyxoma Survivor, said: “As a charity, we are incredibly touched by the effort and generosity behind this fundraising event. What makes it even more special is that it has been organised by someone who knows first-hand what it means to face a diagnosis of PMP.

"Having received support from Pseudomyxoma Survivor during her own journey, Claire has now turned that experience into an opportunity to give back and support others who are walking a similar path. This is truly commendable and a wonderful example of how personal experiences can be transformed into something that brings hope and support to others.

"For a small charity, the £16,002 raised is incredibly significant and will have a lasting impact. It will help us continue our mission of providing support to people affected by PMP, raising awareness of this rare disease, and contributing towards vital research that can make a difference for the future.

Article continues below

"However, just as important is the much-needed awareness Claire has created by organising and delivering this event. For a rare disease like PMP, every person who learns about the condition helps to increase understanding and could make a life-changing difference by helping someone recognise the signs, seek support, or feel less alone following their own diagnosis.”

You can donate through Claire's Just Giving page.

News.title: Two police officers accidentally found missing England fan while on holiday in Spain
News.content:
Two police officers accidentally found missing England fan while on holiday in Spain

Michael Hewitt, known as Little Mick, was travelling to Boston through Barcelona to watch England play Ghana but lost his phone and was being unaware of the search for him

View 2 Images Michael Hewitt was found safe and well in Barcelona (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

Two Birmingham officers have been praised after reuniting a missing man from Leeds with his family as they were all on holiday in Spain.

‌



PC Lamb and PC Somers, of West Midlands Police, were enjoying their time off in Barcelona when they started chatting to a man known as "Little Mick" in a bar. What they didn't know at the time was that the man had been reported missing by his family in Leeds as he vanished on his way to the World Cup and an international search was underway to find him.

‌



After later seeing social media posts about the search, the Birmingham based officers realised who they had been talking to. PC Lamb and PC Somers contacted the local authorities and liaised with police in Barcelona, sharing all the information they had and hoping to reunite Michael Hewitt with his family.

‌



View 2 Images Michael Hewitt, known as Little Mick, had lost his phone (Image: Jam Press)

It was later established that the Leeds man was completely unaware of the large-scale search for him. This was due to the fact he had lost his phone and so hadn't seen any of the coverage about himself online.

Mr Hewitt's disappearance was met with widespread media coverage as he seemingly vanished while travelling to Boston for the World Cup to watch England play Ghana in June. After losing his phone, the 65-year-old stayed in Barcelona as he was unable to access his tickets for the flight to the United States.

‌



In a statement released following the happy ending, Mr Hewitt's brother Gary said: "Little Mick is safe and well in Barcelona, blissfully unaware that the whole world was searching for him.

"As a family, we desperately wanted an embarrassingly simple but happy ending to this horrendous episode and we now have that."

The search for the retired trade union official and Leeds United fan lasted 10 days. PC Lamb and PC Somers have been commended for their actions in helping locate Mr Hewitt.

Article continues below

Birmingham Police Chief Inspector Sean Corrigan said: "The officers’ actions demonstrate our values as a police force, as even on holiday they acted quickly to help a potentially vulnerable man in need.

"By quickly recognising who they’d been speaking to, and immediately informing Spanish authorities, they helped end an international search.

"While the man involved may have just been enjoying a holiday himself, we commend our officers for interrupting theirs and going above and beyond."

News.title: New warning for tenants as they face 'extremely steep' rent rises after rule change
News.content:
New warning for tenants as they face 'extremely steep' rent rises after rule change

New figures released this week paint a difficult picture for tenants

View 3 Images The news for tenants isn't good (Image: Alicia G. Monedero via Getty Images)

Monthly rents have increased by 3.7% as tenants face "extremely steep" and rising rents while house price growth slowed to 2%.

‌



Average UK monthly private rent increased by 3.7%, to £1,393, in the 12 months to July 2026; this annual growth rate is up from 3.3% in the 12 months to June 2026, new Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures released this week show. Average rents increased to £1,451 (3.8%) in England, £843 (4.5%) in Wales, and £1,016 (1.7%) in Scotland, in the 12 months to July 2026.

‌



In Northern Ireland, average rents increased to £875 (2.3%), in the 12 months to May 2026. In England, private rent annual inflation was highest in the North East (6.3%), and lowest in the South East (2.9%), in the 12 months to July 2026.

‌



Average UK house prices increased by 2%, to £272,000, in the 12 months to June 2026; this annual growth rate is down from 3.0% in the 12 months to May 2026. Average house prices increased to £293,000 (1.8%) in England, £213,000 (1.8%) in Wales, and £195,000 (2.3%) in Scotland, in the 12 months to June 2026.

Experts have given their take on the situation. Babek Ismayil, CEO of homebuying platform OneDome, said tenants were struggling with rising rents.

He added: "Tenants in many areas of the country are already facing extremely steep rents, and they continue to edge higher. If more landlords decide to leave the sector and rental supply falls, that could put further upward pressure on rents. For renters hoping to move into homeownership, higher monthly housing costs can make it harder to save and take that next step."

‌



View 3 Images New figures have been released (Image: Mandy via Getty Images)

Rupert Collingwood, founder of The London Broker, said: "It is increasingly acknowledged that the Renters' Rights Act (RRA) may be delivering some well-signposted consequences, which were only 'unexpected' to those in government who wrote the legislation. Landlords are leaving the market, and those who remain are putting their prices up not only due to demand but also because the RRA stopped landlords taking offers over their asking price."

Jamie Elvin, director of London-based Strive Mortgages, said demand was outstripping supply in the rental market.

‌



He added: "House prices are still rising, but the slowdown from 3% to 2% suggests affordability is putting a ceiling on growth. More telling is rents accelerating again, showing the fundamental problem remains: demand continues to outstrip supply.

"For first-time buyers, rising rents make saving a deposit harder while house prices keep moving the goalposts. The long-term answer isn’t just lower mortgage rates — we need more homes, faster planning and a rental market that encourages landlords to stay. Until supply improves, the pressure will continue to show up in either rents, house prices, or both."

Katy Eatenton, mortgage and protection specialist at Eatenton Finance, said the housing market was struggling.

‌



She added: "The property market is certainly not firing on all cylinders but equally prices aren't falling, in no small part due to the ongoing lack of supply. Now is certainly a good time to negotiate hard on price, which many first-time buyers are doing. And vendors need to price realistically or they won't sell."

Evren Ergin, founder and developer at ValuQ, said houses needed to be built near jobs and stations.

He added: "The story is in the gap between the two numbers. House price growth has slowed to 2%, while rents are climbing 3.7% and still accelerating. The cost of not buying is now rising faster than the cost of buying, which quietly punishes the very people waiting for a cheaper moment to get on the ladder.

‌



"Treat the £272,000 average with care, though. It is a national mean, and no one lives in the mean. In the same year, one English city can have its houses rising while its flats fall by double digits. Plan around the headline and you are planning around a number that describes nobody's actual home.

"How do we fix it? Supply where the demand actually is. Rents are rising fastest in the North East, at 6.3%, not because people want to pay more but because there is too little to rent. Build near jobs and stations, and both curves ease. Everything else just manages the symptom."

Patricia Ogunfeibo, founder and non-practising solicitor at London-based tenant2owner, said landlords were struggling.

‌



She added: "This is not surprising; I suspect this is the practical impact of the Renters’ Rights Act coming into force on May 1, and landlords adjusting their prices upwards before then. Though I suspect that rent inflation will stabilise over the next two years."

Darryl Dhoffer, founder of The Mortgage Geezer, said he didn't think landlords were struggling at all.

He added: "The average UK rent has soared to a bargain £1,393 a month. That 3.7% spike means your landlord’s second holiday home is safely funded. England leads the generosity at £1,451, though the North East bags the overachiever award with a blistering 6.3% hike. Meanwhile, house prices slowed to £272k, because why let tenants save a deposit when you can squeeze every spare penny out of them first?

‌



"This reveals our housing market is functioning precisely as designed, which is a relentless wealth extraction funnel trapping millions in long-standing tenancies. The simple fix is to build actual social housing, kill speculative buy-to-let perks and introduce genuine rent caps."

View 3 Images Rents are high in many parts of the UK (Image: Alicia G. Monedero via Getty Images)

Tony Sanchez, founder of Bridging Loan Directory, said costs had gone up across the board.

‌



He added: "These figures show the rental and sales markets moving at different speeds. House prices are still rising, but more slowly, while rent growth has picked up again. Rents increasing faster than property values may improve a landlord’s gross yield on paper, but that is not the same as greater profitability.

"Mortgage costs, tax, insurance, maintenance and compliance all sit beneath the headline rent, while refinancing still depends on the lender’s valuation and affordability calculations. There is no quick fix. Britain needs more homes across different tenures, but new construction takes time.

"In the meantime, policy should avoid unnecessarily reducing the existing supply of rental homes and make it easier for smaller developers to build. Ultimately, sustained additions to supply are the only durable way to ease pressure on both buyers and tenants."

Article continues below

Stephen Perkins, managing director of Norwich-based Yellow Brick Mortgages, said affordable housing was needed.

He added: "The gap between rent growth and house price growth highlights one of the housing market’s biggest problems. House prices may only be rising modestly, but renters are seeing more of their income swallowed by housing costs, making it harder to save the deposit needed to buy. Building more homes matters, but they also need to be homes people can genuinely afford to rent or buy."

News.title: Marcus Wareing ‘I was told to do one thing’ when bankers bought most expensive meal in history
News.content:
Marcus Wareing ‘I was told to do one thing’ when bankers bought most expensive meal in history

The infamous meal, which would cost £85,355.59p in today's money, was so pricey that Wareing positioned chefs near the front door to make sure the diners paid before leaving

View 6 Images Marcus Wareing opened up about the infamous episode at Petrus (Image: 2016 Mike Marsland/Getty)

Marcus Wareing has spilled the beans on the infamous day a group of bankers blew more than £44,000 on a meal which went down in the Guinness Book of Records as the most expensive of all time. The celebrity chef was behind the stove in July 2001 when six investment bankers rocked up to London Michelin-starred restaurant Petrus, reportedly to celebrate a successful bonds deal.

What followed has gone down in history as one of the most notorious, opulent, and expensive meals ever consumed. Astoundingly, the entire bill was made up of top-end booze as the restaurant, which had one Michelin Star at the time, decided to waive the £400 they spent on food.

Even so, the final bill still came to a whopping £44,007, plus an undisclosed 'four-figure' tip. In 2026 money, that comes to £85,355.59p. Not only did the meal write itself in folklore, but it also had severe repercussions for those involved. While the restaurant Wareing shared with celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay and Ramsay's father-in-law, Chris Hutcheson, went from strength to strength following the episode, all but one of the bankers lost their jobs at Barclays Capital.

"It was the Noughties, the Tony Blair years - cash-rich, cigars, smoking, Cognac - the liqueur trolley might as well have been water, the way it was getting drunk," Wareing, 56, told The Go-To Food Podcast.

"It was the time of the banking world and the time everyone was doing really well and cash was king. It was unbelievable."

View 6 Images Marcus Wareing, pictured here in 2007 when he was chef-patron at Petrus (Image: Graham Barclay/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Masterchef's Wareing explained that Petrus wine, which the restaurant was named after, was becoming the drink of choice for the rich and famous. It is named after the Bordeaux wine estate of the same name, and - as of 2024 - a 750ml bottle is priced at an average of $4,112.

However, certain vintages fetch higher prices. The 1947 version was so good that it cemented the estate's name as a titan in the world of wine. You can buy it for a snip at £8,355.44p these days.

"At lunchtime, the sommelier came down and said there was a guy at the bar who had booked a table for dinner tonight and he wanted to look at the wine list, and he was looking at the Petruses," Wareing continued. "Petrus was a very popular name, people were drinking it. It was being drunk every week.

"The guy said, 'I'm interested in Petrus, what have you got?'. My sommelier showed him the list. Then they came back for their meal.

"They were from a very popular bank, and this particular bank had just made 2,000 people unemployed a month earlier. It was quite big news at that particular time."

Barclays - the parent company of Barclays Capital - had at that point faced a storm of criticism after cutting certain jobs across its operations. Reports from the time suggest 1,800 office jobs were cut and branch numbers reduced, although the company's overall workforce - and profits - did grow.

Although lavish meals were nothing new in the City, it was poor timing as the stock market reeled from the collapse of the technology boom at the start of the millennium. Banks were trying to present a more sober, responsible image - which was one of the factors that made the story spread like wildfire.

"These guys came in, sat down, and the guy opened the wine list and he went straight to the page - he knew exactly where he was going - and he said to the sommelier, 'I'll have one of those, one of those, one of those, 45, 46, 47, a 1900 Chateau d'Yquem, and seven beers please'," Wareing explained. "They started off with the beers to whet the palate.

View 6 Images Petrus often sells for thousands of pounds per bottle (Image: VALERY HACHE/AFP via Getty Images)

"The sommelier came down and looked like he'd seen a ghost. A sommelier opening these was like heaven. I was a chef-patron then, and this guy walks in like a mummy and says, 'Er, chef, these guys want these wines'.

"I asked him what they were worth and he told me and I thought, 'S**t'. The first thing that comes into your mind is, 'Can they pay for it?'. We didn't have credit card reservations back in those days.

"I called Gordon (Ramsay), who burst out laughing. I called Chris, our business partner, and asked, 'What should we do? Do we let them have it?'. He said, 'Yes, do it, but do one thing - make sure that nobody leaves the restaurant until they've paid the bill. Make sure you're local, you're around in case something happens, in case they do a runner - you just don't know'.

"We opened the wines and the service fell to pieces. The adrenaline running through me at that point, that was one of the worst services of my life, because it was hard to focus. The sommelier was bringing me the wine and I was trying all these wines.

"They ordered very simply and they weren't interested in the food, they were just bankers enjoying these amazing wines. The sommelier was having the time of his life."

The exact list of drinks was as follows:

1982 Montrachet - £1,400

1945 Petrus - £11,600

1946 Petrus - £9,400

1947 Petrus - £12,300

1900 Chateau d'Yquem - £9,200

Water, champagne, fruit juice, beers - £102

View 6 Images The bankers splashed more than £30,000 on Petrus alone (Image: ERIC PIERMONT/AFP via Getty Images)

The three bottles of Petrus alone came to £33,300. The 1900 Chateau d'Yquem is known as one of the world's finest dessert wines, while the 1982 Montrachet is a 'rare, complex white Burgundy made from Chardonnay grapes' which fetches more than £7,000 a bottle these days.

"And then it came to the bill," Wareing said. "I told Chris the value of it. I thought, 'my god, this is huge. How are they going to pay for it?'.

"We had a corridor upstairs that was next to the restaurant and I got some of the chefs to wait in the corridor by the front door. We had to be ready for it (in case they ran). It sounds weird but you just can't mess around it. They had drunk the stuff - how were they going to pay?

"The bill came out, this massive bill, he puts it on the table and the guy looks at the bill and says, 'No problem - everyone, get your credit cards'. There were all these credit cards on this bill and he said, 'Right, put £4,760 on this, this on this one, this on that one'. The whole bill was broken down into weird numbers. It took 45 minutes to process this because it was more than one credit card.

"Some of them went through, some didn't, but it eventually all went through - although it took forever."

View 6 Images Gordon Ramsay and Marcus Wareing, who later had an acrimonious falling out and legal battle before eventually burying the hatchet (Image: 2025 Dave Benett)

Fortunately for Wareing, the bill was paid, coming out at £7,334.50p per head - although that was not the end of it. The story came out and Barclays later confirmed that five of those involved no longer worked for the bank. One kept his job after the bank decided he could not be held responsible as he had only just joined.

Eventually, they were named in the media - prompting them to threaten to sue Ramsay. "They are seriously cheesed off and obviously blaming me for it. I believe they are in the process of sending a writ. However, the information was not released by me. I have a code and I don't work like that. They will have to prove their case but I shall fight it to defend myself and my staff," the famously fiery chef retorted.

Barclays later insisted that the meal was privately paid for and did not come out of the bank's coffers.

View 6 Images The Petrus restaurant in its new location of Kinnerton Street, Belgravia. It was at 33 St James's Street when Marcus Wareing was head chef (Image: Dave Rushen/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"I don't know what happened to them," said Wareing. "This story came out - I have no idea how it got out, but it got out - and it went global. It put that restaurant on the map. We were selling Petrus like it was bloody water after that. We couldn't buy enough of it.

"We'd asked permission from the Petrus chateau - you can't just choose their name - and they gave us the opportunity to use the name, Petrus. It's quite unusual for that to happen. Monsieur Moueix, the owner, gave his permission for us to use it. He used to come over and drink some of his wine.

Article continues below

"It was Gordon who came up with the name. We were in the cellar of Aubergine, in the wine cellar, and he pulled out a bottle and said, 'Listen, that's going to be the name of your next restaurant'."

Reach has reached out to Barclays for comment.

News.title: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions
News.content:
Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.

The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.

Mayors in 13 areas including Manchester, Liverpool, the West of England and the West Midlands will gain similar powers to Sir Sadiq Khan in London, who is already able to "call in" planning decisions.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said the powers were an "essential part of the toolkit that mayors need to effectively deliver new homes and regeneration".

The Conservatives questioned whether it was right for councils to lose the "ability to make planning decisions in their own communities".

The powers will also be available to mayors in the Combined Authorities in North East England, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, York and North Yorkshire, Hull and East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midlands, and Tees Valley.

Housebuilding has fallen in London in recent years, but Pennycook insisted the "call in" powers had helped the mayor "unblock strategic growth sites" in the capital.

In the 2024 general election, the Labour government promised to build 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade but housebuilders have warned the target could be missed.

Pennycook said the government was "absolutely determined to stick with that ambition".

He acknowledged the target was "really stretching" but said nearly 180,000 children were in temporary accommodation and "any smaller target wouldn't be commensurate with the scale of the challenge".

In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".

A consultation on how the powers will work is due to be published next week.

The government has sought to stress that local councils will continue to decide the majority of applications and that all decisions must still follow planning rules.

It has also said mayors will get a "bigger say" over how housing funding is spent in their area, with the government directing national agency Homes England to focus on local mayors' priorities.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who served as mayor for Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, has repeatedly expressed his desire to transfer more powers to local mayors.

"Challenge does need to be made to local decision-making and actually it cuts both ways," he told the Sunday Times.

"Sometimes it's the other way round. It's the local authority putting forward something that's unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community. It's a two-way street."

Last month, Burnham promised to give all mayors a share of income tax revenue, saying he wanted to "bring power home" to "every postcode".

Earlier this week, he announced a secondment programme to send high-performing civil servants to work in mayoral offices.

The approach has faced criticism from some in his own party and the Liberal Democrats, who fear it could create a "two-tier system" that discriminates against those areas that do not have an elected mayor.

News.title: Plan to restrict serious offenders to certain areas to start in October
News.content:
A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October, Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced.

Government ministers say this is designed to give victims greater freedom and further reduce the possibility of unwanted contact

The intention to introduce "restriction zones" for violent offenders who leave prison and who are on probation was first announced by the government last year.

Probation officers will be able to limit where serious offenders can go for as long as it is deemed necessary. Those who breach their new boundaries could be recalled to prison.

This would go beyond the current practice of imposing "exclusion zones" which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim's home or place of work.

Norris is expected to come up with proposals to further restrict the early release of some prisoners when Parliament resumes next month.

But the Conservatives say that the best thing Labour could do to protect victims is to bring forward emergency legislation which would stop the early release of thousands of criminals.

There is a risk that serious sexual and violent offenders and victims could encounter one another outside exclusion zones.

The new scheme will specify confined areas for offenders in plans tailored to them and developed in consultation with victims.

Norris said the scheme would use GPS technology monitored by probation officers so that "those who step outside the boundaries can be quickly identified and face being sent back to prison".

"Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he added.

Amy Glover, director of domestic abuse services at Advance, a charity supporting women and girls who have experienced domestic abuse, praised the "change in focus".

However, she also called for reform to the criminal justice system saying many survivors of abuse chose "not to pursue a criminal conviction, and for those that do only 5% reach conviction."

A domestic abuse survivor named only as Kristina called the restriction zones a "fantastic concept" but noted that a perpetrator had continuously breached her indefinite restraining order "without consequence".

"The biggest challenge would be to gain victims' confidence in authorities to follow through their promises of protection," she added.

The announcement of the restriction zone scheme's start date comes after a change to the government's early release scheme following a backlash.

Introduced to ease prison overcrowding, on 4 August the policy was updated so people sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would not be eligible for early release.

The Prison Governors' association warned this change to plans at a "very late stage" put further pressure on prison staff.

The restriction zone scheme was criticised when it was announced last year for potentially putting pressure on probation staff, something the government says it hopes to alleviate with more staff and a greater use of technology.

If you are suffering from domestic abuse, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: Iran-linked hackers behind cyber attack that shut down power plant, reports say
News.content:
A small power plant in the UK was shut down during a cyber attack.

The government said that at no point was there a risk to the UK's energy system, but the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has contacted power companies to advise them about the risk of cyber attacks.

The Telegraph reported, external that the attack, which took place last month, was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

For security reasons, neither the government nor the National Cyber Security Centre, which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, would give further details of the site affected. However this was not an attack on an essential service such as a large power station.

According to the Telegraph, the power plant was shut down for four days.

DESNZ said the incident had affected a small-scale generator and at no point had there been a risk to the wider energy system.

The UK's power network has a number of smaller gas generators which provide short-term power when needed.

Protecting the country's supplies is a key challenge for the government. It is updating its regulations for cyber security, and working on a new energy resilience strategy for later this year.

Iran has long been regarded as a capable cyber power but while the Western cyber-security world is braced for attacks either from the state or hackers linked to the state as a result of its conflict with the US this year, there has been little activity so far.

News.title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support over cancer diagnosis
News.content:
It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

She said in that announcement that it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.

Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.

Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.

The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the film's lead role were also on the panel. Davis played Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of the zombie apocalypse, in the cult British movie and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.

Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.

"It was a fun time, we went a bit mad."

The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.

She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.

"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."

David had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.

"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

News.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
News.content:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and Aâlevel students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an examâ¦ so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

News.title: Why we can't look away from hoarder home clean-ups
News.content:
Gordon says the main reason she posts online is to raise awareness, particularly about hoarding disorder and mental health.

According to the NHS, hoarding disorder is a mental health condition, external in which someone collects a lot of things and finds it difficult to get rid of them, even when they negatively affect their daily life.

"I think it's really easy to be quite judgmental," she says.

"People see footage of these homes online and in documentaries, and it's really easy to judge and think the person's lazy.

"There's a lot of stigma behind it and a lot of misunderstanding."

She says the stigma of being a hoarder can stop people from seeking help.

"This is real life. It's mental health. It's people who are finding themselves living in really unsafe, unsanitary conditions through no fault of their own.

"The more we can talk about it, the better. The less we judge, the more we can understand, [and that] is only going to be a good thing."

Gordon says many of her followers are hoarders themselves.

"I get a lot of messages in my inbox saying, 'Thank you so much for your content. That house that you did last week, mine's not dissimilar to that and you're making me feel like I'm not the only one that lives like this'.

"A lot of people have messaged me and said that, because they've seen my videos, they found the courage to ask for help or maybe hire a cleaner.

"So it is having a really positive effect."

Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds and Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: Trump Mobile promoted a 'Made in the USA' phone - but the details kept changing
News.content:
When Trump Mobile was launched by US President Donald Trump's eldest sons in the summer of 2025, the company advertised that a "T1" smartphone would be built in the US and shipped to customers within months.

Over the last year, key details about the phone's manufacture, design and delivery date have changed, and some customers are still waiting for their phones - as Thomas Copeland explains.

Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz.

News.title: Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
News.content:
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.

When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor.

And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.

It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.

News.title: Police officers killed in wrong-way crash mourned in 'unimaginable loss'
News.content:
Two police officers killed in a wrong-way crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough have been remembered as "brave officers protecting our communities" in what has been described as an "unimaginable loss".

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a car driving the wrong way struck a Cleveland Police vehicle at 03:39 BST on Saturday.

Five people in the Volkswagen Passat - said to be in their late teens to early 20s - were also killed. They have not been named.

The BBC understands a police pursuit of the car had ended before the crash, with the police vehicle involved in the crash just happening to be in the South Bank area.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is now investigating.

News.title: Struggling households need more help with bills, energy industry says
News.content:
Higher energy bills this winter mean the government should step in to provide more help for households most in need, the body representing energy firms in the UK has said.

Stubbornly high prices over the last few years have left some people needing "emergency support" over and above the existing Â£150 Warm Home Discount, Energy UK said.

A "better targeted" support scheme that takes into account someone's income, health and energy consumption was needed, it added.

On Wednesday, the energy price cap for October onwards will be announced by regulator Ofgem and is expected to hit a three-year high.

A government spokesperson said that in addition to the Warm Homes Discount it was cutting VAT on electricity bills and would do "everything we can" to shield consumers from global energy shocks.

Energy UK chief executive Dhara Vyas said: "Suppliers continue to do all they can to help their customers but as well as persistently high bills, record levels of debt show how the current system is failing to provide the right support to those in need."

A new "social discount" scheme would result in "a system that works better for everyone", she added.

Ofgem reported at the end of last winter that customers who had fallen behind on their energy bills owed suppliers a record Â£4.7bn. Since then wholesale energy prices have risen, following the start of the Iran war in February.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight predicts Ofgem's cap on household price rises, which is set every three months, will go up by 4% when it is announced on Wednesday.

The rise will apply to household bills during the first half of the coming winter and follows a sharper 13% rise in July.

The energy cap covers around 33 million households in England, Wales and Scotland.

It fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used, but households' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.

News.title: CrossCountry cancels UK services after power cut
News.content:
Trains across the UK have been cancelled after a power cut at train operator CrossCountry's control centre.

The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.

Services across almost all its routes have been cancelled until further notice as it experiences "significant and unforeseen disruption".

Major routes cancelled include services between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh.

"We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible," a CrossCountry spokesperson said.

While the operator usually calls at more than 100 stations, it said that the only route expecting a "near-normal" service was between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport.

The company apologised to passengers affected by the "significant and unforeseen disruption" and said tickets were being accepted by other operators.

Customers are entitled to Delay Repay compensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more, while those who choose not to travel can claim a refund for their journey.

News.title: Baby whose parents feared had just days to live is 'thriving' after life-saving heart operation
News.content:
A baby, whose parents feared had just days to live, is "thriving" after having life-saving operations on his heart.

Macs Green, a previously "completely healthy baby" suffered two cardiac arrests and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy - which can lead to heart failure.

After a struggle to find suitable hospital beds, he has now had device called a Berlin Heart, external fitted, which takes over the function of his heart.

He still needs a transplant and doctors have told his parents Catrin and Dylan they do not know how long the wait will be before he gets one.

But, after his operation in Newcastle's Freeman Hospital, Dylan said Macs was already "completely different" from how he was before.

Before surgery he had been in a specialist unit in Bristol Royal Children's Hospital on an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, external (Ecmo) machine, which helped pump oxygenated blood around his body.

News.title: 'My skin makes me unique and I'm learning to embrace it'
News.content:
A woman born with a rare genetic skin condition that covers 98% of her body in birthmarks has spoken of how she is learning to embrace her appearance after years of trying to hide it.

Laura Kelly, 28, was born with congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN) and underwent 14 operations as a baby, with doctors fearing she may not live beyond the age of eight.

Laura said CMN made her self conscious about how strangers might react and that, growing up as a teenager, she often wore heavy makeup and planned outfits to cover her skin.

She said embracing how she looks and raising awareness of CMN has given her more confidence and hopes sharing her story will help others with a visible difference.

News.title: Vigil held for family who died in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
Alden added: "The way everybody has come together and marked today with this minute's silence, and there were people who met with paddleboards and kayaks over at Kingston Beach as well this morning, it's been a really lovely way to pay to the very sad loss of these lives."

Wesley Horscroft attended on behalf of paddlers in the Kingston beach community.

He said he had originally planned to go out alone and "put some flowers on the water" to honour the family, before he decided to invite others.

"It's kind of grown and a lot of people wanted to turn up to do the same," he said.

He said Saja's death had added an "another layer" to the grief felt in the town.

News.title: I'd swell up once a week - now my life has changed
News.content:
"It's changed my life. I can do everything I want to now. It's brilliant," says Jack Cope.

The 30-year-old joiner, from Bedford, has had hereditary angioedema (HAE), a condition which causes severe unpredictable swelling and painful attacks, since birth.

The swelling occurs all over his body, including in his throat, stomach and face. Even something as simple as using a hammer can cause his hand to swell.

But now, due to a trial at Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, he is trying a new treatment which he says has massively reduced his symptoms.

"I was having about an attack a week and I've gone from that to nothing for nearly a year now," he says.

News.title: Welsh county becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
News.content:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data, external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ãvila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared, which eventually required assistance from the military.

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

News.content:

More and more people over the age of 50 are taking up physical exercise. Medical associations resoundingly agree that this is a good thing. Physical exercise is not only key to disease prevention, but it is also a recommended part of treatment for many illnesses.

However, starting to move at this stage of life requires some care. This is especially true for those who have not previously been physically active, or for people who are overweight or obese.

It has been proven that starting to exercise with routines that are too demanding can lead to significant muscular and skeletal injuries, especially if combined with an inadequate diet. This risk is even greater after the age of 50, as the loss of muscle and bone mass is more pronounced due to natural ageing processes.

Before starting any new exercise programme, it is a good idea to carry out a complete analysis, especially to assess the need for micronutrient supplements.

Protein is key

In addition to micronutrients, the body also needs carbohydrates, fats and proteins – known collectively as macronutrients.

Proteins provide the body with the essential amino acids needed to maintain and develop muscle mass, and to prevent sarcopenia: age-related muscle injury, osteoporosis, and loss of muscle mass and strength (formerly referred to as frailty).

open image in gallery Proteins provide the body with the essential amino acids needed to maintain and develop muscle mass ( Getty )

Protein requirements vary according to an individual’s clinical situation. In people over 50 years of age who are moderately physically active, protein requirements range from 1 to 1.5 grams per kilogram of body weight per day.

However, it is not advisable to increase protein intake without a corresponding increase in physical exercise. Too much protein can actually have harmful effects, especially on bone health, as it has been observed to increase calcium excretion in the urine (calciuria) due to decreased tubular calcium reabsorption.

Animal and vegetable proteins

Protein sources should combine those of vegetable origin – soy, beans, seeds, peanuts, lentils, and so on – with those of animal origin, such as eggs, dairy products, chicken and fish.

While the ideal is to have a balance of both, it has been shown that following a vegetarian diet is compatible with high-performance sports, so long as there is suitable medical and nutritional monitoring.

In addition to what you eat, it also matters when you do it. Spreading protein intake throughout the day is more beneficial than concentrating it in a single meal.

You should also eat protein 30 minutes before or after exercise, as its absorption and availability in the body will be better.

Essential micronutrients: magnesium, calcium, vitamin D

Some micronutrients – by which we mean vitamins and minerals – play a key role in physical exercise at this age. These include magnesium, calcium and vitamin D.

About the author Patricia Yárnoz Esquíroz is a Profesor Clínico Asociado at Universidad de Navarra. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Magnesium aids muscle recovery and bone formation, and can be found in foods such as wheat bran, cheese, pumpkin seeds and flax seeds.

Calcium is essential for maintaining adequate bone mineralisation and preventing loss of bone mineral density (osteopenia) associated with calcium deficiencies in the blood.

Dairy products are known to be beneficial for bone health, both for their bioavailable calcium and the vitamin D content in their whole milk.

Certain plant-based foods, such as tahini (sesame paste), almonds, flaxseed, soya and hazelnuts, are also decent sources of calcium, but their phytate and oxalate content can hinder its absorption.

Lastly, oily fish (tuna, sardines, salmon, and so on) and egg yolks are considered complementary sources of vitamin D in dietary plans focused on people over 50 years of age who do physical exercise.

It is also vitally important to maintain proper hydration before, during and after exercise. Both dehydration and overhydration can affect performance and increase the risk of muscle injury.

open image in gallery Dairy products are known to be beneficial for bone health ( Getty )

Does the type of exercise matter?

So far, we have seen how nutrition influences athletic performance and ultimately the risk of injury. But there is another part of the puzzle: the exercise you do.

There is actually no clear consensus on this, and there is ongoing debate about which type of exercise is the most appropriate according to age, gender or body composition. The question is whether it is better to prioritise strength exercises, alternate with cardio sessions, or do both on different days.

Despite the different theories on the subject, one thing is clear: regular exercise, adapted to the abilities of each individual and with good medical and nutritional monitoring, reduces the risk of multiple diseases and improves quality of life.

Creatine supplementation is booming among those seeking greater muscle size and performance.

Although creatine is certainly not a new discovery, with research dating back to the 1830s, its popularity and sales have continued to grow, and have expanded beyond bodybuilders and athletes to clinical applications and benefits beyond muscle performance.

Today, creatine stands as one of the most researched supplements, and new findings continue to support its use for consistent and measurable results in bodybuilding, fitness and overall health.

While creatine is naturally found in foods like red meat and seafood, and also produced naturally in the body, supplementation has surged in popularity, especially among young men.

This growth in popularity is largely due to young men’s desire to increase muscle size and muscle strength. Several meta-analyses have looked at the effects of creatine supplementation during resistance training on properties of muscle, and support its use and effectiveness when combined with resistance training.

Simply put, creatine can help maintain energy levels, especially during short-duration, high-intensity exercise like weight training.

Creatine’s role in the body

From a physiological perspective, once in the body, the majority of creatine is stored in the muscle as phosphocreatine (PCr). In this form, it can help maintain energy levels through the maintenance of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the body’s primary energy currency.

Because creatine supplementation increases intramuscular levels of creatine, it may enable resistance training at a higher intensity and for longer durations, leading to greater gains in the gym.

Although creatine’s impact on muscle performance may be more well-known, it does not paint the whole picture.

Research is revealing creatine’s positive impact outside the muscular system, showing positive effects on the storage and metabolism of glucose, blood-flow dynamics, anti-inflammatory effects and positive benefits for cognition and brain function, to name a few.

Dosage and safety

About the author Scott Mills is a PhD Candidate in Kinesiology and Health Studies at the University of Regina. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

From a research perspective, dosage recommendations for men can vary, but typically either five grams of creatine daily, or a customized dosage based on bodyweight of (0.1 grams per kilogram per day) has been shown to be well-tolerated and effective for increasing muscle performance.

From a food intake perspective, to consume about five grams of creatine in the diet, an individual would have to consume about 1.15 kilograms of beef, or about a kilogram of pork, for example. This means even a diet that is high in creatine-containing foods may not be enough to maximize its benefits.

The high-calorie content of eating enough of these foods to reach the target creatine intake makes supplementation a practical and appealing option, both for ease of consumption and calorie considerations.

Also, from a cost perspective, at about $0.50 per serving, it’s an easy and cost-effective strategy to reach creatine intake goals. With new forms of creatine seemingly being released all the time (capsules, gummies and flavoured powders), it makes it easy to maintain intake.

Regarding the safety of creatine supplementation, a position stand paper by the International Society of Sports Nutrition concluded that creatine supplementation poses no greater adverse effects in healthy individuals compared to placebo, even with higher dosages.

With that being said, creatine hasn’t been immune to its share of negative claims. Anecdotally, creatine may have some whispers of undesirable side-effects; however, research looking at common myths and misconceptions of creatine (including concerns about water retention, hair loss and dehydration) have largely removed many of the fears.

Resistance training is key

It is largely creatine consumption in combination with resistance training that leads to benefits ( Getty )

It’s important to note that while creatine consumption on its own may still show some positive effects, it is largely creatine consumption in combination with resistance training that leads to benefits.

Resistance training can increase measures of muscle growth and performance (muscle power, muscle strength and muscle endurance) and it’s the combination of creatine with resistance training that will maximize its effects. So resistance training is a paramount component to the positive effects of creatine.

Of course, creatine is not an essential nutrient. Individuals can see improvements in muscle growth and muscle performance while focusing on the intake of high-quality and nutrient-rich foods, a well-designed individualized resistance training program, combined with adequate high-quality sleep and proper stress management without the need to supplement creatine.

A healthy lifestyle is the foundation of well-being, including the groundwork for effectively building muscle.

Creatine supplementation has made its way into the hands of those seeking the secret to greater muscle size and performance. It is well researched and widely accepted, and it continues to increase in popularity due to the positive effects when paired with a solid resistance training program, its safe risk profile when consumed at evidence-based dosages and its low-cost.

While creatine supplementation is not essential, it may be a practical, affordable and effective choice for those seeking muscle growth benefits and beyond.
