Due to geologic processes and most likely providence, the Liberian people inherited certain economic mineral deposits (aka mineral deposits). This policy brief hypothesized that policy makers are transient managers of all inherited economic mineral deposits in Liberia. Mining and exporting minerals for sale without processing them in the country to add values keep Liberia at the bottom of the global mineral supply chain. According to the United States Geological Survey-USGS (USGS, 2025), one fundamental characteristic of countries at the bottom of the Global Mineral Supply Chain is mining and exporting minerals to foreign countries for processing before sale. Leading mineral mining and producing countries tend to have very little to no mineral processing facilities. The same is also true for Liberia. This policy brief is intended to educate, advise, and help modify Liberia’s existing Mineral policy. Instead of waiting to collect nominal annual royalties, land rents, and other fees as the only means of earning income from inherited mineral deposits, this paper recommends the Government of Liberia form and operate Liberian Natural Resources Investment Corporation-LNRIC for profit.

Since all rocks in Liberia do not have anomalous concentrations of minerals such as gold, diamond, and iron ore, it is appropriate to take inventory and determine how much of each mineral deposit we have in Liberia. Reason follows. Each mineral deposit in certain rocks should be viewed as cash deposited in a commercial bank (rock) account. Each week of mining minerals should be considered as a week of withdrawing cash from the bank (aka rock). Before going to the bank to withdraw cash each week, it is reasonable to check your bank account balance first! To keep mining and exporting minerals without taking inventory of each mineral deposit amounts to withdrawing cash from the bank without first checking your bank account balance. Liberia should first take inventory of each mineral deposit before mining.

The goal of this research is to encourage the Liberian people (aka Government) to positively change from: a) waiting to collect insignificantly small annual royalty and taxes as the only means of earning money from the sale of our inherited minerals; b) lacking active participation (aka sit and do nothing) to form and operate the Liberia Natural Resources Investment Corporation-LNRIC for profit. c) watching and noting mining companies haul & sell our minerals weekly, while we wait annually to collect nominal royalty and taxes. In other words, foreign companies make huge sums (money) weekly from selling Liberia’s inherited minerals for themselves, and Liberia waits for the end of each year to earn insignificant income, a pure lose-win state.

Excluding the abstract, this policy brief is divided into 4 interrelated sections: 1) policy issue or problem description; this includes data and proposed policy research questions; 2) current state of research, is a summary of selected publications related to mineral production and short comings of existing research publications; 3) findings and discussions which contains a list of research findings, followed by analyses including scientific justifications for policy recommendations; and 4) policy options or recommendations.

Current State of Research

In March of 2010, the Government of Liberia published a policy document entitled: Mineral Policy of Liberia (MLME, 2010). The vision statement in this document is cut and pasted here for easier reference: “Equitable and optimal exploitation of Liberia’s mineral resources to underpin broad-based sustainable growth and socio-economic development”. This mineral policy document discussed a sustainable and well-governed mining sector that is inclusive, environmentally friendly, and socially responsible. The policy stated that mining in itself is not technically sustainable, as mineral deposits are not finite national assets. It is stated that mineral extraction can indirectly become justifiable in so far as it catalyzes sustainable economic activity in other viable sectors such as the re-investment of the resource rents into sustainable activities. This last statement is similar to item 6 under recommended Policy Options listed below. For the purpose of sustainable mineral deposit management and intergenerational equity, items 1 to 4 of the proposed policy recommendations were not found in Liberia’s National Mineral Policy document.

The United Nation Climate Action home page give a definition: “Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns. Such shifts can be natural, due to changes in the sun’s activity or large volcanic eruptions.” (U.N. Climate Action, 2025). Temperature and weather patterns as used here refer to atmospheric temperature and weather on planet Earth. The impacts of climate change on Liberia and its development are the topic of a World Bank Group report (2024): “Liberia, Country Climate and Development Report-CCDR.” A statement on page 6 of the CCDR reads: “Changing precipitation patterns are expected to lead to more frequent and unpredictable intense rainfall events.” The executive summary of this CCDR concluded: “Global climate change poses an existential threat to peace and prosperity in Liberia.” Many factors leave Liberia particularly vulnerable to climate change. This review found no recommendation suggested to prevent dangerous landslide at former mining areas due to combination of excessive rainfalls and stockpiled unconsolidated soil. Complete reclamation of old mine pits was not discussed.

Adeyeri, et al (2024) published an article in the Science of the Total Environment: “Climate change is intensifying rainfall erosivity and soil erosion (i.e. natural removal of soil from one location to another) in West Africa.” Rainfall erosivity is the ability of rainfall to cause soil erosion or soil loss (Nearing, M. 2017). The 10 West African countries selected for this study were: Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea Bisau, Ivory Coast, Senegal, Gambia, Togo, and Benin. This study used historical meteorological data (e.g. rainfall, major storm, air temperature) from 1982 to 2014. The focus of their study was on impacts of climate change, rainfall, and soil erosion in Liberia and selected West African Countries. Results from computer models concluded that the southern regions of Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Nigeria are projected to receive the highest mean annual rainfall in both near- and far future periods. It was concluded that southern Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and southern Guinea are identified as most exposed to soil erosion due to high erosivity. This review found no evidence of, nor mitigating recommendations for resiliency to overcome impacts of climate change on sustainable mineral deposit management. There were no mitigating actions to foster the prevention of dangerous landslide due to predicted excessive rainfall on unconsolidated soil stockpiled at all old mine pits in Liberia, nor suggestions for reclamation of old mines. Finally, Togbah (2024) published climate change vulnerability research results for Liberia. Results from Togbah’s are similar to Adeyeri (2024) and the World Bank Group (2024).

Towards Liberia Vision 2030: Liberia National Development Plan 2025-2029 (aka The Plan) is published by Liberia’s Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, 2025. Page 14 acknowledged Liberia’s rich natural resources like gold, diamonds, iron ore and other minerals; and, accurately argued that “Effective management and sustainable exploitation of these resources can significantly contribute to revenue generation and (national) development.” Last paragraph on page 55 includes an assertion that mineral beneficiation and other activities have potential for private sector investment. The plan suggests revision to MDAs. This review found no evidence of mineral inventory, construction of steel mill to process iron ore to make iron, steel, recover associated rare metals from steel making process, nor conservation efforts to account for the creation and establishment of sustainable intergenerational equity for Liberia.

Dieudonne C. et al (2013, p. 157) documented evidence of the occurrence of rare Earth elements within iron ore deposits in Southern Cameroun. Additionally, documentary evidence of the association of iron ore processing and rare Earth elements and minerals was reported by the United States Department of Interior-Bureau of Mine (Vierrethur & Cornell, 1993). Mine tailings (waste materials) from the processing of iron ore at Pea Ridge Mine in Missouri contained rare Earth elements-REEs such as Cerium-Ce, Lanthanum-La, Neodymium-Nd, Yttrium-Y and REE- minerals such as monazite, apatite, rutile and xenotime. It was concluded that iron ore mine tailings at Pea Ridge Mine contained elevated sources of REEs. Efficient recovery of REEs from the iron ore tailings was the main drawback in 1993. Inoue et al (2010) page 448 and Table 3 provided more documentary evidence that iron ore contains rare metal elements; and that manganese-Mn, Vanadium-V, and Niobium-Nb are recovered from iron ore using iron and steel making processes. In other words and during the processing of iron ore to make pig iron and steel products, critical REEs are recovered. Please see below under Findings for the applications of REEs which includes electric vehicles. Abaka-Wood et al (2022) also provided the most recent documentary evidence of the recovery of REEs from iron ore tailings. Finally, Djagre et al (2025) also documented that gold mineralization in the Ivory Coast are associated with higher concentrations or enrichment of REEs.

Findings & Discussion Findings “Some rare metal elements such as manganese, niobium, vanadium, phosphorus, and minerals like monazite are contained in iron ore” (Inoue, et al, 2010). There is ample evidence that REE and other valuable chemicals are being recovered from iron ore processing to make steel. Liberia National Development Plan 2025 to 2029 acknowledged (page 11) that with respect to its solid minerals sector and other areas, Liberia’s economic growth is largely concessions-driven with no value addition. Table 5 (Mineral Production in Liberia) on page 79 of Liberia National Development Plan 2025 to 2029 listed primary minerals mined under existing MDAs. Notably, there is no account nor evidence of any recovery of associated valuable minerals nor REEs chemicals. This research found no evidence of the existence of a Liberia-owned and operated Natural Resources Investment Corporation-NRIC. The National Development Plan has no recommendation for such a government- owned and operated company. By processing iron ore to make iron and steel in Liberia, rare metals such as manganese, vanadium, niobium, phosphorus and mineral like monazite can be recovered. Monazite contain rear Earth elements-REE. Niobium and other REE in monazite have key applications in electronics, cell phone, aerospace, medical implants, electric vehicles etc. (Inoue et al, 2010; Balaram, V. 2019). Gold mineralization in the Ivory Coast is associated with REEs and other rare minerals (Djagre et al., 2025). The rocks and tectonic origin (i.e. forces, fracture, deformation, and structure) of Liberia and the Ivory Coast are similar (Brownfield, 2016). Developed countries such as the USA (U.S.G.S., 2025), and the European Union ( EU, 2022) maintained and updated lists of Critical Minerals and Critical Raw Materials. Some REEs and rare metals which are classified as Critical Minerals and Critical Raw Materials are also associated with iron ore and gold deposits. Summary of data (see Table 1 herein) from the Central Bank of Liberia quarterly reports indicate that gold, diamonds, and iron ore mined in Liberia are exported to foreign countries. Importantly, the weight of gold reported by the Central Bank of Liberia is ounce. In commerce, there are two significantly different types of ounces: One type of ounce which is called Troy Ounce (ozt) is reserved only for trading precious metals such as gold, silver, platinum etc. A second type of ounce is the standard ounce-oz, (aka avoirdupois ounce). The standard ounce is used for trading food and shipping. One troy ounce equals 31.10 grams; and one standard ounce equals 28.35 grams. The difference between troy ounce and standard ounce is 2.75 grams or nearly 3.0 grams. Which units of gold is reported to and also reported by the Central Bank of Liberia? The standardization of, accounting of, and transparency of reporting Liberia’s gold is a salient topic for investigation, research, and policy formulation.

Discussion

The principle of intergenerational equity (Kourides, 2025) requires Liberians today to assume the role of responsible stewards, keepers, and managers of its current economic mineral deposits for current and future Liberians, that is those Liberians yet to be born. This is intended to secure current mineral endowment utility and safeguard future prosperity for the Liberian Nation collectively and all its peoples. For these compelling reasons, economic minerals deposited in certain rocks in Liberia should be viewed analogous to cash deposited in a commercial bank (aka rock) saving account. In other words, certain rocks within the borders of Liberia should be viewed as if they were commercial banks; and, economic minerals deposited in those rocks are equivalent to cash deposited in commercial bank saving accounts (see Figure 2 below). Liberians, by virtue of providence inherited these minerals deposits or cash deposited in rocks from our forefathers such as Benjamin J.K. Anderson, Elijah Johnson, Hilary Teage, J.J. Robets, King Boatswain, etc. ( https://liberiadata.com/know-this , 7/2026).

Revenue generation from (1) annual royalty and (2) land rent for mining minerals is a process used by policy makers to withdraw cash from the aforementioned bank accounts without any evidence of mineral or cash “reserved” for future generations. To continuously mine (extract), export, and sell minerals without mineral inventory data is similar to continuous withdrawal from bank saving accounts without first knowing the available saving account balance in the bank. This practice challenges the unsustainability of this activity. In summary, the principle of sustainable development within a nation asserts that the current generation should meet their legitimate needs without jeopardizing or damaging future generations’ ability to meet their needs (UNDP, 2025). The United Nation Development Program’s Sustainable Development Goal #12 deals with responsible production and consumption patterns.

Planet Earth is a whole system. This Earth system consists of 5 interacting components (NASA, 2003): Hydrosphere (i.e. water in all forms), atmosphere (air and other gases), biosphere (all living organisms), geosphere (minerals, rocks & soils), and cryosphere (frozen water/ice). The processes within some components, and interactions among components of Planet Earth over time (million, and billions years) led to the formation of mineral deposits, such as iron ore deposits, petroleum deposits, gold deposits, coal, diamonds, and fertile soil formation, (Wicander & Monroe, 2016). Rocks are made of natural minerals and minerals consist of chemical elements. Based on similarities of properties, the chemical elements are grouped and arranged in a table known as the Periodic Table of Elements (see Figure 3 below). Within soil, rocks and minerals on Earth, similar chemical elements on the Periodic Table formed similar mineral deposits. For instance, platinum (Pt) mineral groups including gold, iron, Pt, Pt-Fe alloys, sperrylite, and other minerals are documented (Oberthur, 2014).

Geologic processes which led to the deposition and enrichment of iron ore, gold, lead, zinc, platinum and other minerals are not adequately efficient enough to single out, separate, and pack iron ore, gold, or other metals in a rock by itself. Geologists have found iron ore deposits with manganese minerals associated. Similarly, copper, lead, zinc and silver deposits are known; gold and platinum deposits are also documented (Janisch, 1986). Iron ore deposit in Cameroun is reportedly associated with monazite and other minerals containing rare Earth chemical elements (Dieudonne, 2013). Is it then conceivable that all iron ore mining companies in Liberia could have also mined and exported associated minerals and other chemicals as well? Most likely, YES (with emphasis). “Some rare metal elements such as Manganese, Niobium, Vanadium and Phosphorus are contained in iron ore”; Inoue et al (2010); Dieudonne C. et al (2013); Vierrethur & Cornell (1993). Gold mineralization in the Ivory Coast is associated with high enrichment of REEs (Djagre et al, 2025).

Iron ore mining in Liberia started in (random order) around 1951 with the Liberian Mining Company-LMC, followed by Bong Mining Company-BMC in 1958, National Iron Ore Company-NIOC in 1961, and Liberian-American-Swedish Mining Company-LAMCO from 1951. LAMCO closed in 1989/90. Loosed soil and rocks excavated from each mine pit are stockpiled near each mine pit. Excessive rainfalls are predicted for Liberia and other West African countries. This rainfall prediction is based on documented recent climate change computer modeling (Adeyeri et al., 2024; World Bank, 2024). When rain water infiltrates unconsolidated soil, rain water adds weight to unconsolidated soil, internal friction (a force) among soil grains can be exceeded, and then soil grains begin to float (Lutgens & Tarbuck, 2016). Dangerous mudslide/landslide will result as shown in Figure 4 below. A more deadlier mudslide occurred at Bomi Hills mine back in October 1982. All mining companies of necessity should be required to deposit surety bonds in the amount of $1,000,000 a year for 10 years, per closed mine pit. Any mining company that fails to dutifully, timely, and responsibly reclaim old mine pits according to Liberia’s specifications would forfeit a minimum of $10,000,000 to the Liberian Government. This measure is a safety deposit against contingencies and is inclusive of all cost related to restoring closed mines and reclaiming sites.

Policy Recommendations/Options Liberians (aka referencing its Government) should not passively idle and wait for annual royalty and rent money for compensation of its valuable mineral endowments worth billions of dollars; while unwittingly and unknowingly transferring its substantial national mineral wealth to foreign corporations. While Liberia is waiting annually to collect penny on the dollar royalty, foreign corporations are digging, hauling, and selling Liberia’s inherited minerals weekly for substantial unmitigated sums. Foreign corporations who mine on Liberian soil operate as actual Buyers and Sellers of high value mineral supplies, having shifted from service providers of mineral extraction implements to mineral wealth suppliers and sourcing. The same mining companies are repositioning to major funders, mineral extractors project in the known MDA arrangement, and commanding controlling shares of the mineral wealth of Liberia which is actually for current and future Liberians.

In order to mitigate this difficulty in mining commerce, Liberia of necessity must assert its sovereign right to form the Natural Resources Investment Corporation (NRIC). One major objective of NRIC is to completely optimize its profits in Liberia mineral sector as part of the national and global marketplace. This is where its mineral endowments can work unhindered for its national interest. Liberia needs to urgently exercise sovereign control of its mineral endowments which is consistent with the United Nation Sustainable Development Goals-SDG #12. NRIC should have 4 main divisions: Mineral Exploration and Production Division; Energy Exploration and Production Division; Forest Products and Deforestation Management Division; Marketing and Human Resources Division. It is urgent & imperative that Liberia modifies existing laws to effectively level the playing field for this new corporation to thrive, to participate in the competitive marketplace, and to grow the mineral sector for the long term.

All MDAs for precious metals such as gold, platinum, silver etc. should specifically require the mining company to publicly and periodically report basic weight of precious metal as troy ounce. For all total weight of gold and precious metals reported to the Liberian Government as kilogram, the government should require the gold or precious metal mining company to explain in writing how the company got the total weight of kilogram, ton, or pound. In other words, breakdown the kilogram, pound or ton unit down to a basic unit of weight measure, sufficiently clear to suit the understanding of Liberian high schoolers. The devil is in the unexplained details, meaning that the details must provide full transparency, uniformity, and clarity in order for reporting and accountability requirements to be fulfilled. All MDAs should specifically state that the basic unit of weight of precious metal reported to the Government of Liberia should be troy ounce , and NOT ounce. Mine Security should commission and track an independently reviewed third-party closure-cost estimate and be updated as the mine footprint and risks change. This approach improves the accuracy of coverage of mine closure events. As a disclaimer, the quoted amount here again is treated as a safety deposit against prevailing contingencies.

Selected photos showing examples of abandoned mine pits in Liberia follow.

Figure 5 above: Mine pit Left by Liberia Mining Company-LMC after closing Bomi Hill Mine; photo by CGTN Africa

Figure 6 above: Photo showing abandoned mine pit from LAMCO mine in Nimba County, Liberia. By Roseline Joseph. 1/18/24

Figure 7 above: Photo showing old mine pit after Bong Mine Company closed. By Lauretta Cisse 2024

10)Accurate Reclassification of Mineral Extraction Service Providers. Mineral extraction service providers rendering mineral extraction capabilities should do just that—provide competence in mineral extraction. To mitigate the prevailing problem and existing confusion of relegating this class of vendors to functional competitors against Liberia in Liberia’s supply chain, and of mistakenly misassigning them as Investors, i.e. venture partners in owning, directing, redirecting, and largely helping themselves disproportionately to Liberia’s sovereign mineral posterity. This correction of role reassignment in the global marketplace eliminates the misdirection of Liberia’s mineral equity to extraction providers who easily transition from the extraction vendor realm to the Buyer / Seller realm. The major goal of role separation is to prevent the natural effect of severely transferring Liberia’s much needed wealth away from its majority underdeveloped, disadvantaged economy, and its Citizens. There is a need to monitor and substantiate unsuspecting efforts of mineral extraction service provider so as to prevent or substantially minimize the risk of mineral wealth flowing from Liberia to external outside sources.

General Procedure for Closing Abandoned Mine Pits

If the Liberian Government had collected in escrow $10,000,000 of surety bond (at a minimum) from LMC by 1961, then LMC would have had good reason ($10,000,000 on hold in account by Liberian Government) to properly close all holes left behind. Suggested procedures to responsibly and properly close all former mine pits follow.

Hire a qualified entity (consulting company) comprising of experienced & licensed professional geologist and an experienced environmental scientist from a reputable entity. Both scientists should collect statistically representative samples of stormwater in Figures 5-7 above and all similar mine pits at Bomi Hills. Use the same team in item a above to collect statistically representative samples of sediments/mud at the bottom of each pit. Perform chemical analyses of the water samples separately from all abandoned holes. Perform chemical analyses of all sediments/mud samples separately from each mine pit. Perform a bench scale treatment test for water from old mine pits. The goal of the treatment test is to substantiate that the quality of water in the old mine pits matches almost exactly the quality of water in the nearest big rivers. While performing the water treatment tests, apply for and obtain discharge permit from Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency-LEPA. Build central surface water treatment facility to treat water from all holes at each mine. Pump water from each mine pit to a central water treatment facility for treatment. Responsibly treat water from all holes at each mine. After treating the water from huge holes at the former LMC mine, slowly discharge the water from the central treatment facility to the nearest big river. The goal of slow discharge is to prevent/minimize erosion and prevent destruction of biodiversity. There should be daily documented quality control tests to ascertain that the quality of discharge water matches that of the receiving river. The discharge should be very slow, and should be done during Liberia’s dry season. After pumping out stormwater from all holes, then use a combination of crushed rocks and soil to backfill each holes at Bomi Hill. Compact each hole to meet Liberia’s predetermined specifications. Legally regulate and enforce all the above stipulations through policy guidance and regulatory oversight of each check listed item. The goal is to ensure good faith use and stewardship of Liberia’s national mineral and mining endowments. This approach should be the mineral and mining strategies and captured in its newly reconstituted NOME Policy, the Liberia National Optimized Mineral Extraction Policy.

How We Got to Where We Are Today and Why?

History tells us that in 1526, the first Portuguese slave ship left West Africa for Brazil. In 1562, Captain John Hawkins of England commanded the slave ship called Jesus of Lubeck that captured or “acquired” 300 African slaves from today’s Sierra Leone and sold them in Spanish West Indies. Another slave ship called the White Lion carrying 20 stolen Africans slaves arrived in Jamestown, Virginia USA in August of 1619. The Portuguese and British (aka white slave traders) established trading relationships with coastal African Chieftains and inland kingdoms. The white slave traders exchanged captured Africans slaves for irons, guns, cloths and whiskey/gin made in Europe. African Coastal Chieftains and native warriors were the middlemen for the Whiteman involved in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade. The slave traders took away as many slaves as they could carry and dispensed of slaves in whatever way the saw fit.

Back in 1967 to 1970, the then vice president of Zambia, Mr. Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe accurately predicted that: “If we don’t handle our independence very well, colonizers will come back in the form of investors”.

Fast forward to today and instead of the slave trade involving white slave traders and African chiefs as middlemen, we now have the mineral commodity trade, white men posting as mineral traders aka “investors”, and African rulers/leaders as middlemen or main actors: descendants from the same root. It appears that white men now posting as natural resources “investor” are taking Liberia’s inherited minerals by first deeply burying our mineral rights in a document called mineral development agreements or MDAs. Those MDAs reviewed for this policy brief had: no mineral inventory requirement, no specified unit of weight to report precious metal excavated, eight cent ($.08) per acre per year of land rent, over 500 acre of land in the case of Bea Mountain; fees paid to members sitting on committees/boards with no authority nor voice, including signature bonuses for signing MDAs, three per cent (3%) royalty annually. The MDAs had no requirement to process minerals in Liberia for value addition.

Hidden ahead of the crevices of two-lane dusty roads, mining concessions areas are populated by unemployed, very low-paid Liberian workers suffering to excavate Liberia’s high-value minerals earmarked to be quickly removed from its soil forever. Today, a segment of short-sighted third world national representatives appear to be the new African Middlemen facilitating economic and mineral extraction or mining schemes with foreign mineral commodity traders or “investors” instead of slave traders.

The institutionalized practice of obtaining inducements by few administrative individuals for the undignified purpose of harvesting Liberia’s much needed minerals and natural resources for pennies on the dollars is most similar to, if not identical to the Trans-Atlantic slave trade: exchange Human Slaves for Artifacts = Highest Value Minerals & REE exchange for Token Gain. Slaves have now been replaced by mineral and natural resources in the mining and mineral sector of the Liberian Economy, while slave traders have been replaced by “investors” in an unsustainable win-lose economic scheme.

Liberian should Collectively remove these shortcomings so as to modernize the transactional aspect of the Liberian Mineral & Mining Economy. By so doing presents a watershed opportunity for all Liberians to jointly plant the Liberian economy on firm footing in the mineral and mining sector. These actions would in turn stabilize and increase Liberia’s wealth substantially, and this will certainly be captured in its GDP growth.

World.title: Liberia: LNP Denies Starlink Use, Clarifies Vehicle Procurement Amid Public Questions
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Liberia National Police (LNP) has clarified questions surrounding the institution’s internet connectivity and procurement of operational vehicles, rejecting claims that its facilities use Starlink internet services and distancing its vehicle purchases and internet arrangements from individuals linked to Liberia’s ongoing narcotics investigation.

In a statement issued Friday, August 21, the police said its internet services are provided through the Liberia Telecommunications Corporation (LIBTELCO/LTC Mobile) under an official institutional contract.

The clarification comes amid public inquiries and discussions concerning the resources being used by the country’s principal law enforcement institution, particularly as authorities continue a high-profile investigation into alleged narcotics trafficking.

The LNP stated that it does not use Starlink internet service at any of its facilities. “The LNP does not use Starlink internet service at any of its facilities,” the institution said, explaining that its internet connectivity is instead provided by LIBTELCO/LTC Mobile through an official agreement.

The police also addressed questions concerning its operational vehicles, confirming that it procured used vehicles from Guardian Fleet, a company based in the United States.

According to the LNP, the vehicles were acquired to strengthen the police institution’s operational capacity, particularly in the areas of mobility, patrols and emergency response.

The police said the procurement forms part of efforts to enhance its ability to respond to security needs across Liberia.

The clarification is particularly significant because public discussions surrounding the LNP’s resources have emerged against the backdrop of an ongoing investigation into an alleged narcotics trafficking network.

The LNP, however, said its official institutional records do not substantiate claims linking either the vehicle procurement or its internet services to individuals associated with the narcotics investigation.

“Official institutional records do not support claims connecting these services or vehicle procurements to individuals associated with the ongoing narcotics investigation,” the police said.

The statement did not identify the specific individuals or claims prompting the clarification, but the institution appeared to be responding directly to questions circulating publicly regarding its procurement arrangements and the source of its internet connectivity.

The police emphasized that its clarification was intended to provide the public with accurate information about the institution’s operational arrangements.

The LNP also reaffirmed its commitment to transparency and accountability, acknowledging the public’s right to seek information about the activities and resources of a national security institution.

According to the police, members of the public are entitled to ask questions about institutional expenditures, procurement decisions and operational resources. At the same time, however, the LNP urged caution in public commentary concerning matters connected to ongoing investigations.

The institution called for responsible public discussion, stressing the importance of protecting the integrity of active investigations as well as the rights of individuals involved. “The LNP respects the public’s right to seek information and remains committed to transparency and accountability,” the statement said.

The police further urged responsible public commentary that protects both the integrity of ongoing investigations and the rights of all persons concerned.

The clarification comes as the LNP and other security institutions remain under intense public scrutiny over their handling of the country’s narcotics investigation.

The investigation has generated widespread public interest, with questions being raised about the movement of suspected narcotics, individuals allegedly connected to the case and the actions of various institutions involved in the government’s response.

Against that backdrop, the LNP’s decision to publicly clarify its internet and vehicle arrangements signals an effort to distinguish its established institutional procurement and service arrangements from allegations or speculation surrounding the narcotics investigation.

The police’s reference to official institutional records suggests that it considers its procurement documentation and contractual arrangements the appropriate basis for determining whether any connection exists between its resources and individuals under investigation.

The LNP’s latest statement therefore seeks to establish a distinction between legitimate public inquiries and claims that the institution says are not supported by its official records.

World.title: Liberia: Bong Native Flomo Calls on Justice Ministry to Release Jewel Howard-Taylor to Her Lawyers
World.content:
MONROVIA — Bong County native residing in the United States, David Flomo, has called on the Ministry of Justice to release former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor into the custody of her lawyers, arguing that the government can continue its investigation into the alleged drug case while ensuring that the former vice president receives proper legal and medical attention.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Flomo made the appeal in a Facebook post amid heightened public attention surrounding Howard-Taylor’s detention and subsequent charging in connection with the government’s ongoing investigation into alleged narcotics trafficking.

“While the fight against drugs in Liberia will have no boundaries and special protections for all citizens, however, the former vice President must be treated with respect and dignity,” Flomo wrote.

He specifically urged the government to release Howard-Taylor to her lawyer and consider placing her under house arrest after she leaves the hospital.

Flomo’s call follows Howard-Taylor’s detention after she was prevented Wednesday by joint security authorities from traveling out of Liberia. The former vice president was subsequently invited by the joint security for questioning as investigators expanded their probe into the alleged drug trafficking network.

Following her appearance before investigators, Howard-Taylor was charged in connection with the ongoing investigation, bringing the former national leader directly into a case that has attracted significant public and political attention.

Howard-Taylor, a native of Sanoyea District in Bong County, has since experienced health complications while in detention and was taken for medical treatment after reportedly falling sick.

Her health condition has become an additional concern surrounding the former vice president’s detention, particularly as authorities and her legal representatives face the next stage of the proceedings.

It is against this backdrop that Flomo is asking the Ministry of Justice to reconsider the conditions under which Howard-Taylor is being held. According to Flomo, releasing her to her lawyers would not prevent the government from continuing its investigation or pursuing the charges against her. Rather, he believes such an arrangement would allow authorities to maintain the legal process while ensuring that the former vice president receives appropriate care and representation.

Flomo also questioned whether Howard-Taylor should be considered a flight risk, arguing that her status as a former senior government official means she continues to benefit from government security protection.

“She isn’t flight risk because she protected for life by government security,” he stated.

His recommendation for house arrest therefore appears to be based on the belief that authorities can maintain sufficient oversight of Howard-Taylor without keeping her in conventional detention, particularly while she is recovering from her reported illness.

The appeal comes as the government continues to defend its broader campaign against illicit drugs and its decision to investigate individuals allegedly connected to the narcotics trade, regardless of their political or social standing.

LiThe former vice president’s case has attracted heightened attention because of her previous position as Liberia’s second-highest constitutional official and her long history in national politics. Before serving as vice president, Howard-Taylor represented Bong County in the Liberian Senate.

World.title: Liberia: Golden Touch Pushes Back Against MPR/APM Investigation, Says Dukuly’s Role Was Lawful
World.content:

MONROVIA — Golden Touch Health Care LLC has mounted a strong defense of its operations and the involvement of Sekou Dukuly, rejecting what it describes as inaccurate implications contained in an investigation published by MPR News and APM Reports.

The healthcare company issued its response Friday, four days after the August 17 publication, maintaining that it has operated with a commitment to providing stable and long-term care to Minnesotans with significant medical and behavioral health needs.

Golden Touch said the report prompted the company to clarify its position, particularly concerning claims surrounding Dukuly and his relationship with the healthcare organization.

At the center of the company’s response is its rejection of the characterization that Dukuly was “moonlighting” in Minnesota while simultaneously living and working in public service in Liberia.

Golden Touch said that description was inaccurate and insisted that Dukuly’s involvement with the company was neither improper nor unlawful.

“There is nothing improper, unlawful, or fraudulent about Mr. Dukuly’s involvement with Golden Touch,” the company said.

The company did not disclose additional details about Dukuly’s specific responsibilities in its statement but maintained that his involvement with Golden Touch should not be interpreted as evidence of wrongdoing.

Golden Touch also defended the structure of its Minnesota operations, emphasizing that it works to comply with applicable assisted living laws and regulations.

According to the company, licensed assisted living directors are present in Minnesota to oversee the care and supervision provided to residents at its facilities.

The company said those arrangements are intended to ensure that residents receive the necessary care and oversight required under Minnesota regulations.

Golden Touch further highlighted its history in the healthcare sector, saying it has provided services since 2017 to residents with complex medical and behavioral health needs.

The company said its work has helped some residents progress toward greater independence, while its directors, caregivers and nurses have remained responsible for providing services throughout the year.

“Our directors, caregivers, and nurses show up 365 days a year,” Golden Touch said, adding that it stands behind their professionalism and compassion.

Alongside its defense of its operations, Golden Touch expressed sympathy to families who lost loved ones while receiving care from the company.

The statement said the company recognizes the significance of those losses and extended condolences to affected families before addressing the issues raised by the MPR/APM investigation.

Golden Touch’s response also took issue with what it described as political implications arising from the report.

The company suggested that some individuals could attempt to use the report for political purposes, but it maintained that such considerations would not change its focus on healthcare delivery.

“It is unfortunate that some may seek political gain based on the inaccurate implications made in the MPR/APM report,” the company stated.

Rather than engage in what it considers political distractions, Golden Touch said it intends to continue concentrating on its healthcare responsibilities and the people who depend on its services.

The company’s statement places particular emphasis on its commitment to Minnesota residents, arguing that its primary responsibility remains providing quality care to people with medical and behavioral health needs.

The dispute highlights the broader importance of oversight, management and compliance within residential healthcare facilities, particularly those serving residents requiring specialized support.

Golden Touch said its continued operations are guided by Minnesota’s assisted living requirements and that licensed professionals oversee care at its facilities.

Golden Touch said it will remain focused on its stated mission rather than the controversy surrounding the report. “Golden Touch will remain focused on what it has always done: providing quality care to Minnesotans in need,” the company said.

World.title: Former Liberian Goalkeeper Melvin King Reportedly Dies in Côte d’Ivoire
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Liberian goalkeeper Melvin King has reportedly died in Côte d’Ivoire, according to reports coming from the country.

King is said to have died several days ago, although details surrounding his death remain unclear at this time.

Reports indicate that the former goalkeeper’s remains are currently in Côte d’Ivoire, with local police reportedly saying that if his family cannot be located within three days, authorities may proceed with his burial.

The development has raised concerns among Liberian football followers, as efforts are reportedly being made to identify and locate King’s relatives.

Further details about his death, including the circumstances surrounding it and arrangements for the return of his remains to Liberia, are expected as more information becomes available.

More to follow as this story develops.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-VP Howard Taylor Remains Hospitalized in Police Custody as Bong Residents Rally Behind Her
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County — In the streets, communities and political circles of Bong County, the detention Wednesday of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has opened a new chapter in a political story that stretches from the civil war years to the highest office in Liberia.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected] & Webster Clayeh

For a county that once gave Howard-Taylor two consecutive mandates to represent it in the Liberian Senate, later rallied behind the political ticket that carried her to the vice presidency and watched her influence produce other elected officials, her current predicament has been met with emotions ranging from disbelief and sadness to defiance, caution and demands for evidence.

Howard-Taylor, a native of Sanoyea District, is facing serious criminal allegations following her detention at Roberts International Airport on Wednesday as she attempted to travel outside Liberia.

Her arrest has placed one of Bong County’s most recognizable political daughters at the center of an investigation the government says is aimed at dismantling an alleged transnational narcotics trafficking network.

But the reaction from Bong County shows that the case is unlikely to be viewed simply as another criminal proceeding. For many residents, Howard-Taylor’s political history has created a deep emotional connection between the former Vice President and the county she represented for 18 years.

Her supporters argue that the allegations must be proven in court. Others are questioning the circumstances surrounding her detention and demanding that the government explain the evidence linking her to the alleged drug network.

Still others say the investigation should be allowed to proceed without political interference, while insisting that Howard-Taylor, like every other accused person, deserves due process.

Howard-Taylor’s political roots are firmly planted in Sanoyea District, where her journey into national politics began to take shape. In 2005, she won election as senator of Bong County by an overwhelming margin, establishing herself as one of the county’s most powerful political figures.

Her victory was not a short-lived political moment. In 2014, she successfully returned to the Senate, winning another nine-year term and reinforcing her position as a dominant force in Bong County politics.

Her two victories meant that for 18 years she was not merely a national political figure with connections to Bong County. She was one of the principal political representatives of the county in Monrovia.

That history has become central to the current reaction. Residents who once saw Howard-Taylor travel between Gbarnga, Sanoyea and Monrovia as a senator and later as Vice President are now watching as she faces detention and criminal charges. Now, she is an accused person in a major narcotics investigation.

The Taylor Legacy and Bong County

Howard-Taylor’s political story cannot be completely separated from the political history of Charles Taylor. Her former husband, Charles Taylor, used Gbarnga as a major base during Liberia’s civil war before eventually becoming President of Liberia. The Taylor movement’s presence in Bong County left a lasting political imprint.

Gbarnga became closely identified with Charles Taylor’s political and military rise, and the Taylor name subsequently carried substantial political weight in the county.

When Howard-Taylor entered politics, that historical connection formed part of the political environment surrounding her. But over time, Howard-Taylor developed a political identity of her own.

Her two Senate victories demonstrated her ability to maintain an electoral constituency in Bong County, while her later selection as George Weah’s running mate in 2017 elevated her from county-level political prominence to national executive power. Her political journey therefore became intertwined with both the history of Bong County and the evolution of Liberia’s opposition politics.

2017 Changed Everything

The 2017 presidential election became one of the defining moments of Howard-Taylor’s political career. George Weah selected her as his running mate on the ticket of the Coalition for Democratic Change, a political alliance that included Howard-Taylor’s National Patriotic Party and the Liberia People Democratic Change. The partnership proved decisive.

In Bong County, the CDC secured victory in both rounds of the 2017 presidential election. For supporters of Howard-Taylor, the result was evidence that her political influence had survived beyond her Senate years.

The former senator had helped position herself at the center of a political movement that eventually captured Liberia’s presidency. Her influence was also reflected in the political careers of other lawmakers.

Edward Karfiah won election as representative of District Five in 2011, while Josiah Marvin Cole later won election as representative of Jorquelleh District Three. Those victories contributed to the perception that Howard-Taylor’s political network extended well beyond her own campaigns.

For years, her supporters viewed her as one of the county’s most effective political mobilizers. Her detention therefore has consequences that extend beyond one individual.

A Sudden Turn at the Airport

The latest chapter began at Roberts International Airport. Howard-Taylor was stopped from leaving Liberia and subsequently taken to the headquarters of the Liberia National Police. The action immediately generated questions among supporters and political observers.

The government, however, says the action was connected to an ongoing investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. Following investigative procedures and a review of evidence presented by the Joint National Security Investigative Team, Howard-Taylor was formally charged.

The Justice Ministry said the charges include offenses under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act of 2023, Liberia’s Penal Law and the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law.

Seven Serious Allegations

Under the Controlled Drug and Substance Act, Howard-Taylor is accused of unlicensed importation of a controlled drug or substance, unlicensed sale, trading, administration, dispensation, delivery, distribution, dispatch in transit and transportation of a controlled drug or substance, and illicit trafficking of a controlled drug or substance.

Under Chapter 10 of Liberia’s Penal Law, she faces allegations involving criminal solicitation, criminal facilitation and criminal conspiracy.

She also faces a money-laundering allegation under the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law. The government has also announced charges in absentia against three alleged members or organizers of the network: Croatian nationals Nikolai Ivancic and Mihovil Vrlovac and Ukrainian national Tara Zaderieko.

Bong County Asks for More Than Headlines

For residents like Marvelene Lepukoi, the seriousness of the allegations makes evidence even more important. Lepukoi has called

on the government to demonstrate independent evidence connecting Howard-Taylor to the alleged narcotics operation. “If Sheikh Basirou is truly the government’s star witness, then the public deserves to know exactly what independent evidence corroborates his claims,” she said.

Her position is that the case should be determined through the courts rather than public accusations. “If there is credible evidence against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, present it before the court and allow it to be properly authenticated, challenged, and tested under the law,” she said.

Lepukoi’s remarks reflect a central concern among some residents: whether the public debate surrounding the case is moving faster than the evidence that will eventually be presented in court. She insists that communication with another person, without more, does not establish participation in an alleged narcotics organization.

He said: “Bring the evidence, establish the connection, and prove the allegations beyond reasonable doubt.”

Emmanuel Weah of Gbarnga said the opposition should not allow Howard-Taylor’s detention to distract from the larger questions surrounding the country’s narcotics investigation. He argued that Liberians still need answers concerning the drug case and that the government must not use prominent political figures to divert attention from unresolved questions.

“The government must not be allowed to shift public attention away from the central questions by turning political figures into scapegoats,” Weah said. His comments reveal a suspicion among some residents that the case could become politically charged because of Howard-Taylor’s history and continuing influence.

But Archie Gboe, a Bong County native residing in Monrovia, approached the issue from a democratic perspective. “What a sad day for Liberia’s democracy,” Gboe said.

He described the repeated emergence of what he considers political witch-hunts as damaging to Liberia’s democratic culture. Although he acknowledged that nobody should be above the law, Gboe questioned the manner in which the former Vice President was stopped at the airport. For him, the government could have used established investigative procedures to request her cooperation rather than allowing the detention to occur in such circumstances.

Ebenezer Gotolo offered another perspective. Rather than immediately defending or condemning Howard-Taylor, he urged Liberians to recognize that being questioned or charged does not amount to being convicted.

“If a former Vice President is invited by the police in connection with an ongoing drug investigation, the matter should be approached through the rule of law and due process—not immediately turned into a political battle,” Gotolo said.

He emphasized that the fight against drugs should not belong to either the government or opposition. “An invitation for questioning is not the same as a declaration of guilt,” he said. Gotolo urged investigators to conduct their work professionally while protecting the rights of everyone involved.

His position may represent the middle ground emerging from the county: support the investigation, but do not abandon due process. Among the strongest reactions has come from Howard-Taylor’s home district.

David Gorlormator, a native of Sanoyea District, questioned the circumstances of the former Vice President’s detention. He asked why Howard-Taylor was allegedly not formally invited before being stopped at Roberts International Airport.

He also questioned the government’s broader handling of the drug investigation and whether all individuals alleged to have connections to the case are being treated equally. For Gorlormator and others, the government must demonstrate that its investigation is not influenced by political considerations.

Dr. George Toto, a native of Totota now living in the United States, responded to the allegations from a deeply personal perspective. Toto said he feels ashamed as a son of Bong County hearing allegations of such magnitude involving a daughter of the county.

For a county that has celebrated Howard-Taylor’s political accomplishments for years, the allegations have created a difficult moment. Residents are now being forced to reconcile the image of the powerful political figure they know with the allegations being brought against her by the state.

Victor Tokpah, a Gbarnga resident and Bong County native, said the government’s announcement has raised questions that should be answered through the legal process. Tokpah said he was neither defending Howard-Taylor nor suggesting that she should be exempt from the law.

He asked what specific drug, quantity, transaction, agreement or alleged proceeds form the basis of the charges. He also questioned whether the case involving Howard-Taylor is directly connected to the approximately US$317 million cocaine investigation or whether that connection is being assumed because the developments emerged around the same period.

Howard-Taylor hospitalized

On Thursday, Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor was rushed to GIMS Hospital in Sophie, Monrovia, after experiencing a medical emergency while in police custody.

Taylor was transported to the medical facility Thursday evening under heavy police escort after health practitioners reportedly observed a significant rise in her blood pressure.

The medical emergency occurred as authorities were preparing to transfer the former vice president to the Monrovia City Court, where she was expected to face proceedings stemming from allegations of drug trafficking and money laundering.

Medical personnel were called to the Liberia National Police Headquarters after concerns were raised about Taylor’s condition.

At the Gomez Institute of Medical Science hospital in Sophie Community, scores of individuals especially from the CDC along with her legal team visited the former Vice President.

Former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwel Saah Kemayah went to the hospital a visit former Vice President Taylor. While Kemayah was allowed entry, three lawmakers were denied.

Frank Saah Foko, Marvin Cole, and Eugine Kollie were prevented from entering the fence of the hospital. “I don’t know the reason for which they are denying me other people went and the police have them assets. But it is ok, at the appropriate time we will have asset,” Montserrado County District 9 Representative Foko said.

He added: “We are to make sure that transparency takes place, that is all we are asking for. We are also asking the citizens of Bong County to be on their alert, to remain peaceful, democratic. The strongest person is the law. We are going to invade the laws; it is our hope that all uphold the dignity of the law.”

While at the Hospital, her legal team issued a statement that it has requested additional time to gather information it says it needed to support the ongoing investigation involving the former vice president.

In the brief statement issued Thursday, August 20, Taylor’s lawyers said she remains at Police Headquarters while they seek additional time to prepare and gather information in connection with the investigation.

“Let it be known that the Former Vice President remains at the Police Headquarters as her counsels have requested additional time to gather information in support of the ongoing investigation,” the legal team said.

World.title: Liberia: First Group of 20 Third-Country Deportees Arrive In Liberia, Secretly Whisked From RIA as Five Reportedly Refuse Disembarked Plane
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia’s controversial deportation arrangement with the United States took effect Thursday with the arrival of the first 20 third-country deportees at Roberts International Airport, but the transfer was overshadowed by a dramatic standoff after five of the deportees reportedly refused to leave the aircraft and were restrained by U.S. federal agents.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The five men were among the 20 deportees flown to Liberia under an agreement between the Liberian government and the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump that could see as many as 1,200 third-country nationals sent to Liberia over the next 12 months.

According to The New York Times, the five men resisted efforts by American federal agents to remove them from the aircraft after it landed at Roberts International Airport.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes and eventually forced them off the plane. However, the five were subsequently returned to the aircraft.

The men were reportedly later flown onward to Equatorial Guinea, although the circumstances surrounding their reported transfer remain unclear.

The Liberian government has not publicly explained what happened to the five men, whether they were formally admitted into Liberia, or why they were reportedly flown to another African country.

Neither Liberian nor U.S. authorities had, as of publication, provided a detailed public account of the incident.

The episode has intensified questions about the implementation of the deportation agreement, including the legal status of the deportees, their consent or otherwise to being transferred to Liberia, and what happens when individuals refuse to disembark.

Five Refuse to Deplane

The confrontation reportedly began after the aircraft carrying the 20 deportees landed at RIA.

According to The New York Times, five men refused to leave the plane when U.S. federal agents attempted to remove them.

The agents reportedly restrained the men for several minutes before forcing them off the aircraft. The five were later returned to the plane, according to the report.

Their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea has raised additional questions about whether Liberia was ultimately their intended destination and whether other countries are involved in the implementation of the U.S. third-country deportation arrangement.

The Liberian government has yet to provide an official explanation.

Deportees Secretly Moved from RIA

The drama surrounding the five deportees unfolded against a backdrop of secrecy surrounding the arrival of the 20-person group.

Airport and state security personnel restricted journalists from accessing the arrival area and prevented local and international media organizations.

including AFP and DW, from observing the deportees’ processing.

According to a FrontPage Africa reporter at the scene, security officers ordered doors closed and were deployed at entry points, restricting movement in and out of the area.

Journalists later discovered that the deportees had already been moved from the airport without media access to their departure.

The group was reportedly transported from the airport in a bus operated by the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission through a back exit, rather than through the main arrival hall.

No interviews were permitted, and journalists were unable to obtain photographs or video footage of the deportees.

The manner in which the group was moved out of RIA has fueled criticism over the government’s handling of the arrangement and its commitment to transparency.

LRRRC Tight-Lipped

Officials of the LRRRC, the government agency responsible for receiving the deportees, declined to provide details about the group at the airport.

Staff referred questions to the commission’s headquarters in Montserrado County but did not provide information about the identities, nationalities or immediate plans for the 20 deportees.

The government had previously stated that the deportees would include nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries, with most expected to come from Latin American countries, including Venezuela, Cuba and Colombia.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah has said the deportees would be received “as guests” and would have the option to apply for asylum in Liberia.

Secretive Arrival Sparks Youth Anger

The secrecy surrounding the arrival has also triggered frustration among some Liberian youths, who argue that the government should prioritize addressing domestic unemployment and poverty before accepting deportees from other countries.

Youth advocate Levi Levala told FrontPage Africa that Liberia is already struggling with unemployment and inadequate social services.

“We, the youth in this country, have nothing right now. No job. No support. And now these people are being brought here? They say America will sponsor them, but Liberia is already suffering. This is not the partnership we need,” Levala said.

“My message to America is: take them back. Liberia is not a dump site,” he added.

Levala and other residents of Unification Town argued that Liberia’s economic challenges make the country ill-equipped to accommodate large numbers of third-country deportees.

How the Deal Came About

The Liberian government announced earlier this week that it had agreed to accept up to 1,200 people deported from the United States who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

The government has described the arrangement as “entirely humanitarian” and not a “quid pro quo,” while acknowledging that Liberia will receive U.S. support to manage the program.

The Ministry of Justice has not disclosed when the next group of deportees will arrive, although the government expects the full group of up to 1,200 to be accommodated over a 12-month period.

Rights Groups Demand Answers

The agreement has generated growing concern among human-rights advocates in Liberia and elsewhere in Africa, particularly over the prospect of countries accepting deportees who have no meaningful connection to them.

Liberian human-rights lawyer and activist Adama Dempster said the government must answer fundamental questions about the arrangement.

“The issue of deportations is raising many concerns that can’t be left unanswered,” Dempster said.

“What conditions will they be held in?” he asked, while questioning other aspects of the agreement.

The identities and backgrounds of the 20 deportees have not been publicly disclosed, making it unclear whether any have criminal records in the United States.

The lack of information has intensified calls for the Liberian government to publish the agreement and explain the legal framework governing the deportees’ arrival, stay and possible departure from Liberia.

A New Test for Liberia

Thursday’s events have placed the Boakai administration under renewed scrutiny over an agreement officials have defended as being in Liberia’s national interest.

But the refusal of five deportees to leave the aircraft — followed by their reported onward flight to Equatorial Guinea — has raised fresh questions about the humanitarian, legal and diplomatic dimensions of the arrangement.

It also remains unclear whether Liberia is simply the destination for the deportees or whether the agreement forms part of a broader U.S. arrangement involving multiple African countries.

As Liberia prepares for potentially hundreds more arrivals, pressure is mounting on the government to disclose the terms of the agreement, explain the treatment of the first 20 deportees and provide a full account of what happened to the five men who refused to disembark at Roberts International Airport.

World.title: Kalumba alleges UPND plot to arrest him for treason as party, police deny knowledge
World.content:
Kalumba alleges UPND plot to arrest him for treason as party, police deny knowledge

Former home affairs minister Katele Kalumba says he has uncovered a scheme by United Party for National Development officials to have him arrested and charged with treason, an allegation both the ruling party and police say they know nothing about.

Kalumba told journalists that he had received information suggesting instructions had already been issued for his arrest, and that his name had been linked, alongside that of former intelligence chief Xavier Chungu, to claims of plotting a coup d’état. He dismissed the suggestion outright, saying it defied both logic and his own political history.

“It is extremely annoying that people want to accuse me and individuals like former intelligence chief Xavier Chungu of plotting a coup d’état,” Kalumba said. “My name has come up that we were trying to plot a coup, which to me is actually nonsense.”

He accused the current administration of running what he described as a witch-hunt aimed at silencing critical voices, and challenged law enforcement agencies to produce evidence for any claims that he had been involved in militia activity. He said investigators should be prepared to prove, rather than simply assert, that offensive weapons had been found or that anything untoward had taken place.

Kalumba pointed to his own record with the ruling party as evidence against the allegations, noting that he had previously supported UPND in Chienge and had contributed financially to the party. He said it was upsetting that his name and Chungu’s were now being associated with illegality after that history of support.

UPND media director Mark Simuuwe, when contacted for comment, said the party had no knowledge of any such plot. He said the investigation and apprehension of lawbreakers fell squarely within the mandate of law enforcement agencies rather than the party itself.

“As UPND, we are not aware of such an activity because, as you are aware, such undertakings are being conducted by law enforcement agencies and not the party,” Simuuwe said.

Zambia Police Service deputy public relations officer Chipo Kaitisha gave a similarly cautious response when asked about Kalumba’s claims, saying her office had no knowledge of any scheme to arrest or detain him, though she said she would look into the matter further.

“I am not aware of any plot to arrest Dr Kalumba. But I will find out,” Kaitisha said.

The allegation surfaces at a moment when concerns over the treatment of opposition and other political figures are already running high. Eleven people arrested in connection with a security operation at opposition leader Brian Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence face treason charges that carry no possibility of bail, while Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu remain at United Nations premises in Lusaka after being summoned for questioning rather than formally charged.

Against that backdrop, the Apostles Council of Churches in Zambia has urged government to extend a hand of reconciliation to achieve national unity and healing following the election. Separately, Apostle Zulu has warned that continued arrests and police summonses of opposition-linked figures risk deepening division rather than promoting the national healing political leaders say they want.

Kalumba’s allegation cannot currently be verified independently, and neither UPND nor police have confirmed any arrest plan or investigation targeting him. Whether the claim develops into a formal case, or fades as an unconfirmed rumour, will likely depend on whether either side produces evidence to support their respective positions in the days ahead.

World.title: Commonwealth demands end to arbitrary arrests as it condemns Kabulonga killing
World.content:
Commonwealth demands end to arbitrary arrests as it condemns Kabulonga killing

The Commonwealth has called on President Hakainde Hichilema’s government to halt arbitrary arrests and release all persons detained for political reasons since the 13 August election, in one of the strongest international rebukes Zambia has faced since the disputed vote.

Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said in a statement issued from London that the Commonwealth was dismayed by the security operation carried out in Kabulonga, Lusaka, in which a police officer was injured and former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya lost his life. She called for a transparent investigation into the incident and urged all parties to exercise restraint.

“The Commonwealth expresses concern at the post-election situation in Zambia and urges full respect for the rights of all persons and for the rule of law, in conformity with the Commonwealth Charter and values,” Botchwey said.

She went further, extending condolences to Kafwaya’s family and wishing the injured officer a swift recovery, while calling for constructive dialogue to de-escalate tensions and safeguard peace and stability in the country.

The intervention places the Commonwealth alongside a growing list of international bodies that have raised concerns over Zambia’s post-election conduct. The United Nations Human Rights Commission, Amnesty International, and observer missions from SADC, the European Union, COMESA and the Great Lakes Region have all condemned aspects of the crackdown that followed the vote.

The security operation at the centre of the criticism took place at the Kabulonga residence of opposition leader Brian Mundubile the day after the election. Government says the raid targeted a suspected militia cell and that officers came under fire from occupants of the property. Kafwaya, a former minister of transport and communications, was shot and killed during the operation.

Mundubile has given a different account, saying he witnessed Kafwaya shot at close range and that the killing has stained Zambia’s democratic credentials. He has also accused the Electoral Commission of Zambia of aiding Hichilema’s victory and has alleged that the military was unleashed on ordinary citizens to help manage the election outcome, allegations government has not directly addressed.

Hichilema, for his part, has accused Mundubile of running a militia together with retired Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, lawyer and former Law Association of Zambia president George Chisanga, Kafwaya, and a Lusaka businessman. Mundubile has dismissed the militia claims as a ruse designed to discredit him ahead of his planned legal challenge.

Eleven people found at the Kabulonga property that night have since been charged with treason-related offences, charges that carry no possibility of bail under Zambian law. Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu have not been charged themselves but have been summoned for questioning over alleged links to national security threats, and are currently staying at United Nations premises in Lusaka rather than returning home.

It is against this backdrop that the Commonwealth’s statement lands with particular weight. Unlike earlier expressions of concern from human rights bodies, the Commonwealth speaks for an association of 56 member states with historical and institutional ties to Zambia, and its language, invoking the Commonwealth Charter directly, signals that Lusaka’s handling of the post-election period is now being measured against standards the country has formally signed up to uphold.

Government has not yet issued a detailed public response to Botchwey’s statement. State House has previously rejected broader allegations of arbitrary arrests, with communication specialist Clayson Hamasaka describing the post-election security operations as lawful investigations rather than a campaign against the opposition, and citing reports of high-grade weapons, alleged mercenary-style training and threats against the Head of State as grounds for the crackdown.

Mundubile is expected to file his Constitutional Court challenge to the presidential result within the seven-day window prescribed by the Constitution, a deadline that falls in the coming days. The Commonwealth’s call for dialogue and restraint, rather than confrontation, will now sit alongside that legal process as Zambia works out how to move from a disputed election toward a settled outcome.

For the family of Kafwaya, the immediate concern remains simpler than the wider diplomatic and legal manoeuvring: an independent, transparent account of what happened at Kabulonga, and confirmation that whoever gave the orders that night will be held to answer for them.

World.title: Kasonde drops citizen election petition as Zambia enters decisive post-poll week
World.content:
Kasonde drops citizen election petition as Zambia enters decisive post-poll week

Zambia begins a new week with one proposed challenge to the August general election now abandoned, while the country waits to see whether Brian Mundubile will proceed with his separate presidential petition.

Prominent lawyer and civil society advocate Linda Kasonde, who had been exploring a citizen-led challenge to the election, has told stakeholders that efforts to build the case have ended because sufficient evidence could not be assembled within the required period.

“It appears that we do not have enough evidence to proceed with the petition challenging the just ended general elections as all efforts to get the Petition off the ground have not succeeded,” Kasonde said in a communication circulated among stakeholders.

Her withdrawal matters because concerns over the election have not gone away. The EU Election Observation Mission reported weaknesses in parts of the results tabulation process, while the Christian Churches Monitoring Group has identified statistical discrepancies in 30 constituencies and called for greater transparency from the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

CCMG has been careful to draw a line under how far those findings go. The group has said the discrepancies it identified do not change the overall winner of the presidential election, even as it presses ECZ to release the underlying polling-station records for independent verification.

Kasonde is now redirecting her energy from overturning the election to the framework that governs future ones.

“Going forward, we hope to shift our focus towards electoral reform challenging decisions, measures and laws taken in the run-up to the August 2026 election,” she said.

Attention now returns to Mundubile. He has rejected the presidential result and has previously said his team gathered evidence for a Constitutional Court challenge. His position has increasingly diverged from figures within the political structure that backed his candidature. Ezra Tembo, NRPUP president, has accepted President-elect Hakainde Hichilema’s victory, while Tonse founder and secretary-general Chris Zumani Zimba has said he will not support a petition.

The clock is running regardless of that internal split. Hichilema was declared president-elect on 18 August after securing 2,965,326 votes against Mundubile’s 1,856,217, a margin of 1,109,109. On the constitutional timetable being applied, the seven-day window for challenging the presidential election expires on Tuesday, 25 August.

A separate but related story is playing out away from the courts. Police have summoned Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu for questioning over alleged links to activities authorities say concern national security. Both men have been staying at the premises of an international organisation in Lusaka. Neither has been convicted of any offence, and Mundubile has firmly rejected government claims linking his camp to an alleged militia.

The new week therefore opens with Zambia edging closer to a political and constitutional resolution, even as key questions remain unsettled. Kasonde’s proposed petition is off the table, and her focus has already shifted to longer-term reform. Mundubile’s challenge, by contrast, remains only an intention until it is formally filed, and the security investigation around him continues in parallel.

Tuesday now stands as the date that decides which of two paths Zambia takes next: another court battle over the presidency, or a final, uncontested road toward Hichilema’s inauguration.
