World.title: GOP lawmakers criticize Trump’s beef import plan amid blowback from ranchers
World.content:
House and Senate Republicans on Friday criticized President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend tariffs on ground beef imports, with lawmakers from agricultural states decrying the impact Trump’s decision will have on farmers.

Nebraska’s GOP senators, Deb Fischer and Pete Ricketts, said in separate posts on X that Trump’s decision was unwise.

“I’m extremely disappointed by this decision from the White House,” Fischer wrote. “We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers. Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry.”

Ricketts wrote: “I appreciate the Administration’s work to lower grocery prices. Short term policy shifts do not equal long term solutions. Flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers.”

The president announced Friday on Truth Social that “the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff. We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

Beef prices have gone up in recent years, in part due to reduced domestic supply. Al Drago / Getty Images

Trump did not say which companies that import beef had agreed to this commitment or what countries would supply the meat.

Explaining his decision, the president pledged that this deal “will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., also cited the hardships American cattle farmers would face as a result of the president’s decision and referred to conversations he’s had with Trump about this issue.

“The President’s heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people, and beef prices have been impacted by the Mexican screwworm,” Sheehy wrote on X. “But the reality is this action will make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down for the American people. And most importantly, this will harm our ranching families who feed the nation.”

Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is running for Senate and received Trump’s endorsement in the race, also panned his announcement, writing in a post on X, “I want to lower prices but this is a bad idea.”

Hinson said that instead of allowing beef imports without tariffs, “We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production, and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers.”

Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, writing in his custom shorthand on X, also expressed concern about Trump’s announcement, writing that “USA cattlemen shld always be put 1st thru America 1st policies.”

Grassley also expressed a “need 2keep up progress fighting screwworm+ expanding domestic herd.”

On Friday, the president defended his decision when asked at Joint Base Andrews about the criticism he was facing from fellow Republicans.

“Well, we want to get the beef prices down, so we’ll get them down a little bit, and that’s what people want. That’s what the voters want, and that’s what I want,” he told reporters. “The ranchers are great. They’re my people. I love the ranchers. They’ve done a fantastic job, but they admit that we need a little help, and in order to get the prices down, so that’s what we’re doing.”

The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on the lawmakers’ criticisms of Trump’s plan.

U.S. cattle ranchers have faced headwinds for years that have sent beef prices higher, including shrinking supply. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation, the United States’ current cattle herd is the nation’s smallest since 1951.

A flesh-eating screwworm that targets cattle was also detected in the U.S. earlier this year for the first time in decades, further threatening cattle herds.

Trump first floated the idea of lowering imports on beef last year, but the notion was quickly shot down by a similar group of GOP senators from agricultural states.

“I represent a beef-producing state. We have four times as many cattle as people,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said at the time, explaining his opposition.

On Friday, leaders for a top industry group representing cattle farmers, the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, also said they were “disappointed” with Trump’s announcement.

“NCBA is disappointed by the President’s statement,” said Colin Woodall, the group’s chief executive officer. “While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd.”

“Today’s announcement and other market interventions throw cold water on the prospect of herd expansion and sacrifices long-term stability for short term messaging,” Woodall added.

World.title: This is what you need (and need to do) to stay safe this hurricane season
World.content:
As a Florida native, I’ve endured a lot of hurricanes and I’ve seen the damage they can cause. If you don’t take proper precautions, the destruction hurricanes leave behind can be catastrophic. This is why it’s important to know how to prepare for a hurricane, and make sure you have all of the supplies necessary to keep you and your family safe. Storms have already started making their way across the United States, with tropical storm Lala impacting Hawaii earlier this week. Plus, a potentially record-breaking El Niño is growing in the Pacific ocean, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Power outages, flooding, broken windows and damage to homes and cars from fallen trees are just some of the things you need to be ready for. And while you may have a generator in case the electricity goes out, it’s important that you know how to use it properly to avoid carbon monoxide exposure.

I talked to a meteorologist and professor at the University of Florida to learn what measures you should take to make sure your home withstands a storm, and the best emergency kits and other supplies you should always have handy during hurricane season.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

How to prepare for a hurricane

There are many different ways to prepare your home ahead of a hurricane to prevent damage, and to keep everyone safe, particularly in the event that you lose power during and after the storm.

“If you live by the coast, you should be thinking about storm surge, rainfall, and wind speed,” says Stephen Mullens, a meteorologist and assistant instructional professor of meteorology at the University of Florida’s Department of Geography. “Most fatalities and property damage comes from flooding as a result of both storm surge (water that has been moved from the ocean onto land) and from too much rain during the storm.”

The below preparedness tips are key for dealing with common problems during a hurricane, including flooding, power outages, broken windows from strong winds and fallen trees.

Watch for an evacuation warning: “If you are by the coast, look up whether you are in an evacuation zone,” says Mullens. “If you must evacuate during a storm, you only need to travel just outside the evacuation zone.” State government officials will traditionally issue evacuation warnings at least a few days ahead of a hurricane if not more, depending on what category the storm falls under. Be sure to stay on top of news updates. “You will need to leave before the wind and rain arrives, so your home preparations must happen with a deadline in mind,” says Mullens.

Prepare for flooding: Flooding is not only dangerous and a threat to your safety, but it can also cause irreparable damage to your home, which, even with insurance, can be extremely costly to deal with. Mullens recommends using things like sandbags to blockade your home if possible. “These can help prevent water from seeping under [home] doors and garage doors. Most of the time, you won’t experience the worst-case scenario, and sandbags can really help when flooding is only a few inches,” says Mullens. “No amount of [sandbags] will allow you to stay in an evacuation zone [though]. If flooding is forecast to be more than a foot, then plan to evacuate in case the forecast gets worse or your emergency management deems evacuation to be mandatory.”

Mullens also recommends preparing other areas around your home for excess water, too. “Outside your home, clear your gutters and drainage areas of leaves and other debris,” he says. “You don’t want water backing up and pooling in ways you don’t expect.” If your home does get flooded, there is a very short window of time before it will cause mold growth and become a pain to handle, according to Mullens. “It’s a race against time to prevent the build up of mold in drywall and furniture. If your roof has been damaged, a large tarp will prevent future rain from entering your home,” he says. “Inside, fans and a lot of towels will help dry things out.”

Prepare for strong winds: “To prepare for wind, trim branches on trees and bushes so they won’t hit the house. Bring furniture and outdoor decorations inside,” says Mullens. “For large items, stake and tie them down or they will likely fly away. If you live near the coast, nailing plywood over your windows can prevent damage inside your home from flying debris.” Additionally, make sure your cars aren’t beside trees, especially ones with coconuts or large branches that could fall during the hurricane and damage the body, windows or windshields.

Keep electronics charged: Make sure all your electronics are charged before the storm arrives and be sure to stock up on batteries as needed for things like flashlights and other essential devices. “Charge phones while power remains,” says Mullens. “Write down important information in case your phone’s battery runs out before power is restored.” Depending on the severity of the storm, a power outage is very likely, even if it’s just temporary.

Gas generators are one of the most common appliances that people use to restore power in their homes during and after hurricanes, according to Mullens. If you don’t have or plan on using a generator, there are alternatives you can consider, too. Some batteries work for home appliances, not just small handheld electronic devices, according to Mullens. “Today, large batteries can power an air conditioner, well pump, refrigerator, oven, or microwave for several hours,” says Mullens. “It’s important to assess what you most want to have power during an extended power outage, your ability to store the unit when you don’t need it, and cost to guide your purchases.”

Prepare for a disruption in water supply: A loss in access to clean water is also a common issue during and after a hurricane, so it’s important to make sure you have a plan in case you don’t have water for a few days. “Buy large water jugs for drinking and sanitation. Fill them with water prior to a storm,” says Mullens. “You can also fill a bath tub with water so you can flush your toilets. Most storms won’t be the worst-case scenario, but if it does happen you will want enough water for drinking and food for seven days.”

Buy non-perishable foods: Since losing power is common during and after hurricanes, you won’t have access to traditional kitchen appliances like a refrigerator to keep food fresh, an electric stovetop and oven or microwave, unless you find batteries or power stations suitable for powering them. Be sure to buy shelf-stable foods that don’t require cooking or refrigeration after opening, including canned vegetables and soup, cereal, granola bars, chips and crackers. “All these items can be stored at room temperature for a year unless otherwise noted,” says Mullens. “In the summer, before hurricane season, purchase one to two of these items each shopping trip instead of right before a storm.”

Your hurricane supply list

All of the products below are either recommendations from our experts, NBC Selected staff and/or highly-rated on Amazon and other retailers.

The Jackery Explorer is a large portable power station, similar to a portable power bank you’d use to charge your phone, except it has the ability to juice up home appliances like electric grills and portable air conditioners — though you can also use it to charge a phone. In addition to multiple USB-C ports and a USB-A port, it has three AC wall outlets (the same type you’d use to charge the power station itself), which are suitable for charging kitchen appliances like air fryers and mini fridges for example.

It’s available in versions with higher wattages and ones that come with solar panels to charge the power station. It also has a companion app that allows you to track how much battery it has left and adjust settings like the energy saving mode from your phone.

Brio 5-Gallon Plastic Water Container $ 41.03 Amazon What to know What we like BPA-free

Has a handle

Made of strong plastic Something to note Lids sold separately

To make it easier to store several gallons of fresh water ahead of a hurricane, get 5-gallon jugs like this, which is made of strong BPA-free, polycarbonate plastic. It has a handle on the side for carrying and lifting. Note that it doesn’t come with a lid, so be sure to buy caps along with the jugs.

You can get these 50-pound capacity sandbags in sets of 10 or more. They’re made from strong polypropylene material to protect your home against flooding when placed around the area properly. Each bag comes with a tie to keep the sand inside and is 14 by 26 inches, so it’s tall enough to block a few inches of water. When you’re not using them for hurricane preparedness, the bags can help weigh down tents, trucks, trailers, and awnings, according to the brand.

Shoppers say that the ties on the sandbags do a great job of keeping them closed and that they last at least a few years. Just keep in mind that the bags are not pre-filled, so you will need to purchase sand for them.

This set of batteries from Energizer comes with 24 AA batteries and 24 AAA batteries, all which have a shelf life of up to 10 years, according to the brand. The leak-resistant batteries are suitable for small handheld devices like flashlights, remotes, toys and more. These are also the typical sizes for devices like smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, which are useful, particularly if you plan on using a gas generator when the power goes out.

Thriaid 330-Piece First Aid Kit $ 45.99 Amazon What to know What we like Has handles for carrying

Waterproof

Comes with a handbook Something to note Has a soft-shell design

While a first aid kit is something everyone should have in their home for any and all situations, you should definitely have one ahead of a hurricane. This kit has more than 300 pieces, including several sets of adhesive bandages in multiple sizes and shapes, wound closure strips, gloves, an emergency blanket, a pill box, gauze, wipes and a thermometer.

The kit comes in a rectangular, waterproof bag with a zipper closure and handles for easy carrying. It’s small and weighs less than 2 pounds, so it fits in some glove compartments and backpacks. Its compact size and take-anywhere design is a standout for people who bought it.

In addition to flashlights, you should consider getting a set of bright lanterns to help keep your home illuminated if you lose power during a hurricane. These water-resistant lanterns have strong, 154-lumen LED lights and stand up on their own. They also have handles for carrying that are also suitable for attaching to a belt loop or a loop on a backpack in case you need your hands for something else (they’re also great for camping trips).

The lights come with a set of 12 AA alkaline batteries and each lantern requires three batteries. You can also adjust the brightness of each lantern just by lowering the top of it.

Midland Emergency Crank Weather AM/FM Radio $ 79.99 Amazon What to know What we like Comes with batteries

Has a siren

Has a flashlight Something to note Small

In addition to making sure your phone is charged, you’ll want to have some sort of communication device that you can use during a hurricane, like this crank radio from Midland. The device is around the size of a modern portable speaker, but you can use it to communicate with emergency responders by turning the crank on the side. It’s connected to emergency radio channels so you can stay aware of weather updates, including from the NOAA, according to the brand.

It has a flashlight and tactile (not digital) buttons that adjust the volume and change the channel. Plus, it has an antenna and an automatic siren that turns on to let you know when severe weather is coming, according to the brand.

Frequently asked questions How do you stay safe during a hurricane? It’s extremely important to not wait until the last minute to buy emergency hurricane supplies, since options will be very limited. Be sure to prepare for the most common problems, like flooding, lack of access to fresh water (including for your toilet), fallen trees and branches and power outages, says Mullens. You can do this by buying things like non-perishable foods, bottled water or gallons of water, medication, power stations and making sure your electronics (including your phone) are fully charged. What should you stock up on before a hurricane? Since hurricanes often lead to power outages, you should stock up on things that being without power would affect, Mullens. This includes getting multi-gallon water jugs from stores like Home Depot, Lowe’s or Amazon so you can keep a large supply of water. You should also buy non-perishable foods that don’t have to be refrigerated, including canned foods and dry pantry items. Lastly, you should also stock up on energy by charging all of your portable devices, including a portable power station, and have enough batteries for emergency devices like flashlights. Do you have to worry about hurricanes if you don’t live on a coast? Yes. While hurricanes are definitely a threat to coastlines, areas far from coasts aren’t exempt from experiencing their effects. Additionally, trailers and mobile homes are particularly vulnerable to damage from hurricanes, according to Mullens. "Trailers and mobile homes are lighter and more likely to be damaged than homes built on a foundation. Thinner walls mean debris thrown in the wind are more likely to damage walls and windows,” says Mullens. “Being lighter means wind and flood water is more likely to lift the home off its supports. There may be less to do inside and outside to prepare the home itself, but you will likely need to evacuate earlier than recommended.” How do you use a generator safely during a hurricane? While generators are a great appliance when it comes to providing a lot of power during a hurricane, they also can be dangerous when used improperly because they can expose you to carbon monoxide, according to Mullens. "If you are using a gas-powered generator, the unit must be placed outside with cords running from the generator into the house. It is very common for people to operate generators indoors or in a garage, resulting in the resident dying due to a build-up of carbon monoxide,” he says. “If you are using a large battery, you may want to incorporate solar panels or another method to recharge it in case of an extended outage.”

Meet our hurricane expert

At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

Stephen Mullens is an assistant instructional professor of meteorology at the University of Florida’s Department of Geography.

Why trust NBC Selected?

I’m a commerce editor at NBC Selected, where I write about home, cleaning and kitchen appliances. I also write about storage and organization, wellness and home renovations. For this story, I talked to a meteorology expert for their guidance. I’m also a Florida native who has experienced and prepared for several hurricanes.

World.title: This is the dorm registry I wish I had as a college freshman
World.content:
When I moved into my college dorm as a freshman, I remember wishing there was a simple way to send friends and family a list of everything I still needed — similar to the registries people create for weddings and baby showers. Between bedding, storage, laundry supplies, toiletries and all the little things I didn’t realize I’d need until move-in day, the shopping added up quickly. I wanted a way to make a cohesive list that everyone could shop while avoiding bad communication that resulted in duplicates and deficits.

Since then, I’ve led the back-to-school shopping for my family. I handled my own college shopping and helped my brother, who’s now a senior in college, with his move in. Next up is my sister, who’s a senior in high school, and I’m already thinking about what she’ll need when it’s her turn to move into a dorm. This time, though, I’m making a registry.

A dorm registry can serve two purposes: It keeps your college shopping organized in one place, and it gives friends and family who want to support you an easy way to buy something you’ll actually use. Most if not all retailers keep track of what requests have been fulfilled so there won’t be any duplicate purchases and, depending on the retailer, you may also be able to have items shipped or picked up at a store near your college, which can be particularly helpful if you’re moving far from home or need to fly to school.

As someone who worked for her campus Residential Life office throughout all four years of college and helped support countless move ins and move outs, I know which dorm essentials students actually use (and which ones they probably don’t need). So below, I’ve rounded up places where you can create a dorm registry or shareable wishlist, along with the essentials I’d recommend adding before move-in day.

Pictured here is an ancient photo of me and my suitemate on move-in day, freshman year of college. I was 18 with an overpacked car, adult braces and a dream. Courtesy Jem Alabi

Want more from NBC Selected? 

Where can you make a dorm registry?

Not every retailer offers a dedicated dorm registry, but that doesn’t mean you can’t make one. Many stores offer shareable wishlists that accomplish essentially the same thing: You can add the dorm essentials you need, send the list to friends and family and keep everything organized in one place. Below are the retailers I recommend for creating a dorm registry or wishlist, including options that offer shipping or pickup near campus.Note that all these retailers require an account, but the wishlist creation tools are free.

Amazon $ 0.00 Amazon What to know Why I like it for college: Amazon is probably one of the easiest options for a dorm registry because you can put a wide variety of dorm essentials (bedding, storage, school supplies, tech accessories, toiletries and more) in one place. You can also assign priorities to items, which I like for distinguishing between the things you need before move-in and the things that would simply be nice to have.

Amazon doesn’t have a registry specifically for dorm rooms, but you can create a Gift List or Wish List and use it like one. To make a Gift List, go to Amazon’s Registry & Gifting page, select “Create” and choose the occasion you’re celebrating; you can also create a List through “Account & Lists” or directly from a product page. Once it’s set up, add dorm essentials as you shop.

How friends and family shop it: You can make an Amazon Gift List public and searchable or keep it shareable and send the link directly to who you want to have it. Amazon also tracks purchases, which helps prevent loved ones from buying the same items.

Shipping/pickup: You can assign a shipping address to an Amazon List, which makes this particularly useful if you want gifts sent to the address you’ll use while at college or mail room once your mailing ID is assigned. Items can be sent directly to your home address which is nice if you want to have safely, securely packaged boxes ready to go for move-in day.

Target $ 0.00 Target What to know Why I like it for college: Target has nearly everything you might need for a dorm, but its large store footprint is what makes it particularly convenient. If you’re attending college away from home, you can shop before you leave and potentially pick up things closer to school instead of packing every pillow, storage bin and bottle of detergent into the car. Target has almost 2,000 locations across the U.S.

Target is one of my favorite options for this because it actually offers a College Wish List specifically designed for school planning. You can create one on Target.com or in the Target app, then add products online or by scanning items in a Target store. Target also offers college-focused checklists to help you figure out what you might be missing.

How friends and family shop it: You can send friends and family a direct link — including a customized URL — or make your list searchable on target.com and in Target stores. When someone buys an item directly through the list, Target updates it to help keep track of what’s already been purchased.

Shipping/pickup: This is where I think Target really shines for college students. Gifts can be shipped to the address attached to your list, and shoppers can also purchase registry and wishlist items online for order pickup. Target also offers drive-up pickup and same day delivery, depending on the order and location.

Walmart $ 0.00 Walmart What to know Why I like it for college: Walmart is especially useful for the less exciting dorm purchases that are just as important as your bedding and decor — think cleaning products, toiletries, laundry supplies, snacks and class supplies. Its pickup option also makes it useful for replenishing essentials once you’re already on campus.

For dorm shopping, I’d recommend creating a Walmart Wishlist. Walmart says its former “Any Occasion” registries are now wishlists, which can be created on walmart.com or in the Walmart app by going to lists under the “My Items” tab, and then “Create a Wishlist.” You can add products online, through the app or even in store by scanning a product’s barcode.

How friends and family shop it: Once you’ve created your wishlist, you can share it via a copied URL, email or social media. Unlike Walmart’s traditional gift registries, wishlists aren’t searchable by friends and family, so you’ll need to send them the link. Gift givers can purchase products, mark them as purchased and have eligible items shipped directly to you.

Shipping/pickup: Walmart offers both shipping and local pickup/delivery services, although fulfillment options depend on the product and location. For pickup orders, you select a local store and time slot and Walmart notifies you when the order is ready.

Dormify $ 0.00 Dormify What to know Why I like it for college: Dormify takes a lot of the guesswork out of college shopping because you aren’t sorting through products intended for an entire house. The site is centered on dorm-friendly categories and features an extensive checklist for students that helps structure shopping plan — including twin XL bedding, storage and organization, bath and laundry, lighting and no-nails decor — so it’s a particularly good option for first-year students furnishing their space for the first time.

Unlike most of the retailers on this list, Dormify is specifically focused on college living and has a dedicated Dorm Wishlist. You can create and manage your wishlist through Dormify’s site and add items from its assortment of twin XL bedding, storage, bath and laundry products, seating, decor, lighting and other dorm essentials.

How friends and family shop it: Dormify has a “Find a Wishlist” tool that lets friends and family search using the student’s name, with optional filters, including state. That means relatives don’t necessarily have to keep track of your individual wishlist link to find it.

Shipping/pickup: Dormify also advertises a Pick Up Near Campus program, which is particularly helpful if you had to drive far or fly to school. Dormify does not have standalone brick-and-mortar stores but you can have items shipped to partner retailers by your school, such as Williams Sonoma, Pottery Barn, or West Elm.

MyRegistry.com $ 0.00 MyRegistry.com What to know Why I like it for college: College students rarely buy everything from one store. A universal registry lets you make one master dorm list without limiting yourself to a single retailer’s inventory. You can also sync existing registries from other retailers into MyRegistry.

MyRegistry is different from most other options on this list because it isn’t a retailer — it’s a universal registry platform. You create a free account and can then use its browser tool or mobile app to add products to one registry from virtually any online retailer. That means your Target sheets, Amazon desk lamp and highlighters from Walmart don’t need to live on three separate lists.

How friends and family shop it: Instead of sending everyone multiple wishlist links, you share one MyRegistry link. When someone chooses an item, they’re directed to the original retailer to complete the purchase. MyRegistry tracks purchased items on the universal list to help prevent duplicates.

Shipping/pickup: It’s important to note that MyRegistry doesn’t fulfill the order itself. Because shoppers ultimately purchase through the retailer that sells the item, shipping, delivery and pickup options are determined by that retailer.

Pottery Barn Teen $ 0.00 PBTeen What to know Why I like it for college: PB Teen is particularly useful if you want to make your dorm feel more put together while still shopping for practical necessities. Its dorm assortment covers everything from mattress toppers and twin XL bedding to under-bed storage, laundry supplies, shower caddies and desk accessories, so you can build most of your room from one wishlist. I also like that its site has dedicated dorm-shopping tools, including a dorm checklist and Build Your Bed tool, which can be helpful for first-year students who aren’t sure where to start.

Pottery Barn Teen has a dedicated Dorm Wishlist, making it one of the most college-specific options on this list. You can create a wishlist online and add products from PB Teen’s Dorm Shop, which includes twin XL bedding, storage and organization, bath and laundry essentials, lighting, desk accessories and decor.

How friends and family shop it: Once your Dorm Wishlist is set up, friends and family can search for it on PB Teen’s website using your first and last name, with optional filters for your state, birth month and year. PB Teen also lets you manage your list online and link a wishlist that was originally created in one of its stores.

Shipping/pickup: This is one of the biggest reasons I like PB Teen for college students: The retailer has a Pick Up Near Campus program and lets shoppers filter dorm products based on whether they’re eligible for the service. PB Teen also promotes the option to ship orders to a store, which can help you avoid packing bulky dorm purchases and transporting them from home. Availability varies by product and location, so I’d check what’s eligible near your school before placing an order.

Crate & Barrel $ 0.00 Crate & Barrel What to know Why I like it for college: I see Crate & Barrel as less of an “everything you need for freshman year” option and more useful for higher-quality items that can follow you beyond the dorm. Think bedding, bath essentials, organizers or kitchenware you’ll eventually use in an apartment. Group gifting is also useful for pricier items.

Crate & Barrel doesn’t have a college-specific registry, but it does allow registries for occasions beyond weddings, including housewarmings — consider dorm room shopping like a mini-housewarming. It is an option for someone furnishing their first space. You can create and edit a registry online or through the Crate & Barrel app and add items digitally or with help from an associate in the store.

How friends and family shop it: Friends and family can search for a registry and purchase directly from it, and Crate & Barrel keeps track of purchased gifts. It also offers group gifting, which lets multiple people contribute toward certain higher-priced registry items.

Shipping/pickup: Eligible registry purchases of $49 or more ship free, according to Crate & Barrel.

The Container Store $ 0.00 The Container Store What to know Why I like it for college: Storage space is one of the biggest challenges in a dorm room, and organization is where The Container Store really stands out. Its dorm checklist includes under-bed storage, bed risers, desktop organizers, hampers, shower caddies, hanging closet organizers, over-the-door storage and stacking drawers — basically the products that help you make use of every inch of a small room. The retailer even recommends choosing free store pickup at a location near campus in its dorm-shopping materials.

The Container Store doesn’t have a college-specific registry, but you can create a Wish List and use it as a dorm registry. You can name your list — something as simple as “[Your Name]’s College Dorm” works — and add the storage and organization products you want to it. The retailer specifically says its wishlists can be used for occasions like graduations and shared with family and friends.

How friends and family shop it: Once you’ve made your list, The Container Store lets you send it via email to friends and family so they can shop from it. Unlike PB Teen’s Dorm Wishlist, however, this isn’t a full-fledged college registry program; it’s better thought of as a shareable wishlist that you can adapt for dorm shopping.

Shipping/pickup: The Container Store offers free in-store and curbside pickup for online orders. You select the store at checkout, and the retailer sends an email or text when the order is ready. That makes it especially helpful if there’s a Container Store near your college: Instead of filling your car with bulky bins, drawers and organizers, you can order online and pick them up closer to campus. Local delivery is also available in select markets.

What to put on your college dorm registry

This is my official packing list for my family and friends (and the exact one I used a few years ago as a freshman). These picks are shopping-expert, residence life-assistant and big-sister approved.

Room Needs/Storage

I tested this clock for our 2026 Wellness Awards (it won for best alarm clock and sound machine) and I consider it one of the best alarms in general, especially for students. I used to think sound machines were redundant with a phone, but the Hatch Restore changed my mind. Its wind-down routine encourages stepping away from screen time before bed to build healthier nighttime habits. The sunrise light is especially helpful in winter for waking up calmly and naturally. While an optional paid app subscription offers extra sounds and podcasts, it isn’t required to benefit from the clock. Additionally, its sleek, minimal design suits any bedroom decor, and it’s HSA/FSA eligible.

Linens/Laundry Supplies

I have tested many towels, and these are at the top of my list. Made from 100% Supima cotton, the sturdy fibers far outperform standard cotton in strength. This ensures the set endures repeated laundering over the years without sacrificing its softness or drying efficiency. It serves as a practical, durable, and comfortable upgrade from basic bath towels, offering an everyday dorm essential that truly lasts.

Where thick, conventional towels stay damp for hours, the open weave allows optimal airflow to deter odors and hamper the growth of mold, mildew, and bacteria. This rapid-dry feature is ideal for compact dorm spaces where towels typically end up on wall hooks rather than wide towel bars. From personal experience, these towels absorb water effortlessly but dry remarkably fast and maintain their quality over long-term use. I also highly recommend their Antimicrobial Gauze Robe.

Office/Desk/Classroom Supplies

NBC Selected page, Morgan Dawson used this metal desktop organizer all four years of college. She says “the minimalist design kept my desk clutter in check, and with seven compartments, there was enough space for pens, pencils, sticky notes, paper clips and miscellaneous knick knacks. The mesh metal material was also easy to clean and prevented dust or pencil shavings from accumulating over time.”

Tech

I never went anywhere without my iPad when I was in college. It became my notebook, planner, TV and second monitor. It’s a powerful, space-saving tool, versatile enough for all aspects of student life. With the iPad Air, students can take handwritten notes, annotate assigned readings, and keep coursework digitally organized, significantly reducing the burden of heavy notebooks and binders. When paired with a physical keyboard, it seamlessly doubles as a laptop replacement for drafting papers, responding to emails, and managing daily assignments.

Outside the classroom, it easily adapts to dorm room living. Whether for streaming TV shows, video calls with family, playing music, or working on assignments on the move, the iPad Air serves as an all-in-one hub. Its all-day battery life ensures students stay powered through back-to-back classes without constantly searching for power outlets, while its lightweight build makes it easy to carry across campus.

The Apple Pencil Pro is a must-have with an iPad and you can get a free engraving at Apple.

Toiletries

There’s nothing like a stomach ache when you’re far from home, and it happens more often than you’d think in college — after all, you don’t get the freshman 15 from eating too many salads. I always had these chewables in my bag because they actually work. I would take two of these whenever I had nausea, an upset stomach, indigestion, runny stools, cramping or heartburn, and I would get relief in minutes. I much prefer these over the liquid version and they are so easy to travel with.

Cleaning Items

Clorox disinfecting wipes are one of those dorm products you may not realize you need until you really need them. They’re a single-step solution for keeping clean, whether that’s wiping up a spill or disinfecting surfaces on a routine basis. Dawson likes the crisp lemon scent, because it feels fresh and clean without the overwhelmingly chemical smell.

Non-essential nice-to-haves

How to shop for dorm essentials

Shopping for a dorm is different from shopping for a bedroom at home: You’re working with limited space, may be sharing that space with someone else and will likely have to move everything again at the end of the school year. Before you start adding items to your dorm registry or wishlist, these are the factors you should consider.

How much should you budget for dorm essentials?

Set a budget before you start shopping and prioritize necessities over decor and convenience items. Bedding, bath essentials, laundry supplies and a few storage solutions are worth budgeting for first; you can always buy additional organizers, decorations and accessories after you’ve moved in and know what you actually need.

You also don’t need to buy everything new. If you already own towels, hangers, a desk lamp or other items that work for your dorm, bring them rather than replacing them simply because you’re going to college. A registry can also be a good place for more expensive essentials that friends or family may want to contribute to.

How should your dorm room’s size and floor plan affect what you buy?

Check your school’s housing website for your residence hall’s floor plan, room dimensions and a list of included furniture before buying larger dorm items. Knowing the size of your bed, what’s already provided and how much floor and closet space you’ll have can prevent you from buying things that won’t fit.

I recommend waiting until move-in to buy some organizers for this reason. It’s much easier to determine whether you need another rolling cart or set of drawers once you unpack and can actually see the space you’re working with.

What should you check before buying dorm appliances and furniture?

Read your college’s residence hall policies before buying appliances, furniture or anything that attaches to the walls or doors. Schools can have specific rules about items like microwaves, mini fridges, coffee makers, extension cords, candles and wall-mounted products, and your school may already provide some of the larger items you’re considering.

Don’t forget about your actual dorm room door, either. Check rules and measurements before buying over-the-door organizers, hooks and similar products, since door dimensions and policies can vary.

What dorm essentials should you share with your roommate?

Coordinate with your roommate before buying anything you only need one of, such as a rug, vacuum, trash can or other shared supplies. Decide who will bring each item rather than splitting the cost of everything, if possible — it’ll make figuring out who takes what at the end of the year much easier.

I’d also avoid relying on your roommate for personal essentials you’ll use frequently. Sharing a vacuum is one thing; having to track down your roommate every time you need laundry pods or utensils is another.

How often will you actually use an item in your dorm?

Before buying something, consider how frequently you’ll use it and whether your college already gives you access to one. Many campuses have resources like printers and other school supplies in libraries, computer labs or residence halls, so you may not need your own version of everything.

For inexpensive items you’ll use constantly, having your own may still be worth the convenience. But if something is expensive, bulky and only useful a few times a semester, check what’s available on campus first.

How durable should dorm essentials be?

Prioritize durability for products you expect to use throughout college, especially items that will be packed, unpacked and transported repeatedly. Hampers, storage bins, luggage and organizers can take a beating during move-ins and move-outs, so spending a little more on sturdy versions may make sense if you plan to use them for several years.

For inexpensive items you don’t expect to keep after college, durability may matter less. Think about the item’s expected lifespan before deciding where it’s worth spending more.

Where will you store your dorm essentials over the summer?

Think about where everything will go when you move out before buying bulky furniture, storage or decor. If you’re flying home, live far from campus or don’t have much storage space at home, you’ll need to either transport your belongings, pay to store them near school, sell or donate them or replace them the following year.

Collapsible, stackable and multipurpose products can be especially useful for this reason. The less space something takes up when you’re not using it, the easier your end-of-year move will be.

What dorm essentials should you wait to buy until after move-in?

Wait on nonessential storage, decor and convenience products if you’re unsure whether they’ll fit or whether you’ll actually use them. Moving in with the basics and shopping for the rest afterward can save you money and keep you from overcrowding your room.

This is also where ordering for pickup near campus can come in handy. Instead of transporting every possible item from home, you can make a list of things you may need and order eligible products once you’ve seen your room and figured out what’s missing.

Frequently asked questions What is a dorm registry? A dorm registry is a shareable list of items you need for your college dorm room. It works similarly to a wedding or baby registry, allowing friends and family to see what you need and, depending on the retailer, which items have already been purchased. Is a dorm registry the same as a wishlist? Not necessarily, but a shareable wishlist can work essentially the same as a dorm registry. Some retailers offer dedicated college registries or dorm wishlists, while others let you create and share a general wishlist with friends and family. When should you make a dorm registry? You can start making a dorm registry once you know where you’ll be living and what your college provides or allows in its residence halls. Starting early also gives you time to compare prices and coordinate larger purchases with your roommate. Can you make a dorm registry at more than one store? Yes, you can make dorm registries or wishlists at multiple retailers. You can share each list separately or use a universal registry service, like MyRegistry.com, to combine products from multiple stores into one list. What should you buy before moving into a dorm? You should buy the essentials you’ll need immediately, including bedding, toiletries, towels, laundry supplies and basic organization products. You can wait to buy some storage, decor and other nonessential items until you’ve seen your room and know how much space you actually have. What should you not put on a dorm registry? Don’t add appliances, furniture or other large items until you’ve checked your college’s residence hall rules and what your room already includes. Schools may prohibit certain appliances and often provide items like a desk, chair, dresser or mini fridge. Do you need a dorm registry if you're not a freshman? You might. A dorm registry or wishlist can be useful for returning college students who need to replace or upgrade their essentials. It can also be helpful for someone moving into a different type of housing or whose needs have changed.

Why trust NBC Selected?

I am the editorial operations associate for NBC Selected. For this article, I did extensive research and pulled from my years of experience with back-to-school shopping and working in residence life to give you the most practical, helpful recommendations for how to create a dorm registry and what to put on it.

World.title: Trump administration's 75-country visa ban was illegal, judge rules
World.content:
Trump administration's 75-country visa ban was illegal, judge rules

toggle caption David J. Phillip/AP

A federal judge has struck down a Trump administration ban on issuing immigrant visas to people from 75 countries, saying the policy violated federal immigration law by discriminating on the basis of nationality.

The State Department said earlier this year that it was halting immigrant visas for citizens of Afghanistan, Brazil, Yemen and dozens of other countries because the Trump administration determined people from those nations were likely to need public assistance if they came to the United States.

The policy would have barred the U.S. government from issuing immigrant visas even in cases where consular officers individually assessed applicants and determined they were likely to be self-sufficient in the U.S., according to a ruling Friday by District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas in the Southern District of New York.

Sponsor Message

"In many ways, this is not a challenging case," Vargas wrote. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 prohibits discrimination on the basis of nationality in the issuance of immigrant visas, Vargas said. However, the Trump administration's policy banned certain people from receiving immigrant visas "based solely on their nationality," the judge wrote.

Vargas cited a U.S. diplomatic cable that instructed consulates to refuse immigrant visas to applicants who had already been approved but whose printed visas hadn't left the consulate.

Vargas said the Trump administration's policy was "contrary to law" and exceeded the authority of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The judge's ruling vacated the visa ban and also set aside visa denials that were based only on the policy.

A State Department spokesperson told NPR the Trump administration is "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants," adding that the administration doesn't comment on ongoing litigation. When the State Department issued the ban, it said the policy would "remain active until the U.S. can ensure that new immigrants will not extract wealth from the American people."

The ban was part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to limit legal and illegal immigration. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional right to birthright citizenship , rejecting an executive order Trump signed that tried to bar citizenship for babies born in the U.S. to parents who either entered the country illegally or who are living and working here legally with temporary visas. The executive order never went into effect because lower court judges ruled it was unconstitutional.

Sponsor Message

Susan Welber, supervising attorney at The Legal Aid Society, which represented plaintiffs in the lawsuit against the federal government, says the 75-country visa ban was "premised on a fiction" that residents of the targeted nations are likely to use public resources if they come to the U.S.

"Any time that we can fight back against policies that are based on fictions and untruths and prejudices, I think we're making for a more just immigration system," Welber says.

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit included the Catholic Immigration Legal Network and African Communities Together, which provide immigration legal services, as well as six U.S. citizens who filed family-based immigration petitions on behalf of relatives and five "intending immigrants" who filed employment-based petitions on their own behalf.

"The suspension of lawful visa processing across 75 countries separated spouses, parents, and children who were simply following the legal immigration process," Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, said in a statement .

Plaintiffs' lawyers said Friday's ruling will allow their clients to proceed through the immigration process.

"For 75 countries' worth of families, this decision means a return to fair, case-by-case review, and a chance to be reunited with their loved ones," said Antionette Dozier, senior attorney for Western Center on Law & Poverty, which represented the Catholic Legal Immigration Network. "No administration gets to override the law because it deems an applicant's nationality unacceptable."

World.title: Opinion: Mr. Rogers keeps finding a new neighborhood
World.content:
Opinion: Mr. Rogers keeps finding a new neighborhood

toggle caption Duane Burleson/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

It's been a full and frenetic few weeks for Jake Rogers, a catcher for the — well, who knows by the time we're off the air today? Mr. Rogers recently changed his neighborhood — and his teams — four times in 21 days. That's a major league record, though perhaps not the kind a player seeks.

He told Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic, "it's been…a whirlwind, to say the least."

Rogers had been with the Detroit Tigers since 2017, beloved by fans and teammates for his positive attitude and sculpted mustache. But his batting average drooped this season. On July 29, the Tigers blew a lead against the Baltimore Orioles and lost in extra innings. Late that night, Rogers was told the team had to let him go. He flew to his home in Dallas, and was signed the next day by the Baltimore Orioles. They must have seen something they liked.

Sponsor Message

Rogers appeared in just 3 games with Baltimore, where he reportedly had to borrow catching gear from a teammate. Just before the Aug. 3 trade deadline hit, he was told he'd been traded to the Boston Red Sox.

So Jake Rogers flew to Boston — flight crews must have known by then if he preferred pretzels or a Stroopwafel — and played the last few innings of a 13-inning game against the Chicago White Sox. He also brought home a run with a sacrifice fly.

But the Red Sox were mostly waiting for another catcher they had just acquired to return from an injury. And so after just three games with them, the team put Rogers on waivers, where he could be claimed by another team.

And he soon was — by the Chicago White Sox. Red Sox, White Sox, Rogers didn't have time to rinse his own socks back in Dallas before joining the White Sox on their road trip…which, it turned out, was to Detroit. The stadium where his saga began.

I wonder if over the last few weeks Jake Rogers has asked himself, "Do I need to change my mouthwash? My cologne? Is it something I said?" Or have managers told him as they let him go, time and again, "It's not you, Jake. It's us."

Sponsor Message

His former home crowd in Detroit gave Jake Rogers a standing ovation as he stepped up to the plate in his 4th uniform in 21 days. And just last night, he hit a home run to win the game for his new team, the White Sox. Maybe there ought to be a special Most Valuable Player award for the people in our lives who are there when they're needed most.

World.title: As Flock battles public scrutiny, other police surveillance companies see an opening
World.content:
As Flock battles public scrutiny, other police surveillance companies see an opening

toggle caption Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Dozens of people crammed into a conference room for a gathering at a public library in Washington, D.C.

The topic? Automated license plate readers, such as the ones sold by Flock Safety, a company facing major backlash from residents in communities across the country who find themselves deeply unsettled by privacy concerns.

On Monday, members of DeFlock DC, a grassroots group dedicated to ending all contracts between the Metropolitan Police Department and Flock, explained to the group how these controversial cameras work and where they are located throughout the city.

But as Loreal Hawk, a member of DeFlock DC, told the group gathered, automated license plate readers are neither new nor unique to Flock. Competitors such as Axon, Motorola Solutions and Verkada, offer similar products to law enforcement agencies, and have for years.

Sponsor Message

"We need to cancel these contracts," Hawk said.

Flock has been the target of much of the public's ire, but its rivals have largely avoided it. Now, some of those competitors are trying to cash in on Flock's fall from grace.

More than 130,000 automated license-plate readers, or ALPR's, can be found in cities and towns across the country, according to the crowdsourced database DeFlock.org . The cameras take images of the backs of cars. Law enforcement has increasingly turned to this tool to help solve crime.

"The Flock ALPR technology has captured the public's attention" and spurred a realization that "maybe we don't want to be surveilled all the time," said Andrew Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University.

But now, he said, Flock is the one that has "the target put on its back."

Why is Flock facing so much heat?

Flock CEO Garrett Langley regularly posts on social media extolling the benefits of his company's tech , often noting that communities are safer because of it. Flock was credited with helping to track the suspect in last year's Brown University shooting, which killed two students and injured nine other people.

"On a very personal level, I go to bed every night very proud of the impact we have in the world," Langley told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Many automated license plate readers, including Flock's, use AI to capture information such as a vehicle's make, model and color. Police can search Flock's shared national database of these images — including vehicles outside of their own jurisdiction.

That national database is a core point of contention for Flock opponents.

"People got really mad at Flock because they realized that it was a window into a whole network of surveillance," said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy advocacy group. He strongly opposes the technology broadly, not just Flock's version of it.

With this network "suddenly your cameras are being used to enforce things that you don't agree with or that are not illegal in your town," he said.

In Texas, for instance, deputies used Flock data to help investigate a woman suspected of traveling to have an abortion.

Hits against Flock keep coming. Police officers have been found to use this technology to stalk women. And while Flock allows customers to control the information they share on its network, there are some cases where information was unknowingly shared more widely, including with federal immigration agencies.

In response, the company last week announced a host of changes , including reducing its data retention period and emphasizing safeguards around local data searches.

The ACLU said the changes were largely unsatisfying.

Competitors step in

License plate readers are only one piece of a growing police surveillance industry.

Many law enforcement agencies use integrated tools such as facial recognition , gunshot detectors , predictive policing , drones and real-time crime centers that pull all this information into one central hub used by investigators.

Ferguson, who is also the author of Your Data Will Be Used Against You: Policing in the Age of Self-Surveillance, says in his view, those integrated systems raise far more red flags for privacy than license plate readers alone. Yet, they've drawn almost no large-scale public protest.

toggle caption PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images





Guariglia believes Flock is at the center of the license plate reader firestorm, in part, because of its cameras' visibility.

Sponsor Message

"Once you know what they look like, you become aware of how ubiquitous they are," he said.

Dozens of communities have turned against Flock amid widespread public backlash. About 100 cities have deactivated cameras, rejected deals or cancelled contracts, according to DeFlock's database . Some, such as Denver and Longmont, Colo. , signed contracts with Flock competitors this year, including Axon, a trend reported by 404 Media .

Axon, a multibillion dollar company that provides tech and weapons to law enforcement and the military, says it's positioned to step in amid the "deFlock movement." During Axon's most recent earnings call, CEO Rick Smith told investors that law enforcement agencies are making the switch.

"We're seeing a significant number of agencies want to come over to Axon and convert from existing license plate readers to us." He credited the company's "controls and privacy work."

Axon declined to say how much business the company has gained from cancelled Flock contracts.

When asked how Flock is responding to other providers swooping in on their departing business, Langley said he is unconcerned.

"We will have added seven times the number of new customers that have left us this year," he said.

Langley said he was especially surprised about Denver's move to sign a one-year deal with Axon, after residents voiced concerns over data sharing for immigration enforcement.

"I guess in some ways I scratch my head because that company works with ICE," he said. "They lack the accountability and transparency we have, and so I don't know why they made that choice."

Axon holds several multimillion dollar contracts with the Department of Homeland Security for its products, including body cameras and Tasers.

"For more than 30 years, we've built products to protect life," Axon spokesperson Kate MacKinnon said in an email to NPR. "As new technologies emerge, we know that our customers require solutions that protect data and privacy."

But privacy experts warn the switch to other police surveillance technologies isn't a fix.

"You're just replacing one color of camera for another," Guariglia said. "Those dangers you were concerned about are still going to be there."

World.title: Hours after U.S. imposes tariffs, Canada says it'll strike back starting Sept. 8
World.content:
Hours after U.S. imposes tariffs, Canada says it'll strike back starting Sept. 8

toggle caption Graham Hughes/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says his country will initiate retaliatory tariffs against U.S. imports starting Sept. 8. The move came hours after the Trump administration began enforcing 50% tariffs on a slew of Canadian goods.

Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada fell apart Friday night, shortly before a midnight deadline for the 50% tariffs to take effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, including some dairy products, alcoholic beverages, cement and hockey equipment.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a bulletin to businesses Friday warning that its officers would be ensuring importers complied with the new rates starting immediately after the deadline passed.

Sponsor Message

Carney said Friday night that "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses." He later said the retaliatory tariffs set to kick in next month will focus on American sectors such as "steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics."

In a statement shared on social media, Carney said important progress had been made in recent weeks toward "improving Canada's position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S." That progress, however, did not meet Canada's objectives, he said, adding: "As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed negotiators to return to Ottawa."

The prime minister blamed the U.S. for the collapse in negotiations. "Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said, concluding, "Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future."

On Saturday morning, Carney wrote on social media that his negotiators had worked "in good faith" for more than a year, and his government would in the coming days "release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labour Day."

Sponsor Message

The U.S., in turn, pointed the finger at Canada. Shortly after midnight, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer responded to Carney on social media by saying that Canada had "declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week."

"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said.

He added that earlier this week "the United States agreed to provide even better treatment to Canada, offering significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber."

"The offer would have led to supply chain coordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals cooperation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labor, and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations," Greer said in his statement.

Overnight Saturday, President Trump posted on social media saying: "Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!! President DJT."

NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.

World.title: A battle over 'Italian brainrot' could shape who owns AI art
World.content:
A battle over 'Italian brainrot' could shape who owns AI art

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images/Collage by Emily Bogle/NPR

Around the world, kids are going crazy for a set of characters collectively known as "Italian brainrot." These memes are generated using artificial intelligence, and they're appearing on social media and YouTube, as well as in video games.

Now their popularity has sparked a fight over who, if anyone, owns them.

A legal battle unfolding in a California courtroom could determine whether several prominent brainrot characters can be used in games and other media without paying or acknowledging their creators. On one side is a company that made a hit game using Italian brainrot characters. On the other is a French startup representing the young creators of several of the characters that appear in the game. At stake is potentially many millions of dollars in revenue.

Sponsor Message

The fight comes at a crossroads for AI-generated art and raises the question of whether prompts to a chatbot can be considered artistic expression. A 2024 case ruled that a chatbot cannot be the sole inventor of a product or piece of art, but it left open the possibility of humans using AI to produce copyrightable works. Last year, the U.S. Copyright Office affirmed that AI-assisted work could be copyrighted but added: "Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis."

"We're still in the middle of figuring out, as a copyright matter, how much human involvement there has to be" for AI art to be legally protected, said Mark McKenna, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles who co-directs the university's Institute for Technology, Law and Policy. McKenna thinks the day will come when an AI drawing, story or song is copyrighted, but he said, "I don't have some specific prediction of how many prompts it's going to take."

Ballerina Cappuccina

Italian brainrot burst forth on the internet in early 2025. The memes are weird, AI-generated characters with faux Italian-sounding names. A cow with the body of the planet Saturn and large human feet is known as La Vaca Saturno Saturnita, while a frothy coffee in a tutu is called Ballerina Cappuccina.

Sponsor Message

Grown-ups can find Italian brainrot confusing, but kids love the Dadaist characters. And sensing an opportunity, products geared toward a younger audience are regularly using brainrot characters.

That includes Steal a Brainrot, a video game made by a company called Do Big Studios and launched last year, shortly after brainrots took the youth internet by storm. In the game, different brainrot characters come out on a conveyor belt and players pick them up. But they can also steal brainrots from each other. Steal a Brainrot is one of the top games on the online gaming platform Roblox, with hundreds of thousands of players logging on at any moment to steal each other's characters.

toggle caption Screenshot by NPR/YouTube

After Steal a Brainrot rocketed to the top of the charts, Sam Brakta (aka SpyderSammy), the creator of Steal a Brainrot and owner of Do Big, received a letter from a French company called Mementum Lab asking the company to enter into licensing negotiations for one of the characters in the game: Tung Tung Sahur.

Tung Tung Sahur (sometimes called Tung Tung Tung Sahur) is among the biggest characters in Italian brainrot. He looks like a wooden stick with a face, human feet and human arms, holding a baseball bat.

Licensing requests are nothing new: If someone wanted to put Darth Vader in a video game, for example, they'd have to pay a fee to Disney, which currently owns the intellectual property for Star Wars.

But rather than pay a license fee, Do Big decided to take Mementum Lab to court. In an amended complaint filed in July, the company stated that "Mementum's claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify."

"It's our client's position that the various brainrots that are featured in this game, because they were created by AI, are not protectable — they're not owned by anybody," said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer at the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp, which is representing Do Big and SpyderSammy.

Young creators use AI

Mementum Lab, the company representing the creators of several characters that appear in Steal a Brainrot, takes a different view. Brainrot characters are already known to millions of children globally and are potentially worth hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, argues Eben Jeda, a co-founder of Mementum.

Sponsor Message

"Our position has always been that if these characters become global entertainment franchises, the original creators should be part of that success," he wrote to NPR in an email.

In the case of Tung Tung Sahur, Jeda argues, there's a lot more to him than meets the eye.

According to court records, Tung Tung Sahur's creator is a young Indonesian man named Fernanda Bagas Indrastata who goes by the online name Noxa. Noxa made the character in 15 minutes using just seven prompts with an AI image generator.

It turns out the character isn't a wooden stick after all. It's actually a type of Indonesian drum called a kentongan. During Ramadan, kentongans are used to wake up people for sahur, the early-morning pre-fast meal. The "tung tung" noise that the drums make became Tung Tung Sahur's first name.

toggle caption Anadolu via Getty Images

Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the law firm representing Mementum Lab in U.S. court, said that Tung Tung Sahur's origin story proves the character was made by a human and that even if it didn't take much effort to create it, that still counts under the law.

"If I sat here right now and drew a picture of something and spent 30 seconds doing that, that could be copyrightable," he told NPR.

Copyright vs. trademark

While Do Big Studios, the creator of Steal a Brainrot, is trying to invalidate any copyright for Tung Tung Sahur, Mementum has countersued, claiming trademark infringement. The difference is significant: Copyright is typically used to protect creative works (like the Harry Potter books and characters) from being plagiarized or duplicated without permission, while trademark has historically been used to protect consumer brands (like Coca-Cola).

Stein said that Mementum is using trademark law because, so far at least, it has not tried to register a copyright for Tung Tung Sahur in the United States. The trademark claim, he asserts, allows the company to focus more directly on whether the company can receive damages from unauthorized use of Tung Tung Sahur, without pursuing the larger philosophical question of whether an AI-generated character is copyrightable under U.S. law.

Sponsor Message

"Mementum has to be strategic about the fights it has in this litigation while preserving its full suite of rights to pursue claims abroad," he said.

Moss, representing Do Big, said he believes the other side is pursuing a trademark claim because it knows it will lose under current copyright law. "The U.S. Copyright Office has been clear that simply typing prompts into an image generator is not authorship," he said.

Because of the counterclaims by both sides, it remains unclear how the case will shape the legal understanding of AI art, but UCLA legal expert McKenna says cases like these will likely be pivotal in creating precedent in the courts.

McKenna said using trademark law to sidestep copyright questions is not an uncommon strategy, but he thinks it's an abuse of the system. "Trademark is supposed to identify the origin of tangible goods and services," he said. "Falling back on trademark so as to avoid the hard questions in copyright, to me, is a misuse of trademark law."

At the same time, McKenna said, he thinks Tung Tung Sahur could have a shot at securing a copyright under U.S. law.

"In general, the standard for originality is pretty low," he said. "It doesn't have to be, like, the most creative thing in the history of the world."

World.title: Supreme Court allows Trump's ballroom construction to continue for now
World.content:
Supreme Court allows Trump's ballroom construction to continue for now

toggle caption Alex Wong/Getty Images

The Supreme Court ruled Friday that President Trump can — for now — move forward with construction of his ballroom on the site of the former East Wing of the White House without needing approval from Congress.

The new ballroom is estimated to cost taxpayers at least $300 million, despite the president saying repeatedly that taxpayers would not foot the bill.

The ruling comes after months of back-and-forth between the Trump administration and the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued to stop the construction of the ballroom. The nonprofit organization has argued that the president must get approval from Congress to build over the East Wing, the side that held offices for the first lady.

Sponsor Message

The ballroom is expected to be a 90,000-square-foot addition to the White House and twice the size of the main part of the White House complex.

Trump has argued for months that the new ballroom is a necessity, often pointing to the lack of space to host events with foreign dignitaries. He has also said that the ballroom will house critical national security benefits, including bomb shelters, a hospital, sniper nests and a drone port.

The Supreme Court had until Friday to weigh in after lower courts had differing rulings on the ballroom for the last few months.

In a brief order, signed by Chief Justice John Roberts, the court stayed the lower court ruling to pause construction.

In its brief filed earlier this week, the trust asserted that if the Supreme Court allowed construction to continue at this time, the court was effectively ending the case.

"Rather than obtain permission from Congress, Petitioners have instead decided to try to outrun judicial review" by accelerating construction. "It is clear that in Petitioners' view, if the Court grants their stay application, this case is over—despite every court to have reviewed their project having found it to be patently unlawful, and no matter the fact that this Court has not reviewed those decisions on the merits," the brief states.

Sponsor Message

Trump praised the decision on social media, saying, "We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court. The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!"

The court proceedings started in March, when Republican-appointed federal Judge Richard Leon ruled against Trump on the ballroom, saying the construction needed to stop unless it was additions to the White House that involved safety and security. The ruling then went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which decided that construction could temporarily continue. Leon then clarified and said below-ground construction of the ballroom could continue but above-ground could not.

Trump responded on social media, writing, "It's all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations of the United States of America!"

The case then went back to the appeals court, but the Trump administration requested an emergency appeal with the Supreme Court.

Construction of the ballroom began last July and has involved closing off access to the north side of the White House and Lafayette Park, which were previously open to the public. Polling shows the project, along with many of Trump's other efforts to remake the capital city, are unpopular among voters.

An April poll from Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos showed 56% of Americans did not approve of Trump's decision to tear down the East Wing and build the ballroom.

NPR's Emily Feng contributed reporting from Washington.

World.title: Beatty files emergency request to stop Trump's name from returning to Kennedy Center
World.content:
Beatty files emergency request to stop Trump's name from returning to Kennedy Center

toggle caption Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images

Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, filed an emergency motion late Thursday evening asking a federal judge to stop the trustees of the Kennedy Center from putting President Trump's name back on the front of the arts complex. She also asked the judge to stop the trustees' plan to rename the physical site of the center the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

If the board's plan moves forward in full, Trump's name would appear on the entryway sign twice, and would appear on a third location on the grounds.

"It's deja vu all over again," Beatty's lawyers wrote to Judge Christopher Cooper in their argument, saying that only Congress can change the name of the center, which by Congressional mandate is a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy. "Now, in a new and breathtaking act of defiance of Congress and of this Court, Defendants have voted to return President Trump's name to the Kennedy Center's facade. This time, Trump's name will appear on the building's front portico not once, but twice."

Sponsor Message

NPR requested comment from the Kennedy Center on Thursday night, but did not receive a reply.

The signage proposed by the center's board, most of whose members were appointed by the president, would eventually read: "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump, Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund." The last line would be added if the fund reaches $100 million in donations. Additionally, the board is seeking to rename the physical grounds of the arts center "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

In May, Judge Cooper ruled that the board's previous attempt to rename the arts institution as the Trump-Kennedy Center was unlawful, writing: "The Kennedy Center's organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it."

The board approved its newest plans for the center in a meeting on Aug. 13 . The Kennedy Center said in previous legal filings that it would not try to add Trump's name back on the building before Sept. 8. In this latest filing, Beatty's team called this September date an "arbitrary deadline," and urged the court to take immediate action, writing: "They have created an unnecessarily fire drill … there is no need for this manufactured emergency."

Beatty is an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board. She filed her lawsuit against the board and Trump as the organization's chairman last December, challenging the renaming of the institution.

Sponsor Message

In a statement emailed to NPR Thursday night, Beatty said: "The board's repeated efforts to break the law are a breathtaking act of defiance, but I will continue to stand up against all unlawful acts—enough is enough. The Kennedy Center is a sacred space that belongs to the American people. At every turn, Trump's handpicked Board has flouted court orders and attempted to circumvent the law and the rulings of the judiciary."

This story was edited by Meghan Collins Sullivan. Additional reporting by Chloe Veltman.

World.title: Top Iran official says U.S. focus on economic warfare shows it has failed militarily
World.content:
Top Iran official says U.S. focus on economic warfare shows it has failed militarily

toggle caption Hadi Mizban/AP

The Iranian regime has dismissed President Trump's threats to crush Iran economically, saying that years of U.S. sanctions have failed.
