World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The story of Zarzaparilla, an Indigenous root beer from Veracruz
World.content:
Mexico’s truest beauty can often be found in its widely diverse, uniquely regional variations of culture and flavors. No two places in Mexico are exactly alike. Whether it’s the way a certain salsa is prepared, the protein of choice used to stuff a tamal or the techniques that may differ from coast to coast, pueblo to pueblo, the country reflects an endless multiverse of realities inside its kitchens. As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me while driving across the desert terrain, you can spend two lifetimes in Mexico and even then, you still wouldn’t uncover all of its secrets and taste all of its idiosyncrasies.

It was a revelation, then, when I learned about zarzaparilla — about its historic origins and regional importance — from one of my uncles who grew up in Veracruz. In the simplest terms, zarzaparilla (referred to simply as zarza by locals) is what modern consumers would likely associate with root beer. But centuries before making its way into European markets via the Spanish — who in the 16th century first encountered the Indigenous remedy in the mountains of what is now Veracruz, and then exported it to Seville, Spain — zarza was a native drink with purported medicinal qualities made from local roots and ingredients that combated syphilis and, according to the American Homebrewers Association, far predates root beer.

A root beer revelation

In an effort to learn more about it, I drove 45 minutes to the source, on a southbound road from my home in Veracruz past two Pueblos Mágicos — first Coatepec, then Xico — until I reached Mexico’s cradle of zarza: Teocelo (or, in Nahuatl, “Tiger God”).

The mountain town of around 11,000 can only be reached through narrow, curving roads that carve through the subtropical terrain at a high elevation — with humid and wet conditions that allow all sorts of vegetation and crops to flourish in the surrounding areas (coffee, in particular, is a notable product from this part of Mexico).

It’s here that zarzaparilla (also confusingly spelled “sarsaparilla”) gained notoriety as a beverage among Spaniards and mestizos, becoming a local commercial industry of sorts that would expand beyond the region. Today, zarzaparilla can be found throughout Mexico, particularly within Veracruz and its neighboring states. But back then, it was — much like jalapeños were until they became commonplace elsewhere — a specialty product known only to those in the greater Xalapa vicinity.

The origins of ‘zarza’

In snooping around the tiny pueblo, it’s easy to find where it all started: Zarzaparilla Flores (a family-owned business that is not to be mistaken for a separate branch of family operations, Zarzaparilla Flores Doña Chabe, which is literally next door, but technically unaffiliated). The original Zarzaparilla Flores is said to have opened in 1920 inside what used to be a storage building for the nearby train yard, which served as a prominent trade route during the Porfiriato era from Xico to the United States. Due to the train, lots of immigrants and outsiders were able to pass through town, bringing a transient mixture of passersby who helped give zarzaparilla its fame beyond Veracruz.

Today, a third-generation family member runs the business — with antique family photos dating back to the Mexican Revolution bedecking the walls (one photo of the original shop owner, Don Manuel Flores, and his wife hangs stoically beneath two old rifles).

Rubén Olivares is the current face of operations. He married into the Flores family and has taken over the zarzaparilla tradition with pride.

A family tradition and recipe

“This region used to be known for cultivating pineapples and oranges, and that created a local exporting economy early on,” Olivares says. “But over time, with climate change and different farming methods, everything shifted, and pineapple exports migrated further south, due to the hotter temperatures down there. And this area, which has always been colder and at higher altitudes, began to grow coffee and other ingredients that were good for making zarzaparilla.”

Without revealing the specifics of their family recipe, he tells me their zarzaparilla is a mix of ginger, cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, lime, jamaica, egg whites and more. They also sell hidromiel (mead) and other liquors made from fermented oranges, arrowhead plants, cherry and crucetillo (a shrub that in the past was used to treat venomous snakebites).

The family’s zarza recipe has remained the same for more than a century and was patented in 1920 by Don Manuel Flores, but according to Olivares, Don Manuel only sold a few liters of it at the time. The family now regularly brews batches of around 1,000 liters and ships it all over Mexico. Predominantly made as a syrupy concentrate, the molasses-like mixture is put into various sizes of plastic bottles and jugs, which consumers can mix with any ratio of filtered or mineral water to their liking.

How the drink conquered the ‘Wild West’

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the beverage was viewed as a medicinal remedy and was brought to the U.S. According to The Seattle Times, “Sarsaparilla was widely consumed all across 19th-century America, easy to find in the local saloon if the one-road town one rode into had no dedicated apothecary or pharmacy, and was supposedly quite popular with cowboys and ranchers looking to tame a rumbling tummy or put a little pep in their step, much as people use kombucha today.” Eventually — and it’s unclear when, why or how — zarzaparilla (made from “dried root bark of several plants in the genus Smilax,” which grew plentifully in Veracruz) was replaced by sassafras, and zarzaparilla became known as root beer. (In 1960, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration banned real sassafras in commercial root beer as safrole in high amounts was found to be carcinogenic.)

Throughout it all, zarza remained the dominant beverage of choice in and around the town of its origin in Veracruz. The Flores family is no longer the only one making it, either: A Google Maps search will reveal no fewer than five other zarzaparilla businesses in the town of about 23 square miles (for comparison’s sake, Mexico City is estimated at 573 square miles, yet according to Google, unfortunately has no official zarzaparilla-dedicated outlets).

Travel attractions in Teocelo

Teocelo has other worthwhile features besides zarza: It’s the site of the Fiesta Patronal, a weekend-long celebration that includes parades, fireworks and religious celebrations in honor of the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion. At the pueblo’s main entrance, there’s a bee sanctuary that produces all kinds of honey products you likely won’t find anywhere else, at least not in abundance — jugs of honey wine, salsa macha made with honey and “honey butter” (akin to peanut butter, with a similarly thick consistency) in variations that range from almond and walnut to berry or garlic.

Note: The honey shop, known as La Mielada, or “The Honeydew,” also has an accompanying restaurant that serves honeyed meats and breads, with an affordable selection of beverages like the aforementioned honey wine or my personal favorite, a mug of locally cultivated coffee with large dollops of organic honey mixed in — a pure delight of sweet and bitter flavors. For outdoor-seeking adventurers, the surrounding area also offers waterfalls, hikes, cabins and whitewater rapids.

To be sure, there’s no shortage of offerings — and mugs of zarza — to enjoy for a weekend in the chilly mountain locale.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let’s start today’s column with a quick quiz:

Pop Quiz Question #1: What is currently the top Mexican export to the United States?

If you are like most people, you are thinking of one of three categories: alcoholic beverages (think tequila, mezcal, Corona beer), food (perhaps avocados, jalapenos, tomatoes) or automobiles. All of those answers are incorrect.

Pop Quiz Question #2: Which country sells more AI servers and equipment to the United States, Mexico or Taiwan?

Of course, most people answer Taiwan. That would also be incorrect.

Mexico’s server-related exports to the US have overtaken autos, underscoring how AI data-center demand is reshaping its export base. Source: @financialtimes https://t.co/QtrH6mKZ0I pic.twitter.com/pyRYc40ktb — (((The Daily Shot))) (@SoberLook) August 7, 2026

Sometimes just one picture, or in this case — one chart recently published by the Financial Times — can be incredibly insightful. Above, you’ll see a chart comparing Mexican exports of two product categories from 2010 to the present day. The blue line shows vehicles, which Mexico has been exporting for over 60 years. Last year, nearly 80% of Mexico’s light vehicle exports went to the United States. The red line shows server-related hardware (think AI data centers). The x-axis shows the years from 2010 to 2026. The y-axis shows monthly exports in billions of US dollars.

As can be clearly seen, exports of server-related hardware have absolutely exploded in the past two years, to the point where they are now surpassing vehicles. Last month alone, over US $15 billion of these products were exported. Think about that for a minute. The news is filled on a daily basis with headlines telling us that Trump has decided not to renew the USMCA or that Trump commented that “we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” Other headlines lead us to believe that tariffs are being slapped on most Mexican goods, significantly hurting Mexico in the process. Neither is true.

That being said, much of the conversation often seems to revolve around two categories of products highly influenced by two distinct voting groups in the U.S. The first is union members and more specifically the members of the United Auto Workers, who have an obvious interest in keeping as much vehicle production as possible in the country. The second is U.S. farmers, who naturally want to keep food production domestic. As a result of these two powerful and influential groups, those segments are what we most often hear about — more specifically cars and tomatoes. And in fact, the U.S. currently has a 17% “antidumping” tariff on Mexican tomatoes and a relatively small and extremely complex-to-calculate tariff on Mexican vehicles. Fun fact: One of the final projects my senior year of college was to analyze the impact of U.S. tomato tariff practices and policies on Mexico. (Yes, I am aware of what an exceptionally boring topic that is for a final project!)

Perhaps not surprisingly, server equipment from Mexico has a 0% tariff from the United States. The most in-demand product on the planet right now has firmly established Mexico in its supply chain, and investment, jobs and exports are all booming in this area. Taiwanese companies are investing heavily in Mexico. It’s all happening very fast. It’s quite exciting and going to be very interesting to continue to follow.

So while most headlines would have you believe that the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship is in shambles, the reality is as follows:

1. Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-moves-past-taiwan-as-top-ai-server-exporter-to-united-states/

2. Mexico is now by far the leading exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-in-numbers-mexico-exports-us-china-canada/

3. Inflation is now lower in Mexico than in the U.S. for the first time: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/inflation-mexico-lower-united-states-why-thats-such-a-big-deal-a-perspective-from-our-ceo/

4. Mexico’s export revenue is up 25% so far this year: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/mexico-export-revenue-this-year/

So what’s the bottom line here? Follow the data, not the noise, and stay tuned to what is the most dynamic segment in the world, growing fast and furious right here in Mexico.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Missed the deadline? Here’s how to get your cell phone service back
World.content:
The first enforced deadline for compliance with mandatory cell phone registration came and went on Aug. 15 and approximately 2.6 million phone lines were suspended, prompting chaos and confusion for users whose now-unregistered phone numbers end in “0.”

Mexico’s Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT) announced on Thursday that nearly 9.7 million users whose number ends in “0” successfully registered their cell phones before the deadline.

The CRT also said that just over 2.3 million users whose lines had been suspended managed to reactivate their phone service by Aug. 19. Another 2.6 million mobile phones are expected to be reactivated in the coming days, while the CRT expects 2.5 million “unused” lines to be decommissioned.

Those who failed to register before the deadline faced plenty of online misinformation, but those whose service was suspended can still recover their service because their phone number was not canceled.

To reactivate the service, users must complete the registration process via their phone company. Prepaid lines must also be registered to remain active.

You can register through the phone company’s registration portal and by verifying your identity. Links to all providers’ platforms can be found on the CRT website here.

You can also complete the process in person at one of your company’s customer service centers, where staff is on hand to assist with the registration.

Mexican mobile phone owners must provide a CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) and a valid official ID, such as the INE-issued voter ID.

Foreigners must also register their phone lines (if it is a Mexican provider) by using the corresponding identity or immigration document, such as a resident visa or a passport.

Procedures vary slightly depending on the phone company, but the process is free.

It is important to note that suspended lines can still make calls to emergency numbers, citizen services and their phone company. They will also continue to receive earthquake alerts and they can be used to complete the registration process.

The government mandated cell phone registration procedures in an effort to eliminate anonymous mobile lines, stop criminal extortion and curb the use of untraceable “burner” prepaid SIM cards.

The CRT had originally established a June 30 deadline for all cell phones to be registered, but when it became apparent that a significant number of users would see their lines suspended, the deadline was extended.

The official schedule to register cell phones now depends on the final digit of your phone number. If your phone number ends in “1,” you must register by Aug. 31. If it ends in “2,” your deadline is Sept. 15, and so on through the end of the year as shown in the graphic above.

In its Aug. 20 report, the CRT said a total of 73.2 million lines — or 60.5% of the total lines expected to be connected in the country — were registered. By the end of the registration process, it expects a purge of around 25 million lines.

With reports from El Universal, Wired and LatinUS

Datafolha presidential polls released on Saturday 22 August 2026 show Brazil split by region. With Flávio Bolsonaro leading in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro while Lula dominates Minas Gerais and Pernambuco.

The state-level numbers, published by Folha de S. Paulo and g1, reveal a country divided along economic and historical lines.

Datafolha Presidential Polls Reveal Regional Divide

Datafolha presidential polls, commissioned by Folha de S. Paulo and TV Globo, covered five states and the federal district.

Fieldwork ran from Tuesday 18 to Friday 21 August 2026, depending on the state. The national survey, released on Friday 21 August, put Lula at 39% and Flávio Bolsonaro at 33% in the first round.

However, the state breakdowns show that this six-point lead is not uniform across the country. The state polls were commissioned by the same clients as the national survey.

However, they were registered separately with the electoral court. The state polls were registered with the electoral court under distinct numbers.

In addition, the national survey was registered as BR-04496/2026.

São Paulo and Rio Favor Bolsonaro

In São Paulo, Brazil’s largest electorate, Flávio Bolsonaro of the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) leads with 37% against Lula’s 33%. The gap of 4 points is larger than the margin of error of 2 percentage points.

Rio de Janeiro shows an even wider lead for Bolsonaro, with 41% to Lula’s 36%. That 5-point gap is larger than the poll’s 3-point margin of error.

São Paulo’s poll was registered as BR-07185/2026, with 1,610 interviews. Meanwhile, Rio’s registration was BR-08448/2026, with 1,204 interviews.

Flávio Bolsonaro is a serving senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Meanwhile, Lula is the sitting president in his third term.

Minas Gerais and Pernambuco Back Lula

By contrast, Lula, the sitting president from the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT), leads in Minas Gerais with 37% against Bolsonaro’s 31%. The 6-point gap is double the 3-point margin of error.

Pernambuco, the only Northeast state polled, gives Lula a commanding 56% to 24% lead. That 32-point gap is far beyond the 3-point margin, making it the strongest result for Lula in this batch.

Minas Gerais registered as BR-04396/2026, and Pernambuco as BR-00109/2026. Both had 1,204 interviews and a 3-point margin of error.

The Northeast is historically pro-Lula, and Pernambuco’s 32-point lead reflects that. However, Minas Gerais, a Southeast state, also backs Lula, showing regional nuances.

Every Gap Is Wider Than the Error Margin

In all four state contests, the gap between the two leaders is larger than that poll’s margin of error. Each result therefore points in a clear direction.

For example, São Paulo’s 4-point gap against a 2-point margin and Rio’s 5-point gap against 3 points both confirm clear leads. Meanwhile, Minas Gerais and Pernambuco show Lula ahead by margins that are statistically significant.

The gaps in all four states exceed their respective margins of error. As a result, each contest shows a clear leader, not a tie.

Each margin of error is specific to its state’s sample size. As a result, these gaps are statistically significant, not ties.

Approval Ratings Mirror the Voting Patterns

Lula’s government approval ratings follow a similar regional pattern. In São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, only 27% rate his government as great or good, while 48% say bad or terrible.

In Pernambuco, 46% approve of Lula’s government, the best score among the five units surveyed. The Distrito Federal, which contains the capital Brasília, shows the worst rejection at 51% bad or terrible.

Lula’s approval in Minas Gerais was not reported in this batch. However, the Distrito Federal showed the worst rejection score at 51%.

Lula’s approval in São Paulo and Rio is low, matching his vote share there. Meanwhile, Pernambuco’s high approval aligns with his strong lead.

Understanding the Regional Definitions

The Southeast (Sudeste) is Brazil’s richest and most populous region, including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Minas Gerais. The Northeast (Nordeste) is poorer and historically pro-Lula, with Pernambuco as one of its states.

The Distrito Federal sits in the Centre-West (Centro-Oeste) region. Although it was polled, no clean Lula-versus-Flávio presidential figure is available for it, only government approval numbers.

São Paulo is called the biggest ‘colégio eleitoral’ in Portuguese. It simply means the largest bloc of registered voters.

The Distrito Federal, containing Brasília, is in the Centre-West. Although polled, its presidential figure is not reported, only approval numbers.

Methodology and Registration Details

Each state poll was registered with Brazil’s top electoral court, the Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), as required by law. The registration numbers allow the public to check the methodology.

Meanwhile, São Paulo had 1,610 interviews with a 2-point margin of error. Rio, Minas Gerais, and Pernambuco each had 1,204 with a 3-point margin.

The Distrito Federal poll had 910 interviews with a 3-point margin. A registration number starting with BR- is filed nationally with the TSE.

The São Paulo survey also carries a state-level number, SP-01806/2026. Datafolha is owned by Folha de S.

Paulo and is a widely cited pollster. The registration numbers ensure transparency, as required by the TSE.

What These Polls Mean for October

Brazil votes in October 2026, and a candidate needs over 50% in the first round to avoid a runoff. These first-round figures are separate from any runoff scenario, so they should not be compared directly.

The regional split suggests that the campaign will be fought on local ground. While Bolsonaro’s son dominates in the Southeast’s biggest states, Lula’s strength in the Northeast could prove decisive.

The regional pattern shows Bolsonaro leading in two Southeast states, while Lula leads in another. Meanwhile, Pernambuco, a Northeast state, gives Lula a 32-point lead.

The regional divide could shape campaign strategies in the coming months. However, these first-round figures do not predict the October outcome.

Datafolha Presidential Polls Summary

In short, Datafolha presidential polls show a Brazil divided by region, with no single candidate leading everywhere. Flávio Bolsonaro leads in São Paulo and Rio, while Lula leads in Minas Gerais and Pernambuco.

These state numbers come from the same field operation as the governor polls but are a separate set of questions. Overall, the picture is one of a fragmented electorate heading into the October vote.

Datafolha is owned by Folha de S. Paulo and is a widely cited pollster.

The state numbers were published on Saturday 22 August 2026. The state numbers were published on Saturday 22 August 2026.

Meanwhile, the national survey, released a day earlier, showed a different overall picture.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the Datafolha presidential polls show for São Paulo?

In São Paulo, Flávio Bolsonaro leads with 37% against Lula’s 33% in the first round. The margin of error is 2 percentage points, so the 4-point gap is statistically significant.

Is Lula ahead in any Southeast state?

Yes, Lula leads in Minas Gerais with 37% to Bolsonaro’s 31%. This is despite Minas Gerais being part of the Southeast, where Bolsonaro leads in the other two states polled.

Why is there no presidential figure for the Distrito Federal?

The Distrito Federal was polled, but the reporting mixes the presidential question with the local governor race. Therefore, only government approval numbers are available, showing 27% approval and 51% disapproval.

What is the margin of error for these state polls?

São Paulo has a margin of error of 2 percentage points. While Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, and Pernambuco each have 3 points.

World.title: Bolsonaro Barred From Voting in Brazil’s October Election
World.content:
Brazil · POLITICS

Key Facts — 2023 TSE ruling Declared Bolsonaro ineligible for eight years for abuse of power, affecting only his candidacy.

— Criminal conviction STF sentenced Bolsonaro to 27 years and 3 months for the coup plot.

— Political rights suspended Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered suspension on 25 November 2025, after conviction became final.

— TSE confirmation The electoral court confirmed in a note to Gazeta do Povo on 21 August 2026 that the suspension stands.

— Election date Brazil votes on 4 October 2026, with a runoff on 25 October if needed.

The former president loses his vote as an automatic consequence of a final criminal conviction. Separate from his earlier ban on running for office.

The Supreme Federal Court in Brasília. Its ruling, not the electoral court’s, cost Bolsonaro his vote.

Bolsonaro barred from voting in Brazil’s October election. As confirmed by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) in a note to the newspaper Gazeta do Povo on 21 August 2026.

The restriction follows the suspension of his political rights by the Supreme Federal Court (STF) after his criminal conviction became final.

Two Separate Penalties

However, the voting ban stems from the criminal conviction, not the 2023 electoral ruling. Although the TSE declared him ineligible in 2023, that decision did not touch his right to vote.

The loss of his vote came later, from the Supreme Federal Court (STF), as an automatic effect of a final criminal sentence. Brazilian law treats the right to vote (capacidade eleitoral ativa) and the right to be a candidate (capacidade eleitoral passiva) as distinct.

The 2023 ruling restricted only his passive electoral capacity, while the 2025 STF order suspended his active capacity. As a result, the two penalties operate independently under Brazilian law.

The distinction matters because each penalty comes from a different court. In addition, the 2023 ruling left his vote intact, while the 2025 order suspended it.

Bolsonaro Barred from Voting

Bolsonaro was convicted in criminal action AP 2.668/DF before the STF, related to the so-called ‘núcleo 1’ of the coup plot. Therefore, the STF published the full written ruling on 22 October 2025.

The sentence was 27 years and 3 months. On 25 November 2025, Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered that Bolsonaro’s political rights be suspended, as the conviction had become final.

The criminal conviction became final, triggering the automatic suspension under article 15, III. Therefore, Justice Moraes acted on 25 November 2025 to enforce this constitutional provision.

The conviction became final at some point after the ruling was published. Meanwhile, the exact date of that finality was not confirmed by the research.

What the Suspension Means

According to O Globo, Bolsonaro loses voting, candidacy, party membership, and posts requiring active electoral capacity. Still, the suspension lasts as long as the criminal sentence’s effects.

This is automatic under article 15, III of the Federal Constitution, which suspends political rights on a final conviction. No separate electoral trial is needed.

The suspension includes the right to vote, to be a candidate, and to join a party. However, it lasts only as long as the sentence’s effects, not permanently.

The suspension also affects his ability to join a political party. However, it does not last forever, only as long as the sentence’s effects.

The TSE’s Role

The TSE is Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which administers elections and keeps the national voter register. Meanwhile, when a criminal court suspends political rights, the TSE records that status.

On 21 August 2026, the TSE confirmed in a written note to Gazeta do Povo that Bolsonaro’s political rights remain suspended. The note said the suspension lasts from the moment the conviction became final until his sentence has been served.

The TSE records the suspension in the voter register, but it did not issue the decision. In addition, the confirmation came as a written note, not a public ruling.

The TSE’s note to Gazeta do Povo was its only confirmation. Still, no public ruling or website statement was found by the research.

The 2023 Electoral Ruling

In contrast, the 2023 TSE ruling only blocked Bolsonaro from running for office. Moreover, the court declared him ineligible for eight years from 2022 on 30 June 2023.

However, this was for abuse of power and improper media use. The court’s wording specified the restriction on his passive electoral capacity, meaning the impossibility of being a candidate.

G1 reported that the decision did not cancel or suspend his political rights, and his ability to vote remained. That ruling’s penalty was ineligibility for eight years, counted from 2022.

Meanwhile, it did not affect his voting rights, as G1 clarified. That ruling came from the TSE, not the STF.

As a result, it did not trigger the constitutional suspension of political rights.

The Clean Record Law

The 25 November 2025 decision also instructed the STF registry to notify the TSE under the Clean Record Law (Lei Complementar 135/2010). This law bars a person convicted by a panel of judges from contesting elections for eight years after the sentence is served.

The notification was for the purposes of Bolsonaro’s ineligibility following the conviction. By contrast, this is separate from the suspension of his voting rights.

The notification under the Clean Record Law concerned ineligibility, not voting. Still, both penalties stem from the same criminal conviction.

The Clean Record Law adds an eight-year ineligibility after a sentence is served. However, this is separate from the suspension of voting rights.

The Upcoming Election

Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October 2026 in the first round, with a runoff on 25 October if needed. The election covers the presidency, governors, senators, and federal and state deputies.

The dates are set by TSE Resolution No. In fact, the number is 23,751. Bolsonaro, as a voter, will not be able to participate in this election.

Bolsonaro will be unable to vote in the 2026 elections, as confirmed by the TSE. Consequently, his participation is barred for this electoral cycle.

The election will take place on 4 October 2026. Consequently, Bolsonaro will not cast a ballot in that vote.

One Person Affected

This restriction applies only to Jair Bolsonaro personally, as a consequence of his own conviction. It does not extend to his family, his party, or his supporters.

Moreover, no other person’s registration is affected, according to the research. The suspension is recorded against his entry on the electoral roll.

The restriction is personal to Bolsonaro, not affecting his family or party. Therefore, no other voter faces this suspension.

The restriction applies solely to Bolsonaro, not to any relative or ally. Therefore, his family and supporters retain their voting rights.

Background on Bolsonaro

Jair Messias Bolsonaro was President of Brazil from 2019 to 2022, losing the 2022 election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He was later convicted by the STF over the plot to overturn that result.

In short, the TSE ruled in 2023, the STF published in October 2025, and Moraes ordered suspension in November 2025. The TSE confirmed the suspension in August 2026, just before the election.

He served as president from 2019 to 2022 and lost the 2022 election. Afterward, his conviction over the coup plot led to these penalties.

He was president from 2019 to 2022 and lost the 2022 election. Afterward, his conviction over the coup plot led to these penalties.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Bolsonaro barred from voting?

Bolsonaro barred from voting is due to the suspension of his political rights by the Supreme Federal Court (STF) after his criminal conviction became final. The suspension is automatic under article 15, III of the Constitution.

Did the 2023 electoral ruling remove his right to vote?

No. The 2023 TSE ruling only made him ineligible to run for office. His ability to vote remained, as G1 reported at the time.

How long will the suspension last?

The suspension lasts as long as the effects of the criminal sentence. The TSE confirmed it remains in effect until his sentence has been served.

Does this affect other people?

No. The restriction applies only to Jair Bolsonaro personally, not to his family, party, or supporters.

Sources: O Globo; Gazeta do Povo; Agência Brasil; G1; Brasil de Fato; Migalhas; Tribunal Superior Eleitoral.

Has flagged a Vaca Muerta espionage risk from Chinese technology in the country’s key shale basin. The United States ambassador to Argentina, Peter Lamelas.

Ambassador Warns of Espionage Risk

However, the US ambassador to Argentina opposed Chinese technology in Vaca Muerta, citing the Vaca Muerta espionage risk. La Nación reported his remarks on 22 August 2026.

In fact, he said high-risk Chinese firms like Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Hytera, Dahua and DJI face communist government designs. Lamelas added that Chinese law forces suppliers to aid Beijing’s spies, creating the Vaca Muerta espionage risk.

However, the ambassador’s warning is not a confirmed finding, but a risk assessment. Still, he has repeated this message, as La Nación noted he ‘volvió a expresarse’.

His warnings were issued in English, not Spanish, according to the sourced reports. However, Argentine outlets translated them for local readers.

Vaca Muerta espionage risk overview

Vaca Muerta is a shale oil and gas formation in the province of Neuquén, in Argentine Patagonia. It is the country’s main unconventional hydrocarbon play.

Therefore, the basin is central to Argentina’s energy ambitions, driving record production and export growth. In the first half of 2026, Vaca Muerta accounted for 68 percent of national oil production and 67 percent of gas extracted.

Meanwhile, the basin’s importance is clear, since it drives record production. As a result, any threat to its development is taken seriously.

The basin’s strategic importance makes such warnings significant for investors. Meanwhile, no espionage has been proven, only the ambassador’s risk assessment.

Chinese Tech Companies Named

The ambassador named six Chinese firms in his warning: Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Hytera, Dahua and DJI. Still, these are the only Chinese companies he cited in the sourced material.

Lamelas issued his warnings in English, in statements and social-media posts that Argentine outlets translated into Spanish. No verified original Spanish-language quotation exists.

In addition, the ambassador’s list includes firms known for surveillance and telecom equipment. After naming them, he linked them to Beijing’s intelligence services.

The firms cited are known for telecom and surveillance equipment. After naming them, Lamelas stressed their obligation to Beijing’s intelligence services.

Earlier Warnings and Huawei Link

Before the La Nación report, Tiempo Argentino reported on 13 August 2026 that Lamelas warned investment would be affected by Huawei equipment. He was quoted as saying China requires companies to give the state access to any data passing through its technology.

The same report identified Huawei as the supplier of network electronics for fibre-optic projects by CALF, the provincial co-operative in Neuquén. Since then, the dispute has escalated, with visas cancelled for CALF directors.

In addition, the Chamber of Deputies summoned the ambassador to explain the pressure. Tiempo Argentino reported his warning on 13 August 2026.

Since then, the dispute has involved visa cancellations and a parliamentary summons.

CALF Co-operative Under Pressure

CALF, the Cooperativa Provincial de Servicios Públicos y Comunitarios de Neuquén, supplies electricity and telecommunications locally. Meanwhile, visas were cancelled for its directors amid the dispute over expanding a fibre-optic network in Vaca Muerta, according to Hoy Rojas.

As a result, Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies summoned the ambassador to clarify alleged diplomatic pressure against CALF over technology agreements with Huawei. The report framed the presence of Chinese state-linked suppliers as a risk to data security and international investment.

However, no outcome has been reported, such as contract cancellation or Huawei removal. Still, the summons shows parliamentary concern over the alleged pressure.

The Chamber of Deputies summoned the ambassador to clarify the pressure. However, no contract cancellation or Huawei removal has been reported.

AmCham Forum Remarks

At the AmCham Energy Forum, Lamelas pressed Argentina to limit Chinese technology in Vaca Muerta and protect Western investment. La Gaceta of Tucumán reported this on 13 August 2026.

He questioned the use of Chinese technology in strategic networks and warned it could hinder the arrival of foreign investment. In fact, this is the outlet’s paraphrase, not a direct quotation.

In fact, his remarks at the forum were paraphrased by La Gaceta, not quoted directly. After that, the ambassador continued to warn about Chinese technology in strategic networks.

La Gaceta paraphrased his remarks at the forum. In addition, he warned that Chinese technology could hinder foreign investment.

Visa Threats and China Reaction

In fact. El País reported on 7 August 2026 that the US threatens to withdraw visas of Argentine business people if they contract Huawei.

Therefore, this provoked a reaction from China. Lamelas told Clarín the matter was a security question for the United States.

Even so, the visa threat and China’s reaction were reported without specific quotations. No Argentine government response to the espionage-risk remarks was found.

Meanwhile, the visa threat and China’s reaction were reported without specific quotations. In addition, no Argentine government response to the espionage-risk remarks was found.

El País reported the visa threat and the Chinese response. Neither government set out its position in detail.

Vaca Muerta’s Economic Weight

Vaca Muerta is the main driver of Argentina’s record oil production, which reached 914,900 barrels per day in June 2026. Overall, unconventional oil accounted for 70 percent of accumulated production for the year.

The basin was the main engine of a record energy surplus in the first half of 2026. The Argentine government expects oil and gas exports from Vaca Muerta to total around US$17 billion in 2026.

In addition, the basin’s contribution to the energy surplus is significant. However, the US$17 billion export projection is separate from the US$14 billion total energy export estimate.

The basin drove a record energy surplus in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the government projects US$17 billion in exports from it this year.

Investment Needs and Projects

A private report cited by Infobae said Vaca Muerta needs US$22 billion of investment to sustain its export leap. YPF, the state-controlled oil company, is weighing investments of some US$130 billion over five years, mostly for drilling.

Compañía Mega S.A. announced an investment of US$360 million to expand production capacity for liquids in the Neuquén field. Two capacity projects are named: the expansion of Oldelval and the VMOS project.

In addition, they will widen crude export capacity towards the end of 2026. After these investments, export capacity will expand, especially with the VMOS project.

However, the report does not define what VMOS stands for. Oldelval’s expansion and the VMOS project will widen export capacity.

However, the report does not define what VMOS stands for.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Vaca Muerta espionage risk?

The US ambassador to Argentina, Peter Lamelas. Has warned that Chinese technology in Vaca Muerta poses a risk of espionage, cyberattacks and network disruptions.

Which Chinese companies did the ambassador name?

Lamelas named Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Hytera, Dahua and DJI. These are the only Chinese firms he cited in the sourced material.

Has espionage been proven in Vaca Muerta?

No. The espionage-risk language is the ambassador’s warning, not a confirmed finding. No Argentine government body, company or intelligence service has substantiated any espionage in the basin.

How significant is Vaca Muerta to Argentina’s economy?

Vaca Muerta drives record oil production, accounting for 68 percent of national output in the first half of 2026. It is expected to generate around US$17 billion in oil and gas exports in 2026.

World.title: Lula Promises Public Security Ministry at Rio Rally
World.content:
Brazil · POLITICS

Key Facts — Promise Lula promised to create a Public Security Ministry at a campaign rally in Bangu, Rio de Janeiro, on Saturday 22 August 2026.

— Condition The creation depends on approval of the public security constitutional amendment (PEC da Segurança Pública) by the Senate.

— Status The amendment has cleared the Chamber of Deputies but is stuck in the Senate, as reported by Folha de S.Paulo.

— Quote Lula said, ‘We are not going to put on a carnival, pyrotechnics, kill 100 or 200 [criminals]. We are going to arrest them.’

— Existing ministry The current federal department is the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, which would be split to create the new ministry.

The pledge depends on a constitutional amendment that is currently stalled in the Senate, according to reports from Folha de S. Paulo and G1.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva promised to create a Public Security Ministry at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Saturday 22 August 2026. The pledge is conditional on Congress approving a constitutional amendment that is currently stalled in the Senate.

Rally in Bangu

According to G1 Rio, Lula spoke at the Bangu Atlético Clube stadium in the Bangu neighbourhood of Rio’s West Zone. The event was a campaign rally, not a government act, as reported by Poder360 and G1 under their election coverage.

The president promised to create a Public Security Ministry, a separate department for security matters, as reported by G1 Rio. This ministry does not exist yet; the current federal department is the Ministry of Justice and Public Security.

The rally took place on Saturday 22 August 2026, according to multiple outlets. Meanwhile, the venue is also known as Estádio Moça Bonita, as reported by Diário de Pernambuco.

Constitutional Amendment Needed

The creation of the Public Security Ministry depends on a constitutional amendment, specifically the public security constitutional amendment (PEC da Segurança Pública). This amendment must pass both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate by three-fifths majorities in two rounds each.

The amendment has cleared the Chamber of Deputies; however, it is stalled in the Senate, according to Folha de S. Paulo.

Lula’s government programme states that once the Public Security amendment is approved, they will create the Ministry of Public Security. A PEC is a proposed amendment to Brazil’s constitution, requiring three-fifths majorities in both houses.

As a result, it is not law while it is in progress, according to the definition.

Lula’s Security Promise

At the rally, Lula said, ‘We are not going to put on a carnival, pyrotechnics, kill 100 or 200 [criminals]. We are going to arrest them.

In short, we will say the neighbourhood, school, and bakery belong to the people. It does not belong to the bandits.

That is what we are going to do. This statement was reported by G1 Rio, and it reflects a rejection of lethal raids in favour of arrests.

Poder360’s headline read ‘Lula says the government will not kill 100 or 200, but will arrest. The verbatim quote in Portuguese was published by G1 Rio on 22 August 2026.

However, the square brackets around ‘criminals’ are G1’s own clarification, not Lula’s word.

Criminal Factions

Moreover, Lula promised to remove criminal factions from Rio and give territories back to the people, as reported by G1 política. He said, ‘We are going to take the criminal out of your territory,’ according to Poder360.

The term ‘facção criminosa’ refers to organised criminal groups, the standard Brazilian term for armed gangs that hold territory. Lula’s promise is part of his broader security policy, which he says will prioritise arresting criminals.

Lula’s promise to remove factions is part of his broader security policy, which prioritises arrests. In addition, the term ‘vila’ refers to the community inside a favela, as defined.

Federal Police Training

In addition, Lula intends to expand federal government action against organised crime, as reported by G1 Rio. He also plans to expand the training of the Federal Police and the Federal Highway Police, according to G1 política.

These measures are part of his campaign platform, which he has been presenting at rallies across the country. At his first campaign rally in São Paulo on 16 August 2026, he made a similar promise, according to G1.

These measures aim to expand federal action against organised crime, as reported. Meanwhile, Lula used a similar formulation at his first rally in São Paulo, according to G1.

Energy Revolution

Lula also spoke about energy, promising to carry out Brazil’s ‘energy revolution’ if re-elected, as reported by Poder360. He said few countries have Brazil’s potential for an energy revolution, citing green hydrogen and solar power, according to Diário de Pernambuco.

However, G1 Rio reported the same passage as ‘energy renewal’ (renovação energética), not ‘revolution’. There is no single official formulation, so the discrepancy remains.

Lula’s energy promise is conditional on his re-election, as Poder360 reported. However, the two outlets used different terms for the same passage, so no single official formulation exists.

Data Centres

Lula mentioned a bill called Redata, which stands for the Special Taxation Regime for Data Centre Services. He said, ‘We are going to talk to the National Congress to approve the Redata bill to bring data centres to Brazil.

The Redata bill is a voluntary five-year tax-break scheme for companies that install or modernise data centres in Brazil. It was first issued as a provisional measure in September 2025, but that lapsed.

Instead, the replacement bill awaits Senate approval, per official records. The Redata bill awaits Senate approval, as it is still pending there.

Meanwhile, the government estimates the tax break at around R$5.2 billion in 2026, per the Chamber news service.

Critical Minerals

According to Diário de Pernambuco, Lula said he has no preference between countries and wants to build partnerships in critical minerals. This is the newspaper’s summary of his remarks, not a direct quotation.

The report does not name any specific country, and no other outlet in the research mentions this topic. Therefore, the details remain limited to that summary.

This summary from Diário de Pernambuco does not name any specific country. Still, it reflects Lula’s stated openness to partnerships in critical minerals.

Public Security Ministry

In short, the Public Security Ministry is a campaign promise that hinges on the public security constitutional amendment. The amendment has passed the Chamber but is stalled in the Senate, so the ministry does not yet exist.

Once the amendment is approved, Lula would create the ministry; however, until then, the existing Ministry of Justice remains responsible. The promise is conditional, and no act creating the ministry has been issued.

The existing Ministry of Justice and Public Security already covers policing and justice. However, the proposed new ministry would be a separate, security-only department carved out from it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Public Security Ministry?

The Public Security Ministry is a proposed federal department that would focus solely on security matters. It would be carved out from the existing Ministry of Justice and Public Security, which currently covers both policing and justice.

Why is the Public Security Ministry not created yet?

The creation depends on a constitutional amendment, specifically the public security constitutional amendment (PEC da Segurança Pública). This amendment must pass both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate by three-fifths majorities in two rounds each.

What did Lula say about killing criminals?

Lula said, ‘We are not going to put on a carnival, pyrotechnics, kill 100 or 200 [criminals]. We are going to arrest them.

What is the Redata bill?

Redata is the Special Taxation Regime for Data Centre Services. A voluntary five-year tax-break scheme for companies that install or modernise data centres in Brazil.

Sources: Valor; G1; Poder360; Folha de S.Paulo; Correio Braziliense; Diário de Pernambuco; Agência Brasil; Câmara dos Deputados; Senado Federal.

World.title: Brazil Fiscal Target Met Only Through Legal Carve-Outs
World.content:
Brazil · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Definition The IFI is a non-partisan technical body attached to Brazil’s Federal Senate.

— Primary result Federal revenue minus spending before interest payments on public debt.

— 2026 target Primary surplus of 0.25% of GDP, or R$34.3 billion, with a tolerance band.

— Precatórios Court-ordered payments excluded from target verification, totaling R$55.7 billion.

— Investor sentiment Negative outlook among fund managers rose from 40% to 54% in July 2026.

The underlying deficit is double the 2025 level, even as the target is formally met.

The National Congress in Brasília. The Independent Fiscal Institution is attached to the Federal Senate.

The Brazil fiscal target for 2026 will be met on paper, but only through legal carve-outs. Underneath them, the country’s finances are getting worse, not better.

The IFI, a technical watchdog attached to the Federal Senate, puts the effective primary deficit at about 0.4 percent of GDP.

The Two Faces of Brazil’s Fiscal Target

Brazil fiscal target for 2026 is set to be met, yet the numbers tell two very different stories. The IFI, or Instituição Fiscal Independente, is a non-partisan body attached to the Federal Senate that monitors public accounts.

According to its Fiscal Monitoring Report No. 115, the effective primary result. Revenue minus spending before interest—will be a deficit of about 0.4% of GDP.

In cash terms, that is a shortfall of R$52.0 billion for the year. Meanwhile, the result measured for Brazil fiscal target verification, after legal exclusions, should be a surplus of about 0.1% of GDP.

That is inside the tolerance band, so the target is formally met. The IFI published its Fiscal Monitoring Report No. 115 on Thursday 20 August 2026.

However, the report shows the effective deficit and the target-basis surplus coexist in the same year.

Brazil Fiscal Target: Primary Result Explained

The primary result is the balance of federal revenue minus spending before interest payments on the public debt. A primary deficit means non-interest spending exceeded revenue, which affects the Brazil fiscal target.

However, Brazil’s law distinguishes the ‘effective’ primary result from the result ‘for the purposes of verifying the target. ‘ The former counts everything and drives the debt path.

As a result, the two numbers for 2026 run in opposite directions: a deficit on the underlying measure. A surplus on the target-verification measure.

The effective primary result drives the debt path, while the target-basis measure is used for legal compliance. Meanwhile, the law allows certain items to be excluded from the latter calculation.

The Role of the IFI

The IFI is not part of the government. Instead, it is a technical body attached to the Federal Senate, the upper house of Congress.

Its projections are its own estimates, not official government figures. In its report, the IFI stresses that the effective deficit of about 0.4% of GDP is what matters for the debt trajectory.

The target-basis surplus is a separate, legally defined measure. The IFI’s criticism is that formal compliance with the primary result target ‘coexists with the realisation of effective primary deficits.

The IFI’s projections are its own estimates, not official government figures. Still, its analysis highlights the gap between formal compliance and the underlying fiscal reality.

The Target and Its Tolerance Band

The 2026 target is set by the LDO, or Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias, the Budget Guidelines Law passed by Congress. The centre of the target is a primary surplus of 0.25% of GDP, or R$34.3 billion.

The target carries a tolerance band of 0.25 percentage point of GDP either side. That gives an upper limit of about R$68.5 billion and a lower limit of R$0—zero deficit still counts as compliance.

Therefore, the projected target-basis surplus of about 0.1% of GDP falls within the band, so the target is met. The lower limit of the tolerance band is zero deficit, so any surplus counts as compliance.

Consequently, the projected surplus of 0.1% of GDP meets the target.

Legal Carve-Outs Explained

The main carve-out identified by name is precatórios, court-ordered payment orders issued when a final judgment goes against the state. These are legal obligations the government must pay, but they sit outside the primary target arithmetic.

The 2026 budget guidelines annex allows R$55.1 billion, equal to 0.40% of GDP, to be compensated out of the target calculation. In execution, the government reports R$55.7 billion of precatórios spending is not counted, citing a constitutional provision.

In short, formal compliance will be reached after legal deductions totalling R$62.8 billion on the government’s calculations and R$69.8 billion on the IFI’s. Plus use of the tolerance band.

Only precatórios are identified by name in the official documents as a deduction. However, the total deductions include other items not itemised in the sources consulted.

The Underlying Deficit Worsens

The IFI estimates a structural primary deficit of 1.4% of potential GDP in the four quarters to June 2026. That is double the 0.7% recorded in the same period of 2025.

This suggests the effective deficit is not a one-off but a trend. The IFI says the improvement in the target-basis result ‘mostly reflects downward revisions in projections of mandatory spending’ rather than a structural reversal.

In short, the legal carve-outs mask a deteriorating fiscal picture. The structural deficit doubled from 0.7% to 1.4% of potential GDP in a year.

As a result, the effective fiscal position is deteriorating despite the target being met.

Government Projections Improve

Moreover, the government’s own Primary Revenue and Expenditure Assessment Report, released in July. Raised the target-basis primary result from a projected surplus of R$4.1 billion to R$10.8 billion.

This came with no need for a spending freeze, known as contingenciamento. However, the IFI attributes this improvement to revisions in mandatory spending projections, not to a real improvement in the effective result.

Still, the government’s numbers show formal compliance is within reach without additional measures. The government’s July report raised the target-basis surplus to R$10.8 billion.

Nevertheless, the IFI says this reflects lower mandatory spending projections, not a structural improvement.

Investor Sentiment Turns Negative

Separately, investor sentiment has soured. Meanwhile.

A survey by XP found that the share of macro hedge-fund managers with a negative outlook for the Brazilian economy rose from 40% in June to 54% in August. The positive view fell from 24% to 8%.

This survey, taken before a Copom meeting, reflects the mood of 23 fund managers, not business confidence broadly. Even so, the pessimism aligns with the IFI’s concerns about the effective deficit.

The survey of 23 macro hedge-fund managers showed pessimism rising sharply. Meanwhile, the positive outlook fell from 24% to 8%, reflecting investor concerns.

What This Means for Brazil

In conclusion, Brazil’s fiscal target for 2026 will be met on paper, but the underlying reality is a growing deficit. The IFI’s projections highlight the gap between legal compliance and economic substance.

The use of carve-outs like precatórios is legal, but it raises questions about the credibility of the target. Investors seem to be taking note, as sentiment has turned negative.

Overall, the fiscal picture is more fragile than the headline target suggests. The fiscal target is met on paper, but the effective deficit persists.

Therefore, the credibility of the target may be questioned, as investors seem to notice.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s fiscal target for 2026?

The target is a primary surplus of 0.25% of GDP, or R$34.3 billion, with a tolerance band of 0.25 percentage point. The lower limit is zero, so a zero deficit still counts as compliance.

Why is the target met despite a deficit?

The target is met because of legal carve-outs, mainly precatórios, which are excluded from the target calculation. The effective primary deficit is about 0.4% of GDP, but the target-basis result is a small surplus.

What are precatórios?

Precatórios are court-ordered payment orders issued when a final judgment goes against the state. They are legal obligations but are excluded from the primary target arithmetic under a constitutional rule.

What is the IFI’s role?

The IFI is a non-partisan technical body attached to the Federal Senate. It monitors public accounts and publishes its own projections, which are not official government figures.

Sources: IFI/Senado Federal; Valor Econômico; Jornal do Comércio; InfoMoney; Brazil’s Ministry of Planning; Presidência da República.

World.title: Nicaragua Constitutional Reform Would Void Foreign Laws

Nicaragua · POLITICS

— Second vote A further approval is reported for September 2026.

— Publication The reform has not yet appeared in the official gazette, La Gaceta.

— Scope The text targets laws, regulations, and rules from other states and international bodies.

— Status The change is a proposal, not yet a constitutional reform in force.

The proposal would strip foreign laws and international rulings of any legal effect inside Nicaragua. But it must pass a second legislative vote before it can take force.

The chamber of Nicaragua’s National Assembly in session.

Nicaragua constitutional reform would void foreign laws if it clears a second legislative vote, according to reports from La Nación and Reforma. The National Assembly gave its first approval on 22 August 2026 to amend article 12 of the constitution.

What the Proposal Says

In fact, the proposed wording, read aloud by Assembly president Gustavo Porras, declares that Nicaragua prohibits the extraterritoriality of foreign laws. Moreover, it states that no foreign or international law shall have effect if it disparages Nicaragua’s sovereignty.

In addition, only agreements signed in the name of the Nicaraguan state would apply under the proposal. These are fragments quoted from the floor, not the full consolidated text of the amended article.

The proposal would declare that no foreign law has legal effect inside Nicaragua. However, it also says only agreements signed in the state’s name would apply.

The proposed wording would make foreign laws ineffective inside Nicaragua. However, it does not name any specific law or international body.

Nicaragua Constitutional Reform: First Step

Under Nicaraguan procedure, a constitutional change cannot take effect on a single vote. It must be approved by the National Assembly, then approved again in a separate, subsequent legislature.

Therefore, the 22 August 2026 vote is only the first of two required approvals. The second vote is reported for September 2026, though no specific day was given.

This two-legislature process ensures the change cannot take effect quickly. Meanwhile, the second vote is scheduled for September 2026.

The first-legislature approval is a proposal, not a reform in force. Therefore, it must be voted again in a second legislature.

Not Yet in the Official Gazette

The reform has not been published in La Gaceta, Nicaragua’s official state gazette. Recent issues from 19 and 21 August 2026 do not contain it.

As a result, the consolidated text of the constitution online still shows the previous wording of article 12. The change remains in process, not yet part of the law.

Since the reform is unpublished, its legal status remains pending. In addition, the online constitution still reflects the old article 12.

The reform has not appeared in the official gazette, La Gaceta. As a result, it has no legal effect until published.

Unanimous Approval in the Assembly

The National Assembly press service reported that the reform plan was approved unanimously. No vote count or breakdown was published.

Meanwhile, the Assembly is controlled by the governing Frente Sandinista de Liberación Nacional, led by Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo. The unanimous vote shows strong backing from the governing party.

Still, this approval does not make the reform law yet. The vote was unanimous, according to the Assembly’s press service.

Meanwhile, no vote count was published.

Scope of the Proposed Change

In addition, the proposal excludes foreign laws and rules from Nicaragua’s legal order. However, this applies only where they act against independence, sovereignty, or peace.

It names no specific foreign law, court, or international organisation. Instead, it refers only to general categories: other states, groups of states, and international bodies.

This means the text is broad but not targeted at any named entity. The text covers laws, regulations, and rules from other states and international bodies.

However, it does not name any specific entity or law. The proposal covers laws, regulations, and rules from other states and international bodies.

However, it does not target any specific foreign law or court.

Part of a Larger Reform Package

The amendment is part of a package called the ‘Propuesta de Reformas Constitucionales y Legales’. It was drawn up by the Assembly’s Constitutional Commission together with the Supreme Electoral Council.

According to the official gazette’s site, the proposal will be sent to the Presidency for review and authorisation. This shows it is still in the legislative pipeline.

This package also includes changes to electoral participation, according to official sources. As a result, the amendment is part of a broader legislative effort.

The package was drawn up by the Constitutional Commission and the Supreme Electoral Council. In addition, it will be sent to the Presidency for review.

Separate Elections Proposal

In a separate strand, President Daniel Ortega said on 23 July 2026 that there would be no more elections, according to EFE. This was part of a speech at the commemoration of the Sandinista revolution’s anniversary.

However, official documents describe reforms that restrict opposition participation and extend mandates, not a technical abolition of all elections. No published reform eliminating elections has been found.

Ortega’s remarks on elections were reported on 23 July 2026, 30 days before the article 12 vote. Meanwhile, the elections package focuses on restricting opposition participation, not abolishing all elections.

Ortega’s remarks were reported on 23 July 2026, 30 days before the article 12 vote. Still, no published reform eliminating elections has been found.

Timeline of the Two Tracks

Overall, Ortega’s remarks were reported on 23 July 2026, and the article 12 vote took place on 22 August 2026. They were 30 days apart.

These are two separate reform tracks that happen to share a reported September voting date. Neither caused the other in any source on this sheet.

So, it would be wrong to see them as directly linked. The two proposals are separate and not causally linked in any source.

Therefore, they should be viewed as independent legislative efforts. The two reform tracks are separate and not causally linked in any source.

Therefore, they should be viewed as independent legislative efforts.

What Happens Next

If the proposal passes a second legislature in September, it would then need publication in La Gaceta to take effect. Until then, it remains a proposal, not a constitutional reform in force.

In short, the Nicaragua constitutional reform would void foreign laws only after these steps are completed. For now, it is a first-step approval with a conditional future.

After a second vote in September, the reform would still need gazette publication. Until then, it remains only a proposal with conditional effects.

If the proposal passes a second legislature in September, it would then need gazette publication. Until then, it remains only a proposal with conditional effects.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Nicaragua constitutional reform propose?

The proposal would amend article 12 to declare that foreign laws and rules from international bodies have no legal effect in Nicaragua. It would apply only to those that disparage the country’s independence, sovereignty, or peace.

Has the reform already taken effect?

No, it has only passed its first legislative vote on 22 August 2026. It requires a second approval in a later legislature, expected in September 2026, and publication in the official gazette.

What is the role of the National Assembly in this process?

The National Assembly is Nicaragua’s single-chamber parliament. It gave unanimous first approval to the proposal.

Does the reform target any specific international body?

No, the proposed wording names no specific court, law, or organisation. It refers only to general categories like other states and international bodies.

Sources: La Nación (Costa Rica); Reforma (Mexico); O Povo (Brazil); EFE; La Prensa Gráfica (El Salvador); Infobae; La Gaceta, Diario Oficial; Asamblea Nacional de Nicaragua; Banco Central de Nicaragua.

— Country risk 505 basis points on Friday 21 August 2026, up 68 points from a month earlier.

— Constitutional rule Article 90 permits one consecutive four-year term, so a 2027 run is allowed.

— Polling 65.3% disapprove of the government, while 33.4% approve, per a Perfil survey.

— Inflation Consumer prices rose 2.1% in July 2026, with 33.8% over twelve months.

President Milei’s statement of intent lands as Argentina’s country risk climbs to its highest level in more than two months. With market analysts pointing to external headwinds and social mood.
