World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: Name of Kazakhstan’s Vice President to be announced within 7–10 days - Tokayev
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 23. The name of the person who will take the post of Vice President of Kazakhstan will be announced within the next week or 10 days.

According to the presidential press service, President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev made the remarks during a briefing for media representatives.

“Everyone is asking about the position of Vice President. Indeed, this is a significant change. We deliberately established this new position in the Constitution. I would not be mistaken in saying that it is extremely necessary. In the current challenging times, such a position is particularly needed by our country. Who will take the post of Vice President will become known within the next week or 10 days. It would be premature to name the person now. I think it will be a well-known person whom you all know well,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev noted that Kazakhstan would implement other reforms as well.

“For example, it is necessary to launch the work of a new state body — the Kazakhstan Halyk Kenesi. As far as I know, some citizens compare it with the Assembly. I believe the Kazakhstan Halyk Kenesi will strengthen and develop the work previously carried out by the Assembly. It can be described as a new multifunctional political mechanism. I am confident that the work of the Kazakhstan Halyk Kenesi will be productive,” he said.

According to the President, plans for the country's further development are ambitious.

“As I have said before, Kazakhstan should turn into a major construction site. Large-scale construction projects will be implemented in every regional center, district and city. Polyclinics, children's rehabilitation centers and other social facilities will be built. In Astana, important facilities such as a new bridge, the Dombra Palace and the Water Resources Research Center will appear. It is necessary to improve cities. We should consistently continue the Taza Kazakhstan campaign,” Tokayev said.

He stressed the need for active efforts to further develop the country.

“We all need to get to work together, as one nation. We have no other homeland but Kazakhstan, and each of us must contribute to its development. Overall, the electoral campaign went well. New figures have entered the socio-political arena, while substantive and constructive ideas were put forward. I think this Kurultai will give new impetus to the development of our country,” Tokayev said.

World.title: Tokayev casts ballot in Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 23. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has cast his ballot in the elections of deputies to the Kurultai.

According to the press service of the President, Tokayev voted at polling station No. 520 located in the Palace of Independence.

“President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev took part in voting in the elections to the Kurultai of the Republic of Kazakhstan at polling station No. 520, located in the Palace of Independence,” the Akorda said.

Following the vote, the Head of State held a briefing for representatives of the media.

“Undoubtedly, today is truly a historic day for our country. For the first time, we are holding elections to a unicameral Kurultai. This is an important historic event. By coming together as a united nation, we are carrying out large-scale reforms. You all know this well and are witnesses to the transformations taking place. We have achieved significant results. At the same time, much work still lies ahead, and the goals we have set are of particular importance. Today's elections are only the beginning of this major work,” Tokayev said.

The elections to the Kurultai, Kazakhstan's unicameral parliament established under the new Constitution, which entered into force on July 1, 2026, began today.

The Kurultai will consist of 145 deputies elected for a five-year term. The elections are being held under a proportional representation system, with deputies elected from party lists in a single nationwide electoral district.

According to Kazakhstan's Central Election Commission, 12,605,788 voters are registered. A total of 10,423 polling stations have been prepared, including 79 polling stations in 61 countries abroad.

Seven political parties are participating in the elections: Adilet, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, the Baitak Green Party of Kazakhstan, the People's Party of Kazakhstan, Auyl, the Ak Zhol Democratic Party of Kazakhstan and Respublica.

International experts are monitoring the voting process. A total of 777 international observers from 42 countries have been registered. Representatives of 13 international organizations are also participating in observation missions.

The Kurultai will replace Kazakhstan's previous bicameral Parliament, which consisted of the Mazhilis and the Senate.

As of 12:00, voter turnout in Kazakhstan's Kurultai elections stood at 37.05%.

World.title: TURKPA Commission Chair highlights strong public interest in Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections

ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 23. The elections should benefit Kazakhstan, Chairperson of the TURKPA Commission on Legal Affairs and International Relations and member of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye Osman Mesten told journalists, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Astana.

“We saw that technology and artificial intelligence are being used to the greatest extent possible as part of the preparations. All necessary measures have been taken to ensure the full participation of citizens in the elections and to ensure that their opinions are reflected at the state level. Necessary measures have also been taken to enable people with disabilities to vote,” he said.

Mesten noted that polling stations had been opened in 61 countries to enable Kazakh citizens living abroad to participate in the elections.

“Necessary measures are also being taken to inform and guide citizens on issues related to participation in the voting,” he added.

According to Mesten, some members of the TURKPA delegation were present at the opening of polling stations in the morning.

“We saw that the polling stations opened in accordance with international standards. Relevant officials, chairpersons, as well as local and international observers were present on site,” he said.

Mesten emphasized that voters were coming to polling stations despite bad weather.

“Voting will continue until 8:00 p.m. Therefore, I expect turnout to be quite high,” he said.

He also noted the strong interest of the Kazakh people in the elections and their active participation in the life of the country.

“In addition to our work observing the elections, we are also conducting social observations. World.title: Kazakhstan knows how to hold elections, many countries have much to learn – observer
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 23. Kazakhstan has demonstrated its ability to organize and conduct elections, and many countries could learn from its experience, international observer from the CIS Interparliamentary Assembly Kazbek Taysaev told journalists, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Astana.

“I am not attending elections in Kazakhstan for the first time. Kazakhstan knows how to conduct elections. Many countries have much to learn from your Central Election Commission and Kazakhstan on how elections should be organized and conducted,” he said.

Taysaev said observers visited a polling station early in the morning and were present for its opening.

“You know, the attitude at the polling station impressed me. Some 15 to 20 people had already arrived before the polling station opened and were standing in line. The opening began with the national anthem of Kazakhstan. To be honest, I was impressed by the respect and love with which people sang their anthem. There were also many young people. For young people to get up and come to vote at 7:00 in the morning is really significant,” the observer said.

According to Taysaev, the active participation of young people demonstrates their interest in the changes taking place in the country.

“This is also a merit of your leadership, the President and his entire team, because fundamental changes are currently taking place in Kazakhstan. Constitutional reforms are very serious; we went through this in Russia. I am very pleased that the young people we spoke with knew what changes had been introduced into the Constitution. They are waiting for changes, they are waiting for a decent life, and they are ready to stand alongside the people and advance the new changes set out in the Constitution,” he said.

Taysaev also recalled that international observers had previously visited Kazakhstan during the constitutional referendum.

“There was also a large number of observers at that time, and support for the constitutional reforms was very strong. The voting is still underway, but it seems to me that the results will be worthy. All parties were represented at the polling stations. Before the elections, we met with representatives and leaders of all the parties. The CIS IPA mission had this opportunity. And it is encouraging that none of them had any complaints about the course of the election campaign,” he said.

The observer emphasized that, according to the party leaders with whom the mission met, all election participants had equal opportunities to present their positions to voters.

“They all had equal and accessible opportunities, at least that is what the party leaders we met with told us. It is very good when there is an opportunity to convey your position to voters. And the fact that people are coming to polling stations and voting calmly and normally is, of course, a great achievement. I repeat once again: for the Central Election Commission to prepare such a large team of heads and members of polling commissions is a major effort,” Taysaev said.

He added that observers had held detailed discussions with members and chairpersons of polling commissions.

“They managed to do it. We asked questions and spoke at length with members and chairpersons of polling commissions. And the hospitality with which they welcomed people was noticeable. People feel it, they come calmly and normally, and everyone votes for the party they choose. Nobody imposes anything on anyone. I liked your elections. You are doing a great job,” Taysaev said.

According to the international observer, more than 60 people are participating in election observation as part of the CIS mission.

“More than 60 people are involved in observation today alone. My colleagues have already mentioned that our representatives will have visited virtually all polling stations. The CIS mission is also operating abroad. So we can already say that, thank God, everything is going well so far,” he said.

World.title: Trump hits back at Canada after retaliatory tariffs announced
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the United States following a breakdown in trade negotiations.

"Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!" Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" he said.

Since beginning his second term, Mr Trump has made numerous references to making Canada the "51st state" of America, which has infuriated the northern neighbours.

Earlier, Mr Carney said that new Canadian tariffs would take effect on September 8, notably targeting the US steel and dairy industries.

New 50 per cent US tariffs impacting about $US20 billion ($28 billion) worth of goods, or 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the US, came into force on Saturday.

Canadian and US steel products will be impacted by the tit-for-tat tariffs. (AP: Nick Iwanyshyn/The Canadian Press)

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, electronics and other products mark a further worsening of relations between the longtime allies and major trading partners.

The two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Friday, with each side blaming the other for derailing three days of intensive negotiations.

The breakdown complicates the future of a US-Mexico-Canada free-trade pact.

Mr Trump's new tariffs hit sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment,

These duties do not exempt Canadian products under the three-nation trade deal, which has shielded most Canadian exports to the US in the past 18 months.

A frosty relationship between Mark Carney (left) and Donald Trump (right) has hit a new low over tariffs. (AP: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press, File)

The new US tariffs cover around 5 per cent of Canada's exports to the US.

They could expose some vulnerable industries such as softwood lumber and wine to severe damage and lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.

PM says Trump considering tariff exemption Anthony Albanese says he has urged Donald Trump to consider giving Australia a full exemption from Washington's sweeping tariffs.

"We will be mobilising our network of businesses in all regions and all sectors to brace for impact and make the best of a bad situation," said Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal opponents of US tariffs, supported Mr Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and the manufacturing sector," Mr Ford said.

There were also US proposals that affected Canadian culture, language and sovereignty, Mr Carney said, without elaborating.

He was elected last year on a promise to be a tough negotiator with Mr Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to the US.

"Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses," Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, said in a statement.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Immersive experiences at heart of Powerhouse Parramatta grand opening
World.content:
A crystal tunnel set within a meteorite, a maze of mirrors and a vintage Qantas plane will be among the exhibits on offer when Powerhouse Parramatta opens its doors on November 7.

The full program for the museum's grand opening was revealed on Sunday, with work continuing to install more than 3,000 objects sourced from Australia and around the world.

The museum is promising an immersive experience, including an exhibition of five major works by British artist Es Devlin.

The Turning includes a labyrinth of mirrors called the Forest of Us.

The Forest of Us artwork involves a labyrinth of mirrors. (Supplied: Andrea Mora)

Visitors will be encouraged to get lost in its light-filled maze, while discovering the "striking visual symmetries" between trees and human lungs.

Powerhouse CEO Lisa Havilah said one of the "beautiful things" about the new space at Parramatta was its flexibility, allowing for large-scale installations.

"We're able to create these exhibitions that people will really be able to immerse themselves in," Ms Havilah said.

" It's also about presenting the collection in new ways as well. "

Devlin's Memory Palace will also feature in the exhibition. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Devlin's other works include Memory Palace, an immersive 3D cityscape, and Collective Portrait, which will invite visitors to draw portraits of strangers.

'Don't be scared' of the dark

An immersive experience catering to children will be an exhibition called The Dark.

"The Dark can be wondrous. There's no need to be scared," the museum's program teases.

The Dark is among the exhibitions catering to children. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Ms Havilah said the exhibition would be set inside a meteorite-like installation, showcasing more than 800 objects including an impressive minerals collection.

"There's a crystal tunnel, there are objects that make noise.

"There are different perspectives of how you imagine the dark, whether it's deep into space, deep underwater or deep in your body."

The Dark will also display the cherished personal objects of children from across Western Sydney.

"We did a call-out and 100 kids … have loaned us their most special object," Ms Havilah said.

"So there's a whole room with these 100 objects, but also the stories behind each of [them]."

One room will feature the favourite objects from 100 children across Western Sydney. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Walking on water

The third of the new exhibitions announced is a First Nations-led work called Overflow.

Through the films of acclaimed director and Kamilaroi man Ivan Sen, visitors can learn about Aboriginal custodianship of the oceans, rivers and other waterways in NSW.

According to the Powerhouse, Overflow will shine a light on cultural practices that foster species protection, flood mitigation, sustainable and commercial fishing and water quality.

Films by Kamilaroi man Ivan Sen are part of the Overflow exhibition. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta )

Ms Havilah said audiences would be invited to "walk on water" as part of the exhibition.

"There will be a huge platform in the middle of the space that will have water in the middle of it," she said.

There will be five opening exhibitions, two of which were previously announced.

Task Eternal will explore the "human ambition to defy gravity", and the display will include a NASA moon rock and original drawings of flying machines by Leonardo da Vinci.

It will also feature the Avro 504K— a replica of the very first Qantas plane.

A replica of the very first Qantas plane will be on display when the museum opens. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta )

Another exhibition, The Mall, will span two storeys of the Powerhouse, exploring the history and evolution of the modern shopping centre.

Western Sydney will get another nod in this exhibition, as the birthplace of the Westfield shopping centre — a concept that was exported to the world.

Rare items from Australian fashion brands will be on show, along with the signature jeans worn by Apple co-founder Steve Jobs.

The display will also include prototypes of the Predator boot, conceived by Australian footballer Craig Johnston and worn by David Beckham.

The Mall will be exhibited over two storeys of the museum. (Supplied: Jo Duck)

Kids see it for free

All of the exhibitions will be free of charge for visitors under 16 years of age.

However, Task Eternal will attract an as-yet undisclosed entry fee for visitors who are 16 years old and over.

Powerhouse Parramatta opening date revealed The NSW government announced in May that construction of the $915 million museum had been completed four years after work began.

Ms Havilah said the museum was designed to increase Sydneysiders' access to "world-class arts and culture."

"It's a really great gift," she said.

"To have four of the five exhibitions free to the public, I think is incredible."

Arts Minister John Graham said the $915 million project, which also includes storage and archiving, would offer good value to families facing cost-of-living pressures.

"We want to ensure that price isn't a barrier for young people to explore the big ideas, the creativity, the innovation that Powerhouse Parramatta will exhibit and celebrate," he said.

World.title: Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
World.content:
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Shoriful's ball of the series

Cameron Green was felled by a brutal inswinging yorker. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.

The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.

With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.

And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.

The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.

The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.

And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …

2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage

Mitchell Starc picked up from where he left off in the second innings. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.

Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.

And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.

He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.

And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.

An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.

Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.

3. Smith takes a screamer after tea

Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.

Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.

And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.

He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.

Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.

4. The shortest session ever?

With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.

However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.

He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.

But it was all over with the very next ball.

Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.

With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.

5. The 29th two-day Test

Australia cruised to victory within two days. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

There have been 2,632 Test matches played in cricket's lengthy red-ball history, with 457 of them held in Australia.

As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.

Only five of those have happened in Australia.

And yet, in the last 20 Tests that have been played on these shores, it has happened four times.

Australia thumped South Africa on a Gabba green top in 2022, and then there were two, two-day Tests during last summer's Ashes, one in Perth and the other at the MCG.

The only Australia-hosted Test to finish inside two days before that game in Brisbane four years ago took place in Melbourne against the West Indies, in February 1931.

Eleven of the two-day Tests in history took place before World War I (between 1882 and 1912), a further three either side of World War II (1931-1946) but then none between 1946 and 1999.

Then, since 2000, there have been 13 two-day Tests. The cost of a fast-paced world, perhaps.

World.title: Swans AFLW captain says support 'just unbelievable' as record smashed
World.content:
Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy wasn't sure what to expect for her side when they ran out for the first instalment of a historic double-header at the SCG.

The Swans dominated headlines across the country all week, filling both front and back pages of every newspaper, for a scandal that called the club's culture into question.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

What the women's team got was an outpouring of support which broke the side's attendance record with 16,672 fans filling the stands to watch them play.

That is more than double the previous club record of 8,264.

"It's amazing. We weren't sure what we were going to expect this week, but to see the support that we've received today is just unbelievable," McEvoy told Fox Footy after the game.

"The members and fans are so tight and they know that we're united as a club and we're better than what we were at the start of the week.

The Swans doubled its crowd attendance record. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

"I'm just so grateful to have the support that we had today and the girls were able to turn it on.

"We had a few nervous girls, that's for sure, but we absolutely turned it on."

The scenes were particularly celebratory on the ground post-siren, after Sydney beat Essendon by 24 points.

It was just the second time the women have played on the SCG for premiership points and the first in a double billing with the men's.

Loading Instagram content

Before locking in to warm up, star men's players Errol Gulden and captain Callum Mills got around the women's players.

Gulden was also seen going up to the crowd giving the fans a big thank you for turning out in droves.

Some of those fans left before the men's game, as a boycott had been suggested in the days before the match as a scandal continues to engulf the club.

It's unclear how many fans left in protest to the scandal, but a steady stream was seen leaving.

Swans players spent time with fans after the game. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Swans fans cheer from the stands. (Getty: Darrian Traynor/AFL Photos)

Lulu Clarke, who has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, was one of the fans who walked out.

Ms Clarke had bought a ticket to the men's game, unaware the women were also playing, but once the news broke of the incident she knew she would not be staying for both games.

"Of late, I've definitely drifted apart from the Swans and the AFL industry as a whole," Ms Clarke said.

"I decided that I'm absolutely not going to the men's game, even if those five players were still stood down. There's no way I could just show up and watch it. It just didn't sit right with me."

Former Matilda Sarah Walsh also left the stadium after the women's game, saying it had been a "tough week", but stressed she was not boycotting the men's team.

"It's not a new story but I have a five-year-old daughter who I brought here today to support the women's team," Ms Walsh said.

"I think you can have a club and not expect someone to be a fan of both teams.

"I think that's the nuance of sport, don't expect Socceroos fans to be Matildas fans … We've got a long way to go in society. I don't think this is a Sydney Swans issue at all … it's a societal issue and we all need to do better."

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia went to the SCG to support the AFLW side. (ABC)

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia told ABC News they were there to support the women and will likely just watch a bit of the men's game.

"It's very disappointing from the men's team … I feel like we were very disappointed in everything that happened," Georgia said.

Kayley said the situation was upsetting.

"We've been supporting the Swans since we were kids as well. So, it was just shocking," she said.

"We never thought that any players from this team could do something like this. It was really upsetting."

Many fans held signs during the game along the lines of "I'm here for AFLW".

World.title: Thousands line riverbank to welcome Spirit IV 'home' to Devonport
World.content:
After years of delays and cost overruns, there was cause for celebration in Devonport today as one of the two new Bass Strait ferries arrived at its home port for the first time.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff was among the crowd welcoming Spirit of Tasmania IV to the north-west coast.

"I was here around 7am and I was with thousands of other Tasmanians … people of all ages," Mr Rockliff told reporters.

"I got the real sense there that this was a dawn of a new era for tourism, for freight, for Tasmania.

"And the sense of occasion was most certainly there.

"People were excited and people were very proud as they could see their ship, Spirit IV, sail up the river, turn on a dime and back in perfectly to the gantry."

Premier Jeremy Rockliff and TT-Line chair Ken Kanofski welcomed Spirit of Tasmania IV to Devonport. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Crowds gathered to watch Spirit of Tasmania IV arrive at its home port for the first time. (ABC News)

But it has not been all smooth sailing to get to this point.

Spirit IV, and its sister ship Spirit V, were initially planned to be ready for service in 2021.

But the ferry replacement program has been beset by delays and cost blowouts relating to both the ships themselves and the wharf infrastructure needed to accommodate them.

In May, state parliament's Public Accounts Committee heard the program, which started in 2018, had cost $717 million more than was forecast in the original business case.

Spirit of Tasmania IV was stored in Scotland before leaving Europe for Australia. (Supplied: TT-Line)

Most of the cost overrun related to the new berth at Devonport.

"You can always look back," Mr Rockliff said today.

"But this is about looking forward … and big projects like this have their challenges, there's no doubt about that.

"But big projects are here for the next generation, the next three decades or more.

"They are the projects that are worth the investment, they're worth the blood, sweat and tears because they always deliver."

Loading...

One of those in the crowd, Rodney Winwood, said "it was nice to see" the ship arrive.

"I had my doubts whether it would fit, but I think a lot of people are here to see whether it would fit really," he said.

Rodney Winwood was among the crowd to see the ship arrive. (ABC News)

Two days of testing

Ferry operator TT-Line's chair, Ken Kanofski, said Spirit IV would be in Devonport until tomorrow afternoon, with its hydraulics, loading systems and the management systems set to be tested.

"The purpose is really to test the gantry and the ship together in a live environment," Mr Kanofski said.

Ken Kanofski says Spirit IV is undergoing two days of testing in Devonport. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

"We've been doing it in Geelong with both ships for a number of times now.

"The gantries are built to designs, clearly, but you want to fine tune the systems, bring the two together for the first time," he said.

Spirit IV will return to Victoria following the testing.

"We'll also bring Spirit V here in September in order to undertake testing of Spirit V with the gantry as well," Mr Kanofski said.

Mr Kanofski said the new ships were still on track to start ferrying passengers in October.

People lined the Mersey River to see the ship arrive. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Emotion and nostalgia on banks of Mersey

Tasmania's Infrastructure Minister Kerry Vincent said there was celebration and nostalgia among the crowd gathered on the banks of Devonport's Mersey River to see the new ship arrive.

"A lot of emotion. There's a lot of old people here that … could remember the Princess and the Empress all talking about the changes and how important these new ships would be for Tasmania," he said.

The Princess of Tasmania and later the Empress of Australia connected Tasmania with Victoria from 1959 until TT-Line's Abel Tasman took over the route in 1985.

The cafeteria on board Spirit of Tasmania IV. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Mr Rockliff said during his first year in politics, he saw Spirits I and II arrive in Tasmania.

"That was also controversial at the time, and I think I might have even broken away from my team at the time as a candidate and supported the two new ferries when our side of politics didn't," he said.

"[To] 24 years later to see brand new ships … and these are purpose-built, brand new for Tasmania and Tasmanians, it's a very proud [moment]."

The ship's arrival has been labelled the "dawn of a new era" by the premier. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Devonport Mayor Alison Jarman said the new ship would be the city's "shining light".

She said there was a sense of celebration around town.

"We're getting hugs, we're getting high fives, we're getting people shaking our hands and congratulating us. And we're just saying to them, 'now, just tell everybody we're ready to go'," Councillor Jarman said.

World.title: Hundreds walk through Brookfield after alleged early morning sexual assault
World.content:
Hundreds of people have walked in solidarity to oppose violence against women following an alleged sexual assault in Brisbane's west.

Crowds gathered in the suburb of Brookfield this morning and walked along Rafting Ground Road in a display of community strength and support.

It comes after a 23-year-old woman was allegedly stalked and sexually assaulted while walking in the area on Thursday morning.

The area where a young women was allegedly sexually assaulted last week is a popular walking spot. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

Police allege 32-year-old Jacob Dave Henry Hauraki had been driving to work and approached the woman from behind, then dragged her into nearby bushes.

He has been charged with six counts of rape, and one count each of stalking, assault with intent to commit rape, assault occasioning bodily harm and deprivation of liberty.

Mr Hauraki remains in custody and is expected to reappear in court on September 18.

Drawing 'a line in the sand'

Event organiser Emily Hall said she wanted to highlight the "spirit of community in Brookfield" in the wake of the alleged assault.

"[We wanted] to put a line in the sand and say as a community we will not stand for violence against anyone, particularly women," Ms Hall said.

Emily Hall organised the event to "highlight the spirit of community" in Brookfield. (ABC News)

"It's an issue for everyone, and we all need to stand up.

"We all need to be prepared to call out behaviours that we don't think are appropriate and support one another when these incidents do occur."

Local state MP Christian Rowan said it was "very encouraging" to see Brookfield residents come together.

"Our community is united," Dr Rowan said.

"It's really important when it comes to ending not only sexual violence against women, but also all forms of violence across communities, not only locally, but throughout Queensland and Australia."

A number of alleged sexual assault incidents have made headlines around the country this month. (ABC News: Emma Johnson)

Hope for change

The alleged rape at Brookfield is one of several alleged sexual assault incidents to make news across Australia in recent weeks.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a Sydney Swans player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

In NSW, three 17-year-old boys were charged over the alleged group sexual assault of a 17-year-old girl in Sydney's south-west last Saturday.

And earlier this month, a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys were charged with the alleged sexual assault of a girl in a Sydney alleyway.

Brookfield resident Debbie Moylan says she regularly walks in the area with her three daughters. (ABC News)

Mother-of-three Debbie Moylan said she joined the Brookfield walk to send a message.

"It really shows that there are a lot of people out here thinking about what's going on in the world at the moment," she said.

"They're worried, they're scared.

World.title: Coalition wants to split Court of Appeal to focus on tougher sentences
World.content:
The Victorian opposition is promising to introduce a specialist Court of Criminal Appeal to deal with serious offenders and sentencing, if it wins the November election.

The Coalition plans to split the existing Court of Appeal into two separate courts, a Court of Criminal Appeal and a Court of Civil Appeal.

It says specialised judges with expertise in criminal prosecutions would be appointed to the new standalone court to handle appeals by offenders and ensure sentencing for serious crime meets community expectations.

The latest crime statistics for Victoria showed youth crime had fallen for the first time in four years, but adult crime rose by 10 per cent due to factors including increases in breaches of bail, retail theft and breaches of family violence orders.

Jess Wilson and James Newbury say they will recruit judges with experience in criminal justice for the Coalition's new Court of Criminal Appeal. (ABC News)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Victoria's criminal justice system was broken and offenders were not afraid of the consequences.

"Victorians are sick and tired of watching offenders walk into our court system and get a slap on the wrist," she said.

"We have a plan to keep Victorians safe, we have a plan to ensure that our court system and our criminal justice system actually meets community expectations."

Former police officer and now Liberal member for Mordialloc, Paul O'Halloran joined Ms Wilson and Shadow Attorney General James Newbury for today's policy announcement.

"Police officers I've worked with over the years are truly frustrated about offenders being bailed, of being released and sentences not reflecting community expectations," Mr O'Halloran said.

"We must have consequences for serious offending."

Paul O'Halloran (centre) joined James Newbury and Jess Wilson at the policy announcement today. (ABC News)

Mr Newbury said he had "consulted with the courts" on the policy but would not say whether he has discussed it with any members of the judiciary.

"I have consulted in the way Victorians would expect," he said.

When new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll took over the leadership from Jacinta Allan last month, he said he was making crime a centrepiece of his leadership.

He said one of his first phone calls was to Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush to talk about police resourcing.

Mr Carroll said the Coalition's plan would cause delays to moving cases through the Court of Appeal.

"The modern-day Liberal party is lacking talent and lacking solicitors, and today's policy announcement shows just that," he said.

"We've seen today the Liberal party searching for a policy idea and not doing any homework."

Slippery slope to 'dangerous policy', legal community says

The Law Institute of Victoria represents more than 22,000 lawyers and people working in the legal system in Victoria.

President Tom Ballantyne said the state opposition had not released a lot of detail about its policy but, from what was available, the proposal appeared to misunderstand how the Court of Appeal functioned.

"The Court of Appeal exists to check whether a judge has made a legal mistake; it's not there to hand down sentences that politicians want," Mr Ballantyne said.

He said there was already extensive criminal expertise among Victoria's appeal judges.

The Law Institute of Victoria says any attempt by a government to influence a decision of a court is a threat to democracy. (ABC News: Karen Percy)

He said he was concerned the opposition was attempting to influence the outcomes of the court or was seeking to choose judges based on the decisions they expected them to make.

"The moment governments start telling courts what outcome to produce, you stop having an independent judiciary," he said.

"It's an extremely slippery slope and not one that can always be reversed."

Mr Ballantyne said any attempt at influencing judicial decision-making would be "an enormously dangerous development" that could undermine democracy.

World.title: Almost two in three youth offenders offending on bail, government says
World.content:
The Queensland government says almost two in three serious youth offenders are committing crimes while on bail, and 38 per cent are committing crimes listed under the Adult Crime, Adult Time legislation.

But the number of serious repeat youth offenders has dropped by 29 per cent, as the government prepares to unveil a tough new stance on bail breaches that would send offenders back to jail.

Premier David Crisafulli said the "most significant reforms to bail" in the state's history will form part of the next phase of the government's Adult Crime, Adult Time (ACAT) initiative.

Minister for Youth Justice and Victim Support Laura Gerber said under the changes, breaching bail by committing a crime listed under the ACAT legislation would become a new offence.

Mr Crisafulli also flagged the legislation could include adult offenders.

Laura Gerber says there has been a 20 per cent drop in repeat offenders since the introduction of Adult Crime, Adult Time laws. (ABC News)

"We are doing the work as to who that applies for and for what period that minimum mandatory will be there, but it is the next step of adult crime, adult time," he said.

With youth justice workers set to go on strike tomorrow, unions have raised concerns about the impact of a potential influx of prisoners on the state's corrective services system.

A report from the state's audit office recently found the number of inmates being held in Queensland prisons had increased by 54 per cent over the past decade.

Before the bail reform changes, Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) was already forecasting the number of extra prisoners in the system to increase by between 1,500 and 5,200 by June 2035.

The latest ombudsman report found Wacol Prison in Brisbane's west was operating at 168 per cent capacity. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

Together Union assistant branch secretary Michael Thomas said the proposed changes would "almost inevitably end up in triple-ups".

Triple-ups are the practice of housing up to three prisoners in a cell designed for one person.

"Even though there is more capacity coming online, there is simply not enough to deal with another 5,000 to 6,000 prisoners," he said.

Michael Thomas says an increase in prisoner numbers will "absolutely" result in corrections officers getting injured. (ABC News)

Mr Thomas said that will put correctional officers at risk.

"We know if we go to triple-up we are going to see more assaults on prison officers," he said.

" This policy will absolutely result in our members being hurt and the government breaching its duty that every employer has to provide a safe workplace. "

Ms Gerber said the government had already brought on "some extra capacity" with a further 1,400 beds to come online "in the next couple of years".

The minister conceded there would likely be more prisoners coming into the system under the bail reforms.

"I'm not saying we're not going to have an increase, because you've seen the data," she said.

A spokesperson for the Australian Workers' Union (AWU), which represents workers in Queensland's youth detention centres, questioned where young people would be held.

"All youth detention centres are at capacity and young people are waiting in watchhouses across the state," AWU secretary Stacey Schinnerl said.

"Every Queenslander deserves to feel safe. That includes our workers in youth detention centres."

Bail reform 'next logical step'

Citing new data, Ms Gerber said the number of serious repeat offenders had dropped by 29 per cent since the introduction of the ACAT legislation.

Ms Gerber said 61 per cent of serious repeat youth offenders went on to allegedly commit an offence while on bail, and 38 per cent committed an offence listed under the ACAT legislation.

"It is a sizeable challenge and the data demonstrates the size of the challenge we're facing," she said.

Mr Crisafulli said bail reform was the "next logical step".

" These will be the most significant reforms to bail in Queensland's history and they will be the strongest bail laws in the country. "

The Queensland government's ACAT laws have already been expanded twice to include a total of 47 offences.

Vyleen White's daughter Cindy Micallef has welcomed the changes. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The changes have been welcomed by Cindy Micallef, whose elderly mother Vyleen White was fatally stabbed by a teenager in a car park in Redbank Plains in 2024.

"For me and my family, had there been stronger bail laws, because our offender had been out on bail three times already, my mother would still be alive," she said.

"There have been so many losses, heartaches and trauma for people that have had a huge miscarriage of justice."

World.title: Mark McVeigh to meet with Essendon board as coach decision edges closer
World.content:
Sydney Swans’ assistant Mark McVeigh will present to the Essendon board on Monday as the club prepares to make an announcement on their new senior coach.

The 45-year-old was in the coaches’ box as the Swans defeated North Melbourne in an emotional encounter at the SCG but will be in Melbourne to make a final presentation to the board before his expected endorsement as coach.

Mark McVeigh is seen as the favourite to win the Essendon coaching job. AFL Photos

McVeigh played 232 matches at Essendon after being chosen with pick No.9 in the 1998 national draft. After retiring in 2012 he moved back to NSW where he became an assistant coach at the Giants when Leon Cameron stood down in 2022.

He coached 13 matches for four wins with former teammates James Hird and Dean Solomon in the coaches’ box alongside him. He then moved to the Sydney Swans where he coached as an assistant under John Longmire and Dean Cox.

World.title: ‘White fragility is crazy in this country’: Rising rap star Miss Kaninna tells it like it is
World.content:
CultureMusicAustralian music ‘White fragility is crazy in this country’: Rising rap star Miss Kaninna tells it like it is Ben Madden August 23, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’ve been given a fascinating tip-off ahead of my interview with proud Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung, Kalkadoon and Yirendali woman Miss Kaninna, as she releases her new mixtape, BLACKPRINT. The follow-up to her 2024 self-titled debut EP, it’s executive produced by Melbourne multi-hyphenate Nikodimos – and he’s suggested I ask about her famous chicken congee. It gets the exact reaction I was hoping for, as she lets out a huge laugh of disbelief. “I’ve just recently been trying to get in the gym, and I’ve found out that oats are not that good for you,” she says. “I think God gave his toughest soldiers the toughest of tummies, and I’m one of those girls that has IBS. I cannot eat anything in bulk without getting super bloated. “A lot of the stuff I say in this mixtape is very much talking the truth,” says rapper Miss Kaninna. Joel Thomas Wilson “I’m Chinese, and I was on TikTok, scrolling, and this woman was talking about how congee is the best breakfast to have when you wake up. I was like ‘bet’ because I don’t even really like oats. I don’t like sweet stuff. But congee, I can get around.” Since emerging in 2023 with her searing debut single Blak Britney, Miss Kaninna has been a name on everyone’s lips. She’s toured relentlessly since, with the songs from BLACKPRINT starting as freestyles. To her, this tape is a chance to channel the energy of her live show into a project that lasts long after the curtain drops.



“I don’t have that much music out, and obviously, I’m a live musician, and so a lot of my focus is on the show and creating an experience for people,” she says. “This mixtape has been a while in the making, and I just want to get it out there so I can start working on my next, which I’ve already been working on.” One of the highlights of the tape is the punk-tinged closer Stolen Wages, one of the most energetic moments in her discography to date. “I stopped making sad music because I’m so sick of looking at people just swaying. Making sad music is cool, but I want to see people jumping around, sweating their holes off,” she says. Late last year, Irish rappers Kneecap brought her as their sole opener across a sold-out tour of the UK and Europe. “They go really hard, and I felt I needed a song that’s bigger than Pinnacle Bitch [her 2024 single and previous set closer] that we can end the set with. “I wrote Stolen Wages in one sitting, and then I called [producer] Lucy Blomkamp, aka Perfectworld, and I was like, ‘I need you to interpolate this right now because I’m going to Europe in, like, two weeks.’ She was so quick. We took it on tour, and I was getting so much positive feedback about that one song.”



Miss Kaninna is one of the biggest and buzziest names in Australian rap, and she’s determined to pave the way for artists to follow. “There’s just not a lot of support for young rappers in Australia,” she says. “One of the first questions I get asked by anybody who’s not in the industry, when I say that I’m a rapper, is ‘Oh, do you want to go to America, or do you want to move?’ “And I’m like, ‘No!’ I very much want to be exported into international markets so that Australian music can benefit from it; it’s not like I just want to get up and leave. I think a lot of people are very focused on just getting out and leaving and not building a good foundation and a good crew here in Australia.” ‘I’m trying to reclaim my body, my space, my mouth and my sexuality, and uplift women to do the same thing.’ There’s no room for misinterpretation on BLACKPRINT. Across the project’s six tracks, Miss Kaninna holds a mirror up to white Australia, and the double standards that permeate every part of Australian culture. From the blink-and-you’ll-miss-it Chat My Shit to the Kobie Dee-featuring Look at Me Now to the slower-burning Mob Ties, she sounds laser focused. While she’s shown off her singing on a couple of occasions recently – including singing backing vocals for Brisbane MC Nerve’s Like a Version cover of Justin Timberlake’s SexyBack on Triple J – she’s rapping with vivid energy across BLACKPRINT. The title of BLACKPRINT is Miss Kaninna’s nod to how Indigenous people across the globe, including Aboriginal people, hold not just the past in their hands but the future. “I think white fragility is crazy in this country, and I think that white people really do think that black power means taking away from them,” she says.



“A lot of the stuff I say in this mixtape is very much talking the truth. It’s not like what I’m saying is crazy. What’s crazy is that the Australian government continues to have a lawless land and illegally occupies this land. Me saying ‘f--- white people’ is not crazy to me. Me saying ‘f--- the government’ or ‘f--- police’ is not crazy. That seems like a pretty normal reaction to what’s going on.” Hailing from Lutruwita/Tasmania, Miss Kaninna’s community has always had her back. Her mother, Ruth Langford, is a prominent First Nations advocate, and she often seeks advice from elders in her community, including Uncle Jim Everett. “Two years ago, I was sitting on a trip with my uncle, and I was feeling a little bit vulnerable and a little bit, like, under a microscope,” she recalls of one such experience. “I had been copping a lot of slack from people saying that, you know, I’m shaking my ass too much and all this stuff, and my uncle was sitting in front of me, and he said, ‘You know, Kaninna, I’m extremely proud of who you are as a woman.’ “He started getting really upset because he was like, ‘Women need to be able to make choices for themselves, and it’s not up to men to dictate what you can and cannot do with your body and your mouth. For the last 250 years, women – Aboriginal women – have been completely objectified and completely sexualised and ripped of any human status, and now you’re reclaiming that back. And however you see fit as an Aboriginal woman, we’ll support you.’



“And that’s what I’m trying to do,” says Miss Kaninna. “I’m trying to actively reclaim my body and reclaim my space and reclaim my mouth and reclaim my sexuality, and uplift women to do the same thing.” Miss Kaninna’s new mixtape, BLACKPRINT, is out now. Her national tour includes shows at Brisbane’s The Brightside on September 11, Sydney’s Oxford Art Factory on September 12 and 13, and Melbourne’s Northcote Theatre on September 18.

World.title: After a week of pain, the healing begins for the Swans and their supporters
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 After a week of pain, the healing begins for the Swans and their supporters Vince Rugari August 23, 2026 — 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For the past week, shattered supporters of the Sydney Swans have been processing their complicated feelings, digesting their mixed emotions, trying to figure out where to put all these broken, jagged little pieces. On Sunday, the best answer anyone’s come up with thus far presented itself at the SCG: here. Put it here. Bring it all to the ground and we’ll sort through it together. Loading In times of trauma, it can help to be with other people. So, on a glorious Sydney afternoon, the broad church that is the Swans’ fan base – sad, angry, hurt, confused, bemused – congregated at its usual location to do what it usually does, unsure if it would still be like it usually is. It was, and it wasn’t.



Were it not for the news that rocked their world on Monday, when the first reports emerged of the night of debauchery that took place at the Pullman in East Melbourne, this all would have been so straightforward. On Thursday, five AFL players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were suspended for the rest of the season for “breaching club standards”. A separate police investigation continues into an alleged sexual assault. Sydney Swans fans on the SCG on Sunday. Janie Barrett The Swans’ first AFLW-AFL(M) double-header at home on Sunday was both an unremarkably normal and singularly bizarre experience. Once the footy began, it felt like practically any other afternoon in the before times. The sights, sounds and smells were all familiar – except for the traditional quarter-time rendition of Sweet Caroline, a beloved Swans ritual that was dropped without explanation.



Oh! And there was a gigantic elephant in the room, too. In the morning, scores of hopeful media roved around Driver Avenue anticipating a frenzy. Fans who came for the 12.30pm start of the AFLW’s round two fixture between the Swans and Essendon were greeted by reporters asking them to explain their decision to turn up, and if they intended to stick around for the men’s game later in the day. Laura Gardiner of the Swans greets fans at the SCG on Sunday. Getty Images This was sporting attendance (and departure) as political statement. Not everyone who arrived early or left between games was making one – but many seized their opportunity to do exactly that, holding aloft cardboard signs bearing messages they would then happily unpack in front of a camera and microphone. “Come down here for some wholesome footy,” a Sydney Roosters fan was heard quipping to them, as he made his way to the NRL double-header next door at Allianz Stadium. It’s amazing how quickly the world changes.



The official crowd for Sydney’s 24-point AFLW win was 16,672 – more than double their previous record, and a clear show of support by the public for a team that was among the week’s indirect victims. Chloe Molloy celebrated a goal by making a “W” with her hands. One supporter had a banner confiscated, but only because it was hung over the sponsor boards. It read: “No more dickheads, please.” Thus began the healing process. “The best way to go about today was to win, really,” said captain Lucy McEvoy. “The girls knew that. To give our members and fans a little bit of joy ... we felt obliged to do that for them and be that beacon for us as a football club.” What followed in the interval was not a mass walkout, as had been feared. Dozens upon dozens of people did exit – and women were, to be sure, overrepresented in that category – leaving behind rows of empty seats in the usually jam-packed members’ stand. But dozens more filed through the turnstiles in the other direction, eager to support another group of players who have also been let down. For them, a crowd of 30,058 was on hand. It was far below the Swans’ usual turnout, but also roughly the same as what they got when the same opponents, North Melbourne, visited last year.



It was a dead rubber, yet the performance and result – a comprehensive 53-point victory for Sydney – were a reminder that there is more talent on their list beyond the five who won’t play again this season. We still don’t know exactly what they did in that hotel room, but we do know it has impacted many people – including the teammates who were sleeping at the time, and who now have to try and somehow win a flag without them. Swans players are cheered as they walk off at half-time. Getty Images They won’t give up meekly. Despite the week they’ve endured, they played with spirit and vigour on Sunday, and the supporters who stuck around responded in kind. In the final minutes, a chant rang through the air: ‘Syyyyyyd-ney! Syyyyyyd-ney!’



In the final seconds, a rare standing ovation, and at the siren, an almighty roar, with tears. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Sydney Swans LIVE updates: Women’s and men’s team play first matches following week of scandal At a function earlier in the day, Swans president Andrew Pridham offered another public apology for the “exceedingly poor decisions by a few [which] have impacted so many”, and said the club would investigate how its proud culture failed to prevent those decisions being made. Pridham also acknowledged that “just words”, lovely and well-chosen as they were, won’t cut it. “It is our future actions that will define us,” he said. On that, we’ll just have to wait. But the Swans will be back at the SCG in a fortnight’s time for a qualifying final. Whatever everyone’s feeling by then, at least they’ll know where to bring it.
