World.title: My suburb gentrified decades ago. Now the people who live here are afraid to walk the streets
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Opinion My suburb gentrified decades ago. Now the people who live here are afraid to walk the streets Ceridwen Spark Contributor August 23, 2026 — 6:30pm

August 23, 2026 — 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Thursday morning, I get a text message. “Heard there’s some nasty crime in your hood. Radio going off about it!” It’s Steve, whom I tease about living in Glen Iris. My “hood” is Footscray, where I’ve lived for 30 years. Victoria Police detectives at Footscray Mall on June 15 last year after an assault that later resulted in murder charges. Penny Stephens Me: “What’s being said?”



Steve: “Antisocial chaos, apparently. Big spike in crime.” I’d like to text “Nah, it’s a beat-up” but can’t. The central business district of Footscray is chaotic and has become increasingly so over the past few years. The name “Footscrazy” has long been used affectionately around the place, but the term feels complicated right now. Whatever the nature of the discussion Steve heard on the radio, this much is true: Sirens, people crazy with meth, street closures, security guards employed at the local Vinnies where I used to volunteer. A couple of weeks ago, our popular shopping and restaurant strip Barkly Street was closed. A mentally unwell man with a toy gun was having an episode on a rooftop near the high school. On a recent Wednesday night the windows of the pizza shop where my daughter’s boyfriend works were smashed in. Police figures from March show Footscray station is one of Melbourne’s worst for incidents of violence, while data from the Crime Statistics Agency shows that crime rates in the suburb have been trending upwards for some time, especially during the past four years, when there’s been a rise of more than 60 per cent.



Police and emergency services respond to an incident in Barkly St, Footscray last month that led to the busy cafe strip being shut down. Nine News The woundedness of central Footscray hurts and not because I’m squeamish. This is not about hatred, blame or judgment. It’s about loss. The place where I’ve lived for almost three decades feels like an open sore. And the care that needs to be shown to reverse the situation requires thought and resources, more than those looking the other way appear willing to invest. Footscray’s CBD streets – beloved and sometimes gritty, but which have offered home to so many from diverse places and for so long – feel abandoned by all but people on the edge. Beyond this central area though, people continue to live, garden and chat in the renovated Victorian homes in streets which began being gentrified in the late 1990s, around when I moved to Footscray. Footscray was never perfect, but those of us who love it are deeply affectionate about the place. Known for being a colourful suburb that’s welcomed migrants from around the world, central Footscray hosts social services that draw those who need them. This includes people I love – I have no interest in demonising anyone needing these services. I’m glad the needle exchange is there; grateful for the gentle volunteers at the op-shop, who offer clothes to those who’ve been robbed while sleeping in the mall. Western Bulldogs player and artist Cody Weightman at a new Salvos cafe offering social services that opened in Footscray in May. Jason South But Footscray has become an expanding sinkhole for suffering since COVID – land squatting, people without homes, insufficient services for those experiencing mental illness and addiction – and all underpinned by fear and racism.



Previously though, the contours of human pain – mental illness, homelessness, addiction, unemployment – co-existed with a joyous, sometimes edgy but always lively and interesting diversity: Vietnamese hairdressers gossiping out the front of the chemist, lanky Sudanese men discussing politics near Maples Café, creative-looking teenagers at the record shop. And mums trekking to Coles and Savers for another round of nappies or discounted toys, or in my case, the day before Steve’s message, an excellent $27 suit for my 17-year-old’s school formal. Footscray is a still a place of great possibilities, as seen by the crowds out enjoying Good Fest in the mall in February 2025. Tom Yau Now though, those of us with money and health and choices tend to do our shopping elsewhere. Sometimes, when the human suffering feels like too much, we head to the overpriced supermarkets in the neighbouring, but less interesting suburb of Seddon. It feels wrong, but it’s easier. Leaving for Seddon, Yarraville or even – god forbid – Brunswick to avoid the horror is a long way from laughing at the “F---ing Brunswick” T-shirt I once saw hanging in a shop in Irving Street, Footscray. The afternoon before the pizza shop windows were smashed, I was in there chatting to Tom, who works alongside my daughter’s boyfriend. He’s seen so much, responded so many times to the distress and violence that plays out in front of the shop, in the heart of Nicholson Mall. Stabbings, being threatened, watching his fellow employees find other work because they’re exhausted. Seeing him in his spunky shorts, adeptly pulling pizzas out of the huge ovens, I want to give him a hug, but can only listen sympathetically. Police tape in Footscray’s Nicholson Street mall on Sunday June 15 last year. Penny Stephens



My neighbour, too, Rosa, an Italian woman who’s lived in Footscray all her life. She holds Footscray stories in her heart. Rosa tells me I can’t remove the pink roses in my garden because they were planted by the former owner as a tribute to the daughter she lost to cancer. Now though, she won’t go to central Footscray because, as she told me, “It breaks my heart.” When I and other people I know who love Footscray go elsewhere, we feel a bit ashamed. It doesn’t take being a cultural geographer to know that to thrive, places need to perform a diversity of functions and be comfortable for a range of people. If the Toms and Rosas abandon the place, it’s only those who can’t leave who remain. Related Article Crime A violent crime shocked this community. Now locals are calling for change There are many good, passionate and active defenders of Footscray who are working to restore the central streets for everyone. Chief among these is Jorge Jorquera, the co-ordinator of Borderlands Co-operative, a local activist organisation, but whom I know as a dad from school. The Maribyrnong City Council tries too – erecting some great art, setting up lively events in and around the Mall. But the problems are bigger than Jorge, than Borderlands and other local organisations, and bigger than local council. Though I understand individual avoidance of the Footscray CBD it’s wrong for those responsible for providing care and solutions to abandon the place. It’s time the Victorian government did more to support local efforts to save this treasured but struggling suburb. It affords belonging to so many – long may it continue to do so.



Associate professor Ceridwen Spark conducts research on urban and social change at RMIT University. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The government’s new gambling ‘reform’ won’t reduce harm
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Peter Hartcher (“Gambling laws’ biggest winners”, August 22) has done us a favour by reporting parliament’s genuine belief that banning gambling advertising would be “a threat to the viability of free-to-air networks” and “the sporting codes, especially the AFL and the NRL”. More important, apparently, than approaching “the issue through a public health lens”. This also helps us avoid the lazy assumption that parliamentarians were “selling out for political donations”. However, both the alcohol and tobacco industries have adjusted to advertising bans which have seen the desired public health effect of significant long-term reductions of public consumption. The current gambling advertising and inducements legislation will almost certainly have little public health impact. David Hind, North Sydney Do we really need ads for these?... Jason South What seems to be forgotten in this debate is that no one is calling for gambling itself to be banned – just the gambling s and their inducements. The Murphy inquiry found that Australians lose more money online gambling than any other people on this planet: something Australians seem very good at, but sadly not a record to be proud of – and a lousy business plan for a punter. More than half a million gambling ads are paid for and screened annually. The funds for that massive spend have to come from somewhere. Just do the maths. Bill Young, Killcare Heights For those who object to the weak gambling legislation, I have a suggestion. Join your local footy or RSL club and start lobbying the board to cut the number of pokies machines. Find like-minded people and swamp the AGM with demands to cut gambling. Accept that subsidised meals and drinks will rise in price. Accept high-priced stars will not be affordable, so results will be down. Accept membership fees will increase. If they cut back gambling, you will blame them for fewer subsidies at your local club. Neville Turbit, Russell Lea Not all five Coalition parliamentarians who crossed the floor to vote against the government’s half-baked gambling laws were Liberals. One dissenter was National Party MP Pat Conaghan.

Col Shephard, Yamba As Peter Hartcher points out, the problem identified by the parliamentary inquiry is not gambling itself, but the torrent of advertising that encourages people to gamble. The freedom to participate should not be confused with a right to promote it. Singapore provides an interesting model. Gambling is legal but tightly controlled, with betting and lotteries confined to licensed operators and approved venues. Why can’t Australia do the same? Adults could still gamble whenever they choose, without subjecting children, vulnerable people, and those with no interest to the relentless bombardment of betting s. John Kempler, Rose Bay Each morning as I pick up my newspaper, I see countless older people with a wallet of the week’s betting dockets, via the lottery/ lotto system. Hundreds of dollars pass the counters of all the lotto agents every day. The minuscule number of winners hardly compensates for the hard-earned cash being lost each week. What is hard to believe is that governments turn a blind eye as a new generation is sucked into the gambling vortex as though it’s a normal part of life. It’s ludicrous, as Tim Costello showed by comparing it to three smoking s an hour not doing any harm either. The bottom line should be no gambling ads at all. How is it that a win on one’s favourite football team has anything to do with the possibility of losing a week’s hard-earned cash? (Money that should be directed to the worth of life and living.) The words “a harmless weekly flutter” just don’t make any sense when the long-term ramifications for most, sucked into gambling, have proven to be so disastrous. Losses of billions each year in NSW is not pocket money. Sadly, the resultant figures have ended up in the wrong pockets for far too long. The spineless approach from the current Labor governments is not going to change one iota of the statistics we now live with, week after week. With the ban on smoking and alcohol advertising now law, it seems that banning gambling ads should seriously be the next move. It won’t stop gambling, but it will put the brakes on, and endorse the fact that the chances of losing one’s entire hard-earned weekly wages is not OK. Greg Vale, Kiama



I was very disappointed to read that the Albanese government has put the interests of the media and the gambling industry ahead of the families of those addicted to gambling and children exposed to gambling. Shame on you. Andrew Macintosh, Cromer Swans can still shine It seems five of the Swans will be known as Ugly Ducklings (“Swans leader apologises for banned stars’ behaviour”, August 22). C’mon, Sydney, support the rest of the squad who now have the chance to shine. Go Swannies. Chris Sinclair, West Pennant Hills A simple, direct consequence for the stood-down Swans members to consider – I am on holiday in Western Queensland, and if I had packed my Swans member cap it would have stayed in my bag. How many thousand more members would feel the same? Malcolm Cato, Westleigh Malcolm Knox has nailed it (“Jeer, jeer the red and white: How the Swans’ faithful were sold a lie”, August 22). For years fans have been force-fed the malarkey of “culture”, not only from the Swans but all the major sporting codes across the country. Manning a kitchen for the homeless or a big night on the drink with teammates? We all know which one the players would choose. Across all codes, over time, we’ve witnessed off-field acts of violence, excessive drinking, drug use, taxi driver abuse, property damage, lewd public behaviour, and extramarital affairs. Are players not merely mirroring society? Salary cap breaches in clubland, bad bank behaviour in real life. The incident is not to be downplayed and obviously has upset a cohort of Swans supporters, but as Knox states, it has exposed the sham the culture thing is. The reality is Australians are watching sport in record numbers. They have long accepted the human failings of those who play it. Winning is the one culture they crave. Mike Kenneally, Manly Howard’s flawed ways Can we please stop the eulogising of John Winston Howard (Letters, August 22)? As treasurer under Malcolm Fraser he led Australia into its worst recession since the Great Depression. Wollongong had an unemployment rate of 25 per cent and youth unemployment rate of 33 per cent in 1982. He has continually demonstrated himself to be a bigot with nothing to be big about. It is arguable he is something close to a war criminal for sending Australian troops into Iraq. Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison were dreadful, but Howard was worse. Tony Doyle, Fairy Meadow



Tariffs or entry tax? The US under Donald Trump has become an unreliable trade and military partner (‴⁣⁣At war’: Canada walks away from US trade talks, retaliates against tariffs”, August 23). Retaliating over tariffs may not work but surely we need to increase customs and quarantine inspections on anyone returning to Australia from the US? Indonesia imposes $A50 cash payment on arriving tourists. We should charge, say, $100 on every arrival to fund greater inspection of bags and persons? If only to control illegal drugs and arms David Neilson, Uralla Badiucao No faith in extremist teachings If Claire Harris learnt bigotry, intolerance, homophobia, and that sexual assaults are caused by women themselves (“Religious private schools like mine must be hauled into line”, August 22), then it is not simply a case of schools like the one she attended being merely “hauled into line”; entrance to them should be avoided by self-respecting families. There are excellent private schools which do promote wholesome attitudes, but let them fend for themselves. Why should governments spend taxpayers’ hard-earned on them while too many public schools attempt to cope with overcrowded classes, understaffing, teacher burnout, classroom and playground violence, inadequate resources and more? Ron Sinclair, Windradyne Former Tangara student Claire Harris: Religious private schools in Australia operate with almost no scrutiny in how they are shaping their students. Stephen Kiprillis



Claire Harris tells a harrowing tale of the metamorphosis that occurs when the teachings of one Jesus Christ are taken by those of His contemporary, medieval and current acolytes, and transformed into their most radical fundamentalist version. Regrettably, it is and has ever been at the heart of Christianity’s core duty to go abroad and “convert the heathen”. Routinely misinterpreted and then taken to its most extreme limits, this has led to the multiple perversions of settler colonialism and rampant exploitation of weaker resource-rich countries by stronger nations. Underlying this process is the assumption that might is right, God-given and, at all costs, authorises crusading Christians to instil not only Christianity but Western “values”, the two perhaps being interchangeable concepts. Frederick Jansohn, Rose Bay After reading Claire Harris’ article while sitting in the sun, in deference to being in my 80th year and having swum one kilometre in the ocean earlier that morning, I took myself off for a mid-morning nap. And there I did dream such a wondrous dream. I was living in an Australia where there were no private schools, teachers all had master’s degrees and were very well paid, and the profession was highly respected. No religion was taught, but a course in ethics, set by a committee of leading ethicists, was mandatory.

Ah, but alas, I then awoke, and to quote Tom Jones, I realised that I had dreamt the impossible dream. Denis Hannigan, Toowoon Bay The recent antics of the Presbyterian synod, the Exclusive Brethren and Catholic Schools NSW reinforce my view that Christian religions are just structures designed to empower and enrich middle-aged white men. If they are so intent on being involved in our political processes while also distancing themselves from societal norms, it is time they paid their own way and were taxed. More tax and greater scrutiny will bring these organisations more into line with the needs and desires of our egalitarian, secular society. John Mizon, Collaroy Walk the talk Much has been said and written about “culture” and “values” in recent years by politicians, the chattering classes and large organisations including religions and schools (“A frightful moment for women and girls”, August 22). Regardless of how vague and non-specific the culture and values are, they have become the fallback position for those claiming the high moral ground.

Perhaps we could accept that both culture and values are those beliefs and actions only truly demonstrated when we believe no one is watching or what we can self-justify. This would lay bare the true culture and values of at least two high-profile schools, sporting teams and fringe religious groups. Very different to what has been said and written. Bernie de Vries, Bolwarra Natassia Chrysanthos, reflecting on writing about sexual assault and consent education five years ago, asks “has anything changed?” In view of the recent events portrayed in this paper, the answer is a clear “no”. It would appear that the pen is not mightier than the sword. Alicia Dawson, Balmain Mums need support

World.title: Mark McVeigh to meet with Essendon board as coach decision edges closer
World.content:
Sydney Swans’ assistant Mark McVeigh will present to the Essendon board on Monday as the club prepares to make an announcement on their new senior coach.

The 45-year-old was in the coaches’ box as the Swans defeated North Melbourne in an emotional encounter at the SCG but will be in Melbourne to make a final presentation to the board before his expected endorsement as coach.

Mark McVeigh is seen as the favourite to win the Essendon coaching job. AFL Photos

McVeigh played 232 matches at Essendon after being chosen with pick No.9 in the 1998 national draft. After retiring in 2012 he moved back to NSW where he became an assistant coach at the Giants when Leon Cameron stood down in 2022.

He coached 13 matches for four wins with former teammates James Hird and Dean Solomon in the coaches’ box alongside him. He then moved to the Sydney Swans where he coached as an assistant under John Longmire and Dean Cox.

World.title: ‘White fragility is crazy in this country’: Rising rap star Miss Kaninna tells it like it is
World.content:
CultureMusicAustralian music ‘White fragility is crazy in this country’: Rising rap star Miss Kaninna tells it like it is Ben Madden August 23, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’ve been given a fascinating tip-off ahead of my interview with proud Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung, Kalkadoon and Yirendali woman Miss Kaninna, as she releases her new mixtape, BLACKPRINT. The follow-up to her 2024 self-titled debut EP, it’s executive produced by Melbourne multi-hyphenate Nikodimos – and he’s suggested I ask about her famous chicken congee. It gets the exact reaction I was hoping for, as she lets out a huge laugh of disbelief. “I’ve just recently been trying to get in the gym, and I’ve found out that oats are not that good for you,” she says. “I think God gave his toughest soldiers the toughest of tummies, and I’m one of those girls that has IBS. I cannot eat anything in bulk without getting super bloated. “A lot of the stuff I say in this mixtape is very much talking the truth,” says rapper Miss Kaninna. Joel Thomas Wilson “I’m Chinese, and I was on TikTok, scrolling, and this woman was talking about how congee is the best breakfast to have when you wake up. I was like ‘bet’ because I don’t even really like oats. I don’t like sweet stuff. But congee, I can get around.” Since emerging in 2023 with her searing debut single Blak Britney, Miss Kaninna has been a name on everyone’s lips. She’s toured relentlessly since, with the songs from BLACKPRINT starting as freestyles. To her, this tape is a chance to channel the energy of her live show into a project that lasts long after the curtain drops.



“I don’t have that much music out, and obviously, I’m a live musician, and so a lot of my focus is on the show and creating an experience for people,” she says. “This mixtape has been a while in the making, and I just want to get it out there so I can start working on my next, which I’ve already been working on.” One of the highlights of the tape is the punk-tinged closer Stolen Wages, one of the most energetic moments in her discography to date. “I stopped making sad music because I’m so sick of looking at people just swaying. Making sad music is cool, but I want to see people jumping around, sweating their holes off,” she says. Late last year, Irish rappers Kneecap brought her as their sole opener across a sold-out tour of the UK and Europe. “They go really hard, and I felt I needed a song that’s bigger than Pinnacle Bitch [her 2024 single and previous set closer] that we can end the set with. “I wrote Stolen Wages in one sitting, and then I called [producer] Lucy Blomkamp, aka Perfectworld, and I was like, ‘I need you to interpolate this right now because I’m going to Europe in, like, two weeks.’ She was so quick. We took it on tour, and I was getting so much positive feedback about that one song.”



Miss Kaninna is one of the biggest and buzziest names in Australian rap, and she’s determined to pave the way for artists to follow. “There’s just not a lot of support for young rappers in Australia,” she says. “One of the first questions I get asked by anybody who’s not in the industry, when I say that I’m a rapper, is ‘Oh, do you want to go to America, or do you want to move?’ “And I’m like, ‘No!’ I very much want to be exported into international markets so that Australian music can benefit from it; it’s not like I just want to get up and leave. I think a lot of people are very focused on just getting out and leaving and not building a good foundation and a good crew here in Australia.” ‘I’m trying to reclaim my body, my space, my mouth and my sexuality, and uplift women to do the same thing.’ There’s no room for misinterpretation on BLACKPRINT. Across the project’s six tracks, Miss Kaninna holds a mirror up to white Australia, and the double standards that permeate every part of Australian culture. From the blink-and-you’ll-miss-it Chat My Shit to the Kobie Dee-featuring Look at Me Now to the slower-burning Mob Ties, she sounds laser focused. While she’s shown off her singing on a couple of occasions recently – including singing backing vocals for Brisbane MC Nerve’s Like a Version cover of Justin Timberlake’s SexyBack on Triple J – she’s rapping with vivid energy across BLACKPRINT. The title of BLACKPRINT is Miss Kaninna’s nod to how Indigenous people across the globe, including Aboriginal people, hold not just the past in their hands but the future. “I think white fragility is crazy in this country, and I think that white people really do think that black power means taking away from them,” she says.



“A lot of the stuff I say in this mixtape is very much talking the truth. It’s not like what I’m saying is crazy. What’s crazy is that the Australian government continues to have a lawless land and illegally occupies this land. Me saying ‘f--- white people’ is not crazy to me. Me saying ‘f--- the government’ or ‘f--- police’ is not crazy. That seems like a pretty normal reaction to what’s going on.” Hailing from Lutruwita/Tasmania, Miss Kaninna’s community has always had her back. Her mother, Ruth Langford, is a prominent First Nations advocate, and she often seeks advice from elders in her community, including Uncle Jim Everett. “Two years ago, I was sitting on a trip with my uncle, and I was feeling a little bit vulnerable and a little bit, like, under a microscope,” she recalls of one such experience. “I had been copping a lot of slack from people saying that, you know, I’m shaking my ass too much and all this stuff, and my uncle was sitting in front of me, and he said, ‘You know, Kaninna, I’m extremely proud of who you are as a woman.’ “He started getting really upset because he was like, ‘Women need to be able to make choices for themselves, and it’s not up to men to dictate what you can and cannot do with your body and your mouth. For the last 250 years, women – Aboriginal women – have been completely objectified and completely sexualised and ripped of any human status, and now you’re reclaiming that back. And however you see fit as an Aboriginal woman, we’ll support you.’



“And that’s what I’m trying to do,” says Miss Kaninna. “I’m trying to actively reclaim my body and reclaim my space and reclaim my mouth and reclaim my sexuality, and uplift women to do the same thing.” Miss Kaninna’s new mixtape, BLACKPRINT, is out now. Her national tour includes shows at Brisbane’s The Brightside on September 11, Sydney’s Oxford Art Factory on September 12 and 13, and Melbourne’s Northcote Theatre on September 18.

World.title: After a week of pain, the healing begins for the Swans and their supporters
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 After a week of pain, the healing begins for the Swans and their supporters Vince Rugari August 23, 2026 — 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For the past week, shattered supporters of the Sydney Swans have been processing their complicated feelings, digesting their mixed emotions, trying to figure out where to put all these broken, jagged little pieces. On Sunday, the best answer anyone’s come up with thus far presented itself at the SCG: here. Put it here. Bring it all to the ground and we’ll sort through it together. Loading In times of trauma, it can help to be with other people. So, on a glorious Sydney afternoon, the broad church that is the Swans’ fan base – sad, angry, hurt, confused, bemused – congregated at its usual location to do what it usually does, unsure if it would still be like it usually is. It was, and it wasn’t.



Were it not for the news that rocked their world on Monday, when the first reports emerged of the night of debauchery that took place at the Pullman in East Melbourne, this all would have been so straightforward. On Thursday, five AFL players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – were suspended for the rest of the season for “breaching club standards”. A separate police investigation continues into an alleged sexual assault. Sydney Swans fans on the SCG on Sunday. Janie Barrett The Swans’ first AFLW-AFL(M) double-header at home on Sunday was both an unremarkably normal and singularly bizarre experience. Once the footy began, it felt like practically any other afternoon in the before times. The sights, sounds and smells were all familiar – except for the traditional quarter-time rendition of Sweet Caroline, a beloved Swans ritual that was dropped without explanation.



Oh! And there was a gigantic elephant in the room, too. In the morning, scores of hopeful media roved around Driver Avenue anticipating a frenzy. Fans who came for the 12.30pm start of the AFLW’s round two fixture between the Swans and Essendon were greeted by reporters asking them to explain their decision to turn up, and if they intended to stick around for the men’s game later in the day. Laura Gardiner of the Swans greets fans at the SCG on Sunday. Getty Images This was sporting attendance (and departure) as political statement. Not everyone who arrived early or left between games was making one – but many seized their opportunity to do exactly that, holding aloft cardboard signs bearing messages they would then happily unpack in front of a camera and microphone. “Come down here for some wholesome footy,” a Sydney Roosters fan was heard quipping to them, as he made his way to the NRL double-header next door at Allianz Stadium. It’s amazing how quickly the world changes.



The official crowd for Sydney’s 24-point AFLW win was 16,672 – more than double their previous record, and a clear show of support by the public for a team that was among the week’s indirect victims. Chloe Molloy celebrated a goal by making a “W” with her hands. One supporter had a banner confiscated, but only because it was hung over the sponsor boards. It read: “No more dickheads, please.” Thus began the healing process. “The best way to go about today was to win, really,” said captain Lucy McEvoy. “The girls knew that. To give our members and fans a little bit of joy ... we felt obliged to do that for them and be that beacon for us as a football club.” What followed in the interval was not a mass walkout, as had been feared. Dozens upon dozens of people did exit – and women were, to be sure, overrepresented in that category – leaving behind rows of empty seats in the usually jam-packed members’ stand. But dozens more filed through the turnstiles in the other direction, eager to support another group of players who have also been let down. For them, a crowd of 30,058 was on hand. It was far below the Swans’ usual turnout, but also roughly the same as what they got when the same opponents, North Melbourne, visited last year.



It was a dead rubber, yet the performance and result – a comprehensive 53-point victory for Sydney – were a reminder that there is more talent on their list beyond the five who won’t play again this season. We still don’t know exactly what they did in that hotel room, but we do know it has impacted many people – including the teammates who were sleeping at the time, and who now have to try and somehow win a flag without them. Swans players are cheered as they walk off at half-time. Getty Images They won’t give up meekly. Despite the week they’ve endured, they played with spirit and vigour on Sunday, and the supporters who stuck around responded in kind. In the final minutes, a chant rang through the air: ‘Syyyyyyd-ney! Syyyyyyd-ney!’



In the final seconds, a rare standing ovation, and at the siren, an almighty roar, with tears. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Sydney Swans LIVE updates: Women’s and men’s team play first matches following week of scandal At a function earlier in the day, Swans president Andrew Pridham offered another public apology for the “exceedingly poor decisions by a few [which] have impacted so many”, and said the club would investigate how its proud culture failed to prevent those decisions being made. Pridham also acknowledged that “just words”, lovely and well-chosen as they were, won’t cut it. “It is our future actions that will define us,” he said. On that, we’ll just have to wait. But the Swans will be back at the SCG in a fortnight’s time for a qualifying final. Whatever everyone’s feeling by then, at least they’ll know where to bring it.

World.title: My suburb gentrified decades ago. Now the people who live here are afraid to walk the streets
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Opinion My suburb gentrified decades ago. Now the people who live here are afraid to walk the streets Ceridwen Spark Contributor August 23, 2026 — 6:30pm

August 23, 2026 — 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Thursday morning, I get a text message. “Heard there’s some nasty crime in your hood. Radio going off about it!” It’s Steve, whom I tease about living in Glen Iris. My “hood” is Footscray, where I’ve lived for 30 years. Victoria Police detectives at Footscray Mall on June 15 last year after an assault that later resulted in murder charges. Penny Stephens Me: “What’s being said?”



Steve: “Antisocial chaos, apparently. Big spike in crime.” I’d like to text “Nah, it’s a beat-up” but can’t. The central business district of Footscray is chaotic and has become increasingly so over the past few years. The name “Footscrazy” has long been used affectionately around the place, but the term feels complicated right now. Whatever the nature of the discussion Steve heard on the radio, this much is true: Sirens, people crazy with meth, street closures, security guards employed at the local Vinnies where I used to volunteer. A couple of weeks ago, our popular shopping and restaurant strip Barkly Street was closed. A mentally unwell man with a toy gun was having an episode on a rooftop near the high school. On a recent Wednesday night the windows of the pizza shop where my daughter’s boyfriend works were smashed in. Police figures from March show Footscray station is one of Melbourne’s worst for incidents of violence, while data from the Crime Statistics Agency shows that crime rates in the suburb have been trending upwards for some time, especially during the past four years, when there’s been a rise of more than 60 per cent.



Police and emergency services respond to an incident in Barkly St, Footscray last month that led to the busy cafe strip being shut down. Nine News The woundedness of central Footscray hurts and not because I’m squeamish. This is not about hatred, blame or judgment. It’s about loss. The place where I’ve lived for almost three decades feels like an open sore. And the care that needs to be shown to reverse the situation requires thought and resources, more than those looking the other way appear willing to invest. Footscray’s CBD streets – beloved and sometimes gritty, but which have offered home to so many from diverse places and for so long – feel abandoned by all but people on the edge. Beyond this central area though, people continue to live, garden and chat in the renovated Victorian homes in streets which began being gentrified in the late 1990s, around when I moved to Footscray. Footscray was never perfect, but those of us who love it are deeply affectionate about the place. Known for being a colourful suburb that’s welcomed migrants from around the world, central Footscray hosts social services that draw those who need them. This includes people I love – I have no interest in demonising anyone needing these services. I’m glad the needle exchange is there; grateful for the gentle volunteers at the op-shop, who offer clothes to those who’ve been robbed while sleeping in the mall. Western Bulldogs player and artist Cody Weightman at a new Salvos cafe offering social services that opened in Footscray in May. Jason South But Footscray has become an expanding sinkhole for suffering since COVID – land squatting, people without homes, insufficient services for those experiencing mental illness and addiction – and all underpinned by fear and racism.



Previously though, the contours of human pain – mental illness, homelessness, addiction, unemployment – co-existed with a joyous, sometimes edgy but always lively and interesting diversity: Vietnamese hairdressers gossiping out the front of the chemist, lanky Sudanese men discussing politics near Maples Café, creative-looking teenagers at the record shop. And mums trekking to Coles and Savers for another round of nappies or discounted toys, or in my case, the day before Steve’s message, an excellent $27 suit for my 17-year-old’s school formal. Footscray is a still a place of great possibilities, as seen by the crowds out enjoying Good Fest in the mall in February 2025. Tom Yau Now though, those of us with money and health and choices tend to do our shopping elsewhere. Sometimes, when the human suffering feels like too much, we head to the overpriced supermarkets in the neighbouring, but less interesting suburb of Seddon. It feels wrong, but it’s easier. Leaving for Seddon, Yarraville or even – god forbid – Brunswick to avoid the horror is a long way from laughing at the “F---ing Brunswick” T-shirt I once saw hanging in a shop in Irving Street, Footscray. The afternoon before the pizza shop windows were smashed, I was in there chatting to Tom, who works alongside my daughter’s boyfriend. He’s seen so much, responded so many times to the distress and violence that plays out in front of the shop, in the heart of Nicholson Mall. Stabbings, being threatened, watching his fellow employees find other work because they’re exhausted. Seeing him in his spunky shorts, adeptly pulling pizzas out of the huge ovens, I want to give him a hug, but can only listen sympathetically. Police tape in Footscray’s Nicholson Street mall on Sunday June 15 last year. Penny Stephens



My neighbour, too, Rosa, an Italian woman who’s lived in Footscray all her life. She holds Footscray stories in her heart. Rosa tells me I can’t remove the pink roses in my garden because they were planted by the former owner as a tribute to the daughter she lost to cancer. Now though, she won’t go to central Footscray because, as she told me, “It breaks my heart.” When I and other people I know who love Footscray go elsewhere, we feel a bit ashamed. It doesn’t take being a cultural geographer to know that to thrive, places need to perform a diversity of functions and be comfortable for a range of people. If the Toms and Rosas abandon the place, it’s only those who can’t leave who remain. Related Article Crime A violent crime shocked this community. Now locals are calling for change There are many good, passionate and active defenders of Footscray who are working to restore the central streets for everyone. Chief among these is Jorge Jorquera, the co-ordinator of Borderlands Co-operative, a local activist organisation, but whom I know as a dad from school. The Maribyrnong City Council tries too – erecting some great art, setting up lively events in and around the Mall. But the problems are bigger than Jorge, than Borderlands and other local organisations, and bigger than local council. Though I understand individual avoidance of the Footscray CBD it’s wrong for those responsible for providing care and solutions to abandon the place. It’s time the Victorian government did more to support local efforts to save this treasured but struggling suburb. It affords belonging to so many – long may it continue to do so.



Associate professor Ceridwen Spark conducts research on urban and social change at RMIT University. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Swans’ AFLW team ride support for win; Collingwood are battling
World.content:
Fremantle have beaten Collingwood by 20 points to get their AFLW season off the mark and condemn the Magpies to an 0-2 start.

The Dockers had a point to prove heading into Sunday’s clash at Victoria Park after losing to Port Adelaide, while the Magpies were well-beaten by Richmond first-up.

But after Collingwood kicked the opening point, Fremantle quickly snatched the lead and never looked back, claiming an 8.2 (50) to 4.6 (30) win.

Powerhouse Fremantle ruck Mim Strom was everywhere with 28 disposals, 28 hit-outs, nine clearances, six tackles and a goal.

Gabrielle Newton (26 disposals), Kiara Bowers (26), Aisling McCarthy (25) and Orlagh Lally (24) were also prolific while Bella Smith (three goals) and boom recruit Eden Zanker (two goals) hit the scoreboard.

In her first AFLW game in 682 days after a horror injury run, Collingwood superstar Brianna Davey had 22 disposals, while skipper Ruby Schleicher kicked two goals.

AAP

World.title: Flights cancelled after severe gales hit parts of the country
World.content:
A number of Air New Zealand flights were cancelled on Sunday after severe gales hit southern and central parts of the country.

The airline said strong winds had impacted its operations in Wellington, Palmerston North, New Plymouth, Blenheim, Invercargill, Dunedin and Queenstown.

Wellington Airport said two flights were cancelled and two others diverted early on Sunday morning.

MetService meteorologist Gerard Bellham said central parts of the country were feeling the effects of "strong, blustery winds". Those severe gusts hit 168 km/h on Sunday morning at Wellington's Mt Kaukau.

An orange strong wind warning was in effect throughout the day for the Tararua district.

A strong wind watch was in place throughout the day for inland Hawke's Bay as well.

The watch and warning were lifted on Sunday evening.

The wind had also been responsible for widespread power outages across the motu on Sunday, Bellham said.

More than 650 customers across the Wellington region had been affected. Almost 400 homes were without power earlier in the day in the Wairarapa, as well as another 200 in Manawatū.

Down south, more than 700 homes had unplanned outages in the Marlborough area, and more than 300 homes in Tasman experienced power outages early Sunday morning.

Almost 400 homes along the West Coast, including Hokitika and Wahapo, experienced wind-related outages earlier in the day. About 20 homes in Christchurch were affected too.

Bellham said better weather was on the horizon, with "spring-like" conditions ahead in the coming days.

Most of the North Island is forecast to be fine this week, with cloudy periods ahead for western parts of the island, becoming isolated showers later on in the week.

World.title: Teenage girls 'violently assaulted' in Auckland robbery
World.content:
Police are investigating after two teenage girls were allegedly violently assaulted by a larger group of girls in a robbery in Auckland's Takapuna last night.

Police say they have identified most of the youths involved, who are aged between 12 and 17.

"The two young victims were hanging out with the group around Takapuna for around an hour on Saturday evening,

"At about 9.30pm the group reportedly turned on the pair," said Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams.

"The victims were separated and reportedly violently assaulted, before having their personal items stolen," he said.

Police said the victims were able to identify a number of young people of interest at a bus station.

Williams said follow-up enquiries were being made, with potential charges being considered.

World.title: Ousted Te Pāti Māori MP Tākuta Ferris to stand as independent candidate
World.content:
Te Tai Tonga MP Tākuta Ferris has confirmed he will recontest the Māori electorate seat as an independent candidate.

Ferris - alongside Mariameno Kapa-Kingi - was ousted from Te Pāti Māori in 2025 following a period of internal conflict and a public falling out with the party's leadership.

In a social media video released on Sunday, Ferris announced his candidacy and said the past 10 months of independence had "tested us".

"But they have also shown us the strength and resilience of those who place their trust in me, and for that I remain deeply grateful.

"Through turbulent waters, it has been our values that have been the compass in this pursuit." he said.

Ferris said being elected as an independent would give Te Tai Tonga an opportunity to "take the voice of the people directly into Parliament".

"A voice uncompromised by party politics, accountable only to the people of Te Tai Tonga, a voice to advocate for Te Tai Tonga-centric solutions and leverage better outcomes for our people from any government."

Ferris said independence did not mean "standing alone".

"It means being free to stand with our people. Ultimately, our aspirations require Te Tai Tonga solutions [and] that must be underpinned by strong kaupapa."

Ferris laid out three kaupapa he said would be at the "forefront" of his campaign, Te Tiriti, Te Tangata, Te Taiao; protecting and enhancing He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti in decision making, developing and growing the potential of Māori and protecting te taiao.

"We are a numerical inevitability and it is time we stood in that power, the power of our collective voice and recognised the opportunity that is before us . An opportunity to carry a mandate into Parliament that is accountable only to the people of Te Tai Tonga. That is why I stand as an independent, to carry your voice, your aspirations and your mandate straight into Parliament.

"To work with anyone who is willing to work for our people and to remain a strong and unwavering voice for te iwi Māori. This campaign is not mine alone. It doesn't belong to a party. It belongs to the people of Te Tai Tonga." he said.

World.title: ACT Party takes aim at 'activist judges', Treaty of Waitangi clauses
World.content:
The ACT Party has released a policy designed to protect core democratic values and property rights, reign in "activist judges" and stop Parliament creating "divisive" Treaty of Waitangi clauses.

"Today's policy is about ensuring New Zealanders can move forward under one law for all with one future together," party leader David Seymour said.

"ACT will add three principles to the Constitution Act, affirming the basic values that Parliament is sovereign, the rule of law is fundamental and all New Zealanders are equal before the law."

Key to the policy is restraining courts from considering Māori tikanga (custom) in decisions.

"Recent Supreme Court decisions have pushed the line further than Parliament ever legislated," Seymour said.

"Parliament has pushed back in some instances, such as Smith v Fonterra and the Marine and Coastal Area cases, but others, such as Ellis, where the Supreme Court widely expanded the use of tikanga in the law, have not been responded to.

"Parliament is elected, judges are not. We cannot allow tikanga to become a separate source of law applying to broad areas of unrelated law without Parliament ever deciding that it should.

"ACT will make clear that tikanga cannot be used to influence court decisions, except where Parliament has expressly allowed for it."

The party would also amend the Legislation Act 2019 to ensure statutes are enacted in the context of the time they were passed. Judges could resolve ambiguity, but not override statutory language.

"Courts are often responding to unclear legislation or Parliament's silence, when they make decisions that substantially change how the law is understood.

"ACT will stop governments writing vague treaty clauses into law that create uncertainty, and leave courts and officials to decide what they mean through divisive interpretations."

Any bill referring to the Waitangi Treaty would require cabinet to agree which interests were engaged, who they apply to and what obligations they created, restoring "clear lines of democratic accountability".

"We won't unlock New Zealand's potential while the political and judicial classes experiment on our basic rights," Seymour said.

"Inventing new legal concepts, dividing us according to some people's version of history and trampling our property rights might be fun for wig wearers in court and lanyard wearers in the public service, but all it does for the ordinary person is created uncertainty and frustration."

Speaking to RNZ, Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngārewa-Packer compared the policy to the Treaty Principles Bill and said Aotearoa had already sent a "very clear" message about it - Hikoi mō Te Tiriti.

"The very government he's in didn't support it, and there's millions of dollars wasted when we've got a nation that's dealing with a cost of living crisis, a fuel crisis, and an opportunity loss crisis.

"What we should be doing is having a government and parties that indicate their willingness to take the country forward and not have this nonsense.

"Show me an instance where a house, a farm, [or] public access has been denied because of the Treaty - it just can't be validated." she said.

Ngārewa-Packer accused Seymour of "dog whistling" and creating a "drama that doesn't exist".

"There's a lot of work to do, there's a lot of maturing to do, but again, Māori are not in the way of the progress of Aotearoa."

World.title: National promises no new taxes if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party is promising no new taxes if re-elected this November, but has not ruled out increasing existing taxes.

The party had already ruled out a bank tax and on Sunday scrapped the idea of an accommodation levy on short-term rentals such as bed and breakfasts.

It comes after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly a fortnight ago about the possibility of three new taxes under National - a bed tax, a bank tax, and a fuel excise increase.

The announcement on Sunday ruled out the first two but was silent on the third, fuel excise.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said policies like a bed tax would only hurt those booking weekends away and the party would instead look at existing mechanisms to help councils cope with tourism costs.

She said the party would continue to invest in front-line services and while National was committed to no additional taxes, she said the Labour Party had left the door open to introducing more than its proposed capital gains tax.

Leader Christopher Luxon said taxes would be a "defining theme" of the election.

"Our promise of no new taxes this election reflects our disciplined economic management, focused on growing the economy, creating jobs, lifting wages and keeping taxes low.

"It's part of National's plan to fix the basics and build the future."

Speaking at the policy announcement and the launch of his own Botany campaign, Luxon said National were "committed to the problem" of high tourism costs, but a bed tax was not the solution.

"We couldn't find a way to do it through an accommodation levy, that would end up hurting everyday Kiwis who are just going away for a weekend in Auckland or Queenstown."

Luxon pointed the finger at Labour and "its mates", which he said would see the introduction of up to nine new taxes.

"We are not introducing a capital gains tax, we're not introducing a wealth tax, an inheritance tax, a gift tax, a 45 percent increase to the income tax, a $5 billion tax on businesses, an increase in business tax rates, and the list goes on and on and on.

"That is not happening," he said.

At Budget 2026 in May, Willis - as finance minister - announced a levy on banks which she said would gather about $200 million over for years.

Willis said she had looked at what banks were currently being taxed and what the "measures" to change that were, but could not find "other measures" that would not result in "additional costs" for Kiwis.

"My concern that there isn't a mechanism that won't end up being borne by everyday people on their mortgage or their bank fees - and I don't want that.

"I'm really concerned that Kiwis not face the cost of additional taxes, and while we looked at alternative mechanisms, none of them stacked up against the simple rule: no more costs for Kiwis," she said.

Asked if National meant no increases existing taxes, levies or fees, Willis did not rule it out.

"We're saying no new taxes." she said.

Luxon said the petrol tax had been a "feature of New Zealand's system for decades" and his government had decided not to increase it in their first term.

"We also need to acknowledge that is the way that we actually fund and invest in our roads as well. But this is about no new taxes, and I can't be clearer, this is the fundamental choice of this election.

"You've seen a Labour Party that wants to spend more, they want to tax more, and they want to borrow more, versus responsible economic management that actually grows an economy and improves affordability for all New Zealanders and stops Labour's tax grab," he said.

Asked how the policy would be received by his coalition partners, Luxon said all three parties signed up to lowering taxes for working New Zealanders.

"It was the first thing we did: first tax relief for New Zealanders in 14 years. All parties signed up for that."

Pushed again on if it the no new tax policy would be "solidified" in a potential coalition agreement, Luxon said it would be.

In a statement, Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said voting for National meant voting for more cuts.

"If you're ruling out revenue, you have to cut spending. So what are you going to cut?

"More nurses? More hospital services? More front-line workers? More support for families?"

McAnulty said New Zealanders had a right to know what "National is planning to take away from them".

"Putting everything on the chopping block is not responsible government," he said.

In response, Willis attacked Labour's newly released fiscal strategy, which looks to hold Crown expenditure at 33 percent of GDP.

World.title: Man in critical condition after being hit by car in Manawatū
World.content:
A man is in critical condition in Wellington Hospital, after being being hit by a car in Manawatū in the early hours of Saturday morning.

He was found after police were called to Halcombe Road, north of Feilding, about 12:20am.

"That person was located with extensive injuries, and is currently in the intensive care unit at Wellington Hospital," Detective David Burrows said.

"The vehicle allegedly involved in this incident left the scene before police arrival - we want to speak with the driver as the information that he has will be vital to our investigation."

Police said there may be witnesses with video footage who were reluctant to come forward.

"There were a number of people in attendance at the time this incident took place, and we believe someone will either have information that can assist us in identifying the alleged driver or any other information that can assist in our investigation," Burrows said.

"We're providing the family of the young person who was injured with the support they need at this time. We're urging people to please consider them and do the right thing and come forward with any information you have."

It was a traumatic incident that "could have so easily been avoided", police said.

"Anti-social road activity is extremely dangerous, whether you are taking part or simply just observing, and this incident should be a reminder of that."

Anyone with information should contact police on 105 by phone or online at 105.police.govt.nz.

Information can also be provided anonymously through Crime Stoppers on 0800 555 111.

World.title: Mediawatch: Are we getting more ‘media mature’?
World.content:
Political twitch on taxing big tech, maturing media Kiwis Mediawatch Download MP3 36m

For years it's been a global mega-trend few media companies could buck - people drawn away in droves from TV, radio and publications by unlimited digital stuff online.

Much of it is fun and free stuff on the likes of YouTube, Facebook and TikTok, fed by billions of users. Fast-proliferating subscription video on demand (SVOD) services have also offered high-quality shows and movies to those prepared to pay a premium.

The biggest survey of news consumption in the world - the Digital News Report 2026 - found social media and video platforms overtook media organisations' own channels this year as the most popular source of information.

While a majority in all 48 countries watched online news video, consumption of video on publishers' own sites and apps fell by five per cent in a year.

As well as the existing audience thinning out, local media face the prospect of following generations never coming to them in numbers. According to the UK's regulator Ofcom, less than a quarter of what 16 to 24 year-olds watch at home comes from broadcasters.

It's not so different here.

"Young people get their news and entertainment from YouTube, Tiktok and Instagram - not Stuff, the Herald and RNZ. Young people thought locally-made content was cringe . . . but a lot of the time, young people didn't know it even existed," The Detail reported in 2023 just after NZ On Air released research on the media habits of 15-24 year-olds.

NZ On Air's bi-annual surveys of people over 15 -

Where are the Audiences? - have also tracked the declining reach of established home-grown media here.

Empire strikes back?

Theo David as Vili in Shortland Street. Supplied / South Pacific Pictures

But two years ago, WATA? 2024 had better news for local media.

"The year-on-year growth of global media platform audiences in New Zealand appears to be slowing - while the decline for local platforms may be stabilising," NZ On Air said at the time.

"We are still engaging with local [media] despite the fact that we are moving more to global and digital," Glasshouse media's Amanda Wisnewski told Mediawatch at the time.

The just-released WATA? 2026 report shows the empire striking back again. The new surveyor Verian concluded "established and emerging platforms increasingly coexist rather than replace one another".

TV broadcasters reached more New Zealanders each day - live and on-demand - than global video platforms, according to the survey of 1700 people in April and May 2026.

Radio is still strong in the mornings, with more people going online and streaming later in the day - and there's an uptick in TV broadcasts in the traditional evening peaktimes too.

News articles (either online or hardcopy) reached over half of New Zealanders.

Fewer of us shelling out for Netflix, Spotify and the rest

Local media - and free platforms - may be benefitting from the cost of living cutting the appeal of streaming services offering premium content for a price. NZ On Air 'Where are the Audiences 2026' survey

Netflix surged after it finally arrived in New Zealand in 2014. By 2020, the WATA? survey found 40 percent of Kiwis using it.

But WATA? 2024 found Netflix used by only 38 percent of us - and fewer New Zealanders paying for SVOD across the board - while 60 percent watched New Zealand TV channels in 2024 for an average of three-and-a-half hours a day, either live or on-demand.

This year, that's up again to 63 percent, and more than one-in-three people surveyed used New Zealand-based broadcast video on-demand (BVOD) such as TVNZ+, ThreeNow and SkyGo daily.

The cost-of-living crisis and rising subscription fees have accelerated SVOD's retreat.

Netflix daily use has dropped to 32 percent. Spotify use is at 27 percent in 2026, down 8 percent since 2024.

This year's survey found 62 percent using global video-sharing platforms daily, with 15-39 year-olds, Māori, Pacific and Asian people heavier than average users.

YouTube now reaches more than half of New Zealanders daily (52 percent), but so does TVNZ (53 per cent) and it is well ahead of other sources of online viewing, and the biggest social platform Facebook.

Four years ago, the survey found almost two out of three people aged 40-59 were using YouTube, and over-60s were going online at record rates too.

Local content in the media mix

Encouraging numbers for local content in NZ on Air's latest 'Where are the Audiences?' survey. supplied

NZ On Air will be heartened by the survey finding local content is widely seen as high quality and that people who have watched local shows recently value them more.

"Most New Zealanders believe NZ music matches international quality, while many also see NZ shows as comparable to overseas content. Both NZ music and NZ shows are strongly associated with national pride," says Verian in WATA? 2026.

"I suspect more and more New Zealanders see our broadcasters as safe havens - delivering familiar fare and greater relevance with local programming," New Zealand Herald editor turned media researcher Dr Gavin Ellis wrote this week.

He believed WATA? 2026 showed local broadcasters "back on top" in a fragmented market, and also highlighted better results for local content.

"Almost half of the sample recently watched a New Zealand-made show. The ratio was even higher among people aged over 60. Almost two-thirds of those surveyed thought local quality was as good as overseas content and 71 per cent said that content made them "a little prouder to be a New Zealander".

But the picture is different when you break the population down, as NZ on Air did with separate survey reports on younger people, Māori (PDF), Pacific (PDF, and Asian New Zealanders (PDF).

These found the global platforms still sit at the centre of young people's media habits.

Māori use most of the same platforms as the wider population, but Netflix is bigger for them - and Facebook use is up there with YouTube.

The platforms Pacific audiences use "most reflect a digital-first and social media ecosystem", the survey concluded. And the likes of YouTube, Instagram and TikTok dominated Asian New Zealanders' daily media habits - and captured more of their time than any other media activity.

These parts of our population are also among the fastest-growing, so can local media keep on clawing back overall attention as recorded in the national surveys?

Dilemma for NZ On Air

Cameron Harland of NZ on Air Copyright 2013

WATA? 2026 also raises questions for NZ On Air. Are people getting the local content they fund, given the ever-increasing range of outlets New Zealanders use? And do they like what they find?

The survey found two-thirds of people can find NZ content easily, though more people said they find out about them via social media - and fewer are alerted by promos on TV.

"I think we're seeing free and paid, local and global, traditional and digital media coexisting rather than simply replacing one another," NZ On Air chief executive Cameron Harland told Mediawatch.

While the reach of Netflix and Spotify was down, the people who are paying for it were using it more. People were also spending more time listening to podcasts, radio and music streaming.

"That's probably one of the fundamental findings from the research. There's not a lot of new customers finding their way into different places, but those that are engaging are engaging for longer - pretty much across the board."

Are local and free platforms getting the benefit of the rising cost-of-living?

"I suspect that there is a little bit of that. I think a little more about if I need to have all of these streaming platforms at the same time. But we're moving into a more sophisticated viewing environment in the way that people are engaging with the many options available."

If the economy improves, could that flip back? People may start spending on offshore platforms' subscriptions again, undermining the domestic media outlets NZ On Air needs to air the content it funds.

"Possibly. But you could say that our local platforms are doing a good job. TVNZ+ is a fantastic streaming platform. ThreeNow is the same."

"They're investing massively in their streaming infrastructure, and the content. The FIFA World Cup went well for TVNZ, but it's also a great opportunity for them to get (more) viewers to the platform and they can cross-promote other content."

Will this change what NZ On Air spends our money on?

"There's a couple of examples in recent years where we have made some tangible changes based upon the findings that we've seen from the research," Harland told Mediawatch.

One is the 2023 youth content strategy Within My Reach (PDF), which states bluntly: "Our research has highlighted that 15 - 24-year-olds have largely disengaged from traditional media platforms, such as television, and are increasingly turning to social media and international streaming services as their primary sources of content."

NZ On Air also funded a recent series about social media mental health aimed at younger people - Under the Influence.

In the past it would have been a TV documentary made for TVNZ or TV3's weekday peaktime. But UTI was broken up into 15-minute episodes on the New Zealand Herald website and also posted on YouTube where it was more likely to reach younger people.

"Those youth-orientated pieces of work need to be where they are. We have a strategy that does allow for that content to go digital-first sort of into social media and also hoping that there might be secondary plays into TVNZ or 3Now or other places."

But if local linear and on-demand TV is edging out the share of the global video sharing platforms, will NZ On Air go back to the future and spend more big money on more productions for television?

"We are definitely not shying away from putting serious investment into primetime shows. That kind of the peak-time TV content is still very much kind of supported by us and delivering significant audiences," said Harland.

"That youth content going into YouTube and the global video players is still a relatively modest level of funding that we're putting in."

For decades, Shortland Street was funded by TVNZ itself from advertising revenue the show attracted in TVNZ2 at 7pm on weekdays.

Now $2.3 million a year goes into the production - described by NZ on Air as a 'life-saving injection' - and it also qualifies for the Screen Production Rebate.

"On one level it's frustrating that we're having to fund something that we didn't need to fund previously," Cameron Harland told Mediawatch.

"But that is also just simply the nature of the commercial environment the broadcasters exist within. The audience for that show is actually significant and relatively young, which are those that are quite hard to find."

Ms. X - funded by NZ on Air - starring Australian actor Melissa George. supplied

$8m was recently devoted to four scripted projects, including Ms. X (on Three right now, starring Australian actor Melissa George) and the return of local comedy Wellington Paranormal.

Reality shows Celebrity Treasure Island and The Traitors - both versions of proven hit international franchises - are funded by NZ On Air too.

"I think most people are acknowledging that it is a tough media environment for these platforms to fund this content themselves. We feel like we have data on our side. We really understand whether audiences are engaging in this content or not - and the fact that they are is really important.

"To a certain extent, our life is about tension. We have a requirement to fund content for a number of different audiences that are listed in our Act.

"Most of our content is still being funded into New Zealand-owned broadcast platforms - by some significant margin. The local platforms are by far and away the best place for the content to sit because they are doing a really good job in promoting it in the really fragmented media landscape that we now operate in."

Partnership with platforms

AFP / NurPhoto / Samuel Boivin

NZ On Air raised eyebrows in the media when it partnered with Netflix on a programme - Toi Atea - to fast-track people into screen production.

Netflix carries few local productions and rarely invests in any. Aren't domestic broadcasters better placed to train and employ people here?

"What you're also hearing, no doubt, is people saying Netflix is not engaging in commissioning local content. Let's get them around the table and have some good conversations about what's going on.

"Netflix have put money into this programme. In turn we are selecting local productions for people to work on - and that the money is paying for those people to engage in that.

"The local productions are . . . for the most part . . . shows that are going to be playing into local platforms. Netflix have just come along and said they are keen to support us financially in this.

"We'd be more than happy for TVNZ or Sky/Three or RNZ to support us financially in this as well.

World.title: Tigers score upset of the NRL season with 79th-minute winner
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have slipped on a Wests Tigers-shaped banana skin in a shock 25-24 loss that could prove fatal in their pursuit of the NRL's minor premiership.

Halfback Jock Madden was the hero for the Tigers on Sunday, kicking a 79th-minute field goal to snap an eight-game losing run.

The Tigers' finals hopes ended months ago and they were ranked $10 outsiders at the Sydney Football Stadium.

But led by co-captain Api Koroisau, Benji Marshall's side produced one of the upsets of the season to turn the make-up of the top four on its head.

With two rounds remaining, the Roosters (38 points, +162) sit third after blowing a golden chance to move clear of the ladder-leading Warriors (38 points, +295) and second-placed Penrith (38 points, +294).

In further bad news for coach Trent Robinson, lock Victor Radley was placed on report and failed to finish the second half as he underwent a head injury assessment.

The Tigers had every reason to not aim up on Sunday, especially when prop Alex Twal was ruled out with a head knock inside 60 seconds and Roosters winger Billy Smith touched down after just three minutes.

The best win of Benji Marshall's tenure has thrown the NRL's top four into chaos. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

But unlike the past few months when they would have gone to water, the Tigers stood up for themselves.

Patrick Herbert was credited with three try assists in the space of eight minutes as the journeyman centre set up Jeral Skelton for a double either side of a short-range try for Tony Sukkar.

Skelton's second in the 26th minute stunned the stadium into silence, but Madden's inability to kick any of the three conversions meant the Roosters only trailed by six.

Smith grabbed a second on the stroke of halftime with Sam Walker converting both of the winger's tries to make it 12-12 at the break.

The Tigers kept the Roosters at bay before Samuela Fainu was able to offload to Jahream Bula, who drew Cody Ramsey and set up Solomone Saukuru.

Koroisau — handed kicking duties after Madden's three misses — converted, before starting and finishing off another spectacular move that edged the Tigers further ahead.

Koroisau looped round to the left edge and played a short side with Saukuru and Junior Tupou, who passed back in field where the Tigers hooker was in support.

After Koroisau converted his own try, Koroisau booted a 40/20 to put his side straight back on the attack.

The Tigers were unable to take advantage of the leg-up in field position and after Luai gave away a penalty, Robert Toia crashed over for the home side.

Walker rattled the conversion into the left upright, meaning the Tigers had to defend an eight-point lead with 15 minutes left.

Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase dropped the ball over the line, but offloaded to Walker, who scored in the 72nd minute and cut the deficit to two points.

After Hugo Savala was tackled off the ball, Walker tied the game with a penalty with less than five minutes remaining.

And the Roosters looked destined to find a winning play but an unforced offload from Naufahu Whyte put the Tigers on the attack with barely 90 seconds left.

Radley was ordered off for a concussion test which gave Madden time to pick his spot and strike the match-winning field goal.

Cronulla did just enough to beat the Titans. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam )

Earlier, Cronulla snapped a shocking two-game losing streak to revive their NRL top-four finals hopes with a potentially season-saving 30-22 win over the lowly Gold Coast.

The victory was anything but convincing as the Sharks recovered from an eight-point second-half deficit to prevail at Skilled Park on Sunday.

Quietening some doubters, Cronulla will nevertheless bank the priceless two competition points and move on after staying in the hunt for an all-important double chance in the looming finals.

No team in NRL history has won the premiership from outside the top four.

AAP
